3	===== PDF 32 (printed 21) =====
4	SUPERTRAINING
5	Figure 1.10 Graphical definition of work as the area under the force-displacement curve
6	Initial Implications of M echanics
7	Because of their fundamental importance in biomechanics, Newton’s Laws of Motion warrant repetition here:
8	Newton / (The Law of Inertia): A body will persist in its original state of rest or motion unless acted on by 
9	an external agency (i.e. a force).
10	Newton //(The Law of Acceleration): Newton stated it thus: “The change of motion is proportional to the 
11	motive force impressed; and is made in the direction of the straight line in which that force is impressed” 
12	(Richards et al, 1962), which in modem terms may be restated as: 
13	The rate of change of velocity 
14	(acceleration) is proportional to the resultant force acting on the body and is in the same direction as the force 
15	or, if suitable units are chosen. Force = Mass x Acceleration ( F = m.a).
16	Newton ///(The Law of Reaction): For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction.
17	Despite the familiarity of these laws, some of their implications appear to be forgotten in the practical setting, in 
18	particular regarding comparison between machine and free weight training. Some machine manufacturers advertise 
19	that their variable resistance machines are superior to free weights, because, in the latter case, the weight remains 
20	constant and does not change in response to altering joint leverages throughout range of any movement. 
21	Newton’s first two laws show clearly that this claim is false, since a load may only be lifted if its weight (due to 
22	gravitational acceleration) is overcome by the lifter with an acceleration which exceeds that of gravity.
23	Furthermore, during the lift, proprioceptive feedback makes the athlete aware that the load is changing and 
24	enables him to intervene voluntarily in the loading process by accelerating or decelerating the bar to increase or 
25	decrease the force involved. This method is sometimes known as Compensatory Acceleration Training (CAT) 
26	and can be useful in altering muscle tension or movement velocity to achieve a specific training goal (see Ch 7.1).
27	Although the role of CAT is well known during concentric movement (in which the load is being overcome), 
28	its vital role during eccentric movement (in which the load overcomes the propulsive force) is inadequately 
29	appreciated. In non-ballistic eccentric motion in which muscle contraction continues throughout the movement, 
30	the muscles try to oppose the effects of the gravity to slow down and ultimately halt the downward motion of 
31	the bar. In ballistic motion in which muscle action is intermittent, so-called antagonistic muscle action comes into 
32	play to slow down and halt the limb to ensure that the joint is not dislocated or soft tissues are ruptured.
33	Even during isometric action (in which there is no external limb movement), compensatory processes are at 
34	play if no movement is to occur, since neural activation changes due to fatigue, altered mental focus or other 
35	physiological processes. This means that the athlete has to maintain adequate muscle tension for the entire 
36	duration of the isometric action, either by means of involuntary conditioned reflex action or by voluntary 
37	intervention. Thus, it might be preferable for the acronym CAT to stand for ‘Compensatory Action Training’.
38	Mass and Acceleration Issues
39	The implication for the well-known Principle of Progressive Overload is that ‘overload’ should refer not simply 
40	to the use of progressively greater resistance over a given period, but also to the progressive increase in muscle 
41	tension, which may be produced by involuntary or voluntary processes. This change in tension may be produced 
42	in ways which relate directly to Newton II and which pose a question which is of fundamental importance to all 
43	strength training. It is relevant to examine this issue before we go any further.
44	21
45	
46	
47	===== PDF 33 (printed 22) =====
48	SUPERTRAINING
49	Since force F = m.a, we may apply it to produce the same magnitude of force F in several different ways:
50	(a) F = M.a 
51	where the mass M is large and the acceleration is small
52	(b) F = m.A where the mass is small and the acceleration A is large
53	(c) F = m.a 
54	where both mass and acceleration are moderate
55	To which might be added force production under isometric or isokinetic conditions where acceleration is zero:
56	(d) F = k.R where k is a factor of proportionality and R is the resistance applied by the apparatus.
57	This might immediately suggest, since the production of an adequate level of muscle tension is necessary for 
58	strength training, that all o f these methods of ‘Force Training* are entirely the same and that is just a matter of 
59	one’s personal choice which method is used. So, the question is: “Does it make any real difference which method 
60	o f strength training is used, as long as adequate muscle tension is produced?”
61	If one attempts to answer this question in purely mechanistic terms, one might be tempted to reply “no" and 
62	qualify one’s reply with qualifying comments about initiating movement against heavy loads with high inertia, 
63	possible detrimental effects of sustained loads on the soft tissues of the body and duration of loading.
64	Interestingly, practical experience from three different competitive aspects of strength training, namely 
65	Olympic weightlifting, powerlifting and bodybuilding, offers some preliminary information. Option (a) with 
66	very heavy loads is most commonly encountered in powerlifting, while the hypertrophy associated with 
67	bodybuilding generally is a product of option (c) training with moderate loads performed for about 8-12 
68	repetitions. Option (b) is characterised by many actions in track and field events. Olympic weightlifting, which 
69	involves lifting heavy loads rapidly, appears to contradict evidence that velocity decreases with load, but this is 
70	because weightlifting is ballistic and relies on the quick movement of the lifter under the bar. It may be concluded 
71	that powerlifting is essentially strength generating, while weightlifting is maximum power generating in nature.
72	Option (d) occurs only under laboratory conditions using special isokinetic devices to control the motion and 
73	correlation of results obtained under these and actual sporting conditions tends to be low, although it may 
74	produce significant increase in non-specific strength (Rosentzweig & Hinson, 1972; Ostemig, 1986).
75	The practical evidence shows that the above ways of generating force do not produce the same results and 
76	research reveals that this is because different neural, muscular and metabolic processes are involved in each ease. 
77	Thus, strength and power training are not simply a matter of using some generalised form of resistance training to 
78	produce adequate physical loading and muscle tension; the principle of specificity o f training is central to the 
79	entire issue.
80	M u scle T e n s io n  a n d  T ra in in g  S tim u lu s
81	Some coaches maintain that maximal muscle hypertrophy depends on tension time, with continuous tension 
82	times of 30-60 seconds per set of any exercise being commonly recommended. The observation that the extended 
83	use of isometric exercises of this magnitude of duration docs not produce the degree of hypertrophy associated 
84	with dynamic exercise (which includes eccentric action) militates against this simplistic claim. The fact that 
85	tension fluctuates from low to high values throughout a movement also militates against this idea. Clearly, both 
86	hypertrophy and strength increase depend on the existence of some minimum level o f tension, but nobody has 
87	identified what this tension threshold should be in the case of hypertrophy. Moreover, it is well known that 
88	novices to resistance training respond to much lower intensities o f loading both in terms of hypertrophy and 
89	strength gains.
90	Research has shown that the threshold training stimulus necessary for increasing muscular strength in the 
91	average person should not be less than one-third of the maximal strength (Hettinger & Muller, 1953). As strength 
92	increases, the intensity of the stimulus required to produce a training effect should be increased, and reach 80- 
93	95% of the athlete's maximum. It may be appropriate that the strength of the training stimulus sometimes equals 
94	or even exceeds the level of the competition stimulus of the given exercise (Verkhoshansky, 1977).
95	Thus, the development of strength requires that the stimulus intensity be gradually increased. 
96	It was 
97	discovered that every stimulus has a changing strengthening threshold, the achievement of which fails to elicit any 
98	further increase in muscular strength (Hettinger, 1961). The less trained the muscles, the further the strengthening 
99	threshold from the beginning state. The rate at which strength increases from the initial level to the strengthening 
100	threshold, expressed as a percentage of the current maximum strength, is independent of sex, age, muscle group
101	22
102	
103	
104	===== PDF 34 (printed 23) =====
105	SUPERTRAINING
106	and the level of the strengthening threshold. After the strengthening threshold has been reached, strength can be 
107	increased only by intensifying the training.
108	In this regard, according to Korobkov, Gerasimov and Vasiliev (Verkhoshansky, 1977), strength increases 
109	relatively uniformly during the initial stages of training, independent of how the load is applied in training, 
110	whether large or small. Approximately equivalent increases in strength arc obtained with loads of 20, 40, 60 and 
111	80 percent of IRM (one repetition maximum). An increase in the intensity of training in the initial stages (e.g. 
112	using a heavier load, faster tempo of movement and shorter intervals between sessions) does not always enhance 
113	the effectiveness of strength development, this becoming effective only later, as strength increases. This principle 
114	is corroborated by the training results of weightlifters (Hettinger, 1961; Verkhoshansky, 1977).
115	Application of Basic Biom echanics
116	This brings us back to the interesting and vitally important question in strength training which was raised earlier, 
117	namely: Should a heavy weight be lifted with a small acceleration or should a lighter load be lifted with a greater 
118	acceleration to produce strength most effectively? Or, is it preferable to train isometrically to produce maximal 
119	strength gains? In all of these cases the force produced may be exactly the same, but the training effect may be 
120	entirely different. What training effect is imposed by the duration of muscle tension, especially since the factor of 
121	strength-endurance becomes increasingly important and maximal strength becomes less important as the duration 
122	of any contraction increases?
123	To answer these questions, it is necessary in later chapters to apply the fundamentals of biomechanics to 
124	strength training (Fig 1.11) and draw a curve of force versus time and examine how each force-time curve or 
125	appropriate portion of this curve best matches the required strength quality, such as static strength, speed- 
126	strength, strength-endurance or strength-spced. In other words, the force-time curve may serve as one of the vital 
127	starting points for understanding the entire phenomenon of sport-specific strength and for prescribing sport- 
128	specific strength training. This curve is used in later chapters to answer the questions posed above and to act as a 
129	framework for resolving many other important strength training issues.
130	Figure 1.11 Summary of the major concepts used in sport biomechanics. Strain is the relative change in length, i.e. the change in 
131	length of a length of material L caused by a force F relative to its original length, d/dt refers to the first derivative with respect to time. 
132	] cfe refers to the integral with respect to displacement s.
133	As mentioned previously, other curves which also provide invaluable information for understanding and 
134	applying sport-specific strength training are the force (torque) vs angular displacement (for each joint), force 
135	(torque) vs velocity, endurance vs force and endurance vs velocity graphs. This information, together with a 
136	knowledge of which muscles are involved statically and dynamically in given complex movements, ftimish the 
137	minimum requirements for drawing up an effective and safe strength training programme for any sport. It is a 
138	major intention of this text to provide the reader with a solid understanding of these and other essential 
139	processes which are central to exercise prescription for enhanced performance or rehabilitation after injury.
140	23
141	
142	
143	===== PDF 35 (printed 24) =====
144	1.3 A Philosophy of Physical Training
145	The success o f any training programme is closely linked to the philosophy of physical training in which it is 
146	embedded. Since this text draws heavily on Russian exercise science, it is enlightening to examine the overall 
147	education system in Russia which produced generations of the world's finest athletes in all sports. The excellence 
148	of their athletes in international competition is a direct result of carefully designed educational programmes aimed 
149	at employing sport, among other activities, to promote its national aims. Russian sport, like any other class of 
150	education, follows the same general principles and stages. The Russians distinguish between physical education 
151	and sport, in that the latter involves specialisation, competition for improving performance, and the acquisition of 
152	maximum physical and mental drive.
153	Several authors (Yessis, 1987; Schneidman, 1979; Matveyev, 1981; Vorobyev, 1978) give useful insights 
154	into the highly organised approach of the Russians, who recognise at least eight interrelated principles in scientific 
155	sports preparation:
156	1. T he P rin c ip le  o f A w aren ess
157	This covers the ideology and the philosophy o f Russian sport as well as the conscious awareness of all processes 
158	involved in acquiring sporting proficiency. The athlete is required to know himself and understand the 
159	physiological and psychological processes taking place in his body to enable him to control and evaluate 
160	objectively his sensations and his capacity for work.
161	2. T he P rin c ip le  o f A ll-round D e v e lo p m e n t
162	This entails building a solid physical and mental foundation on which to found other specialised sporting qualities. 
163	All-round development involves strength, speed, flexibility, endurance, good coordination, strong will-power, and 
164	exemplary moral and cultural development. Psychological preparation involves persuasion, explanation, example, 
165	encouragement, group influence, self-motivation and adaptation to stress.
166	3 . T h e P rin c ip le  o f C o n s e c u tiv e n e s s  (or C o n siste n c y )
167	This refers to the systematic overloading principle in which the intensity and the volume o f physical work, as 
168	well as the degree of difficulty of motor skills, is progressively increased. In all aspects, including strength, skill 
169	and strategy, the athlete moves from the easy to the difficult, from the light to the heavy, from the known to the 
170	unknown. The same principle in reverse is advised so that physical workouts arc not ended abruptly. The 
171	harmony of the body must be maintained by slowing down the exercise tempo after every workout and every 
172	competitive season.
173	4 . T he P rin c ip le  o f R e p e titio n
174	This principle is based on Pavlov's three-stage theory for development of conditioned reflexes. Firstly, novel 
175	activities stimulate large areas of the brain and recruit muscles which are unnecessary for performing a particular 
176	movement. Next, consistent repetition diminishes spurious neuromuscular activity and enables one to concentrate 
177	predominantly on the task being learned. Finally, expertise is established and the movement becomes automatic. 
178	These are the same stages applied in teaching sporting skills, namely:
179	(a) Development o f knowledge The athlete must understand frilly what must be learned before attempting to 
180	master it
181	(b) Development o f motor ability The athlete must acquire the ability to concentrate full attention on 
182	performance of the required physical manoeuvres
183	(c) Development o f automatic motor response The athlete no longer needs to concentrate consciously on the 
184	movements to perform them efficiently. The learned skill has bccome an automatic, conditioned reflex.
185	Not only repetition of exercises, but also proper sequences of work and rest fatigue and recovery, injury and 
186	rehabilitation are vital in producing the proficient athlete.
187	5. T h e P rin c ip le  o f V isu a lisa tio n
188	The athlete must be able to visualise the correct movements in order to master any sport. He must leam these 
189	patterns by observing demonstrations by his coach and other experts, studying films, slides and diagrams, and
190	SUPERTRAINING
191	24
192	
193	
194	===== PDF 233 (printed 222) =====
195	SUPERTRAINING
196	muscle stimulation changcd according to the weight (3.3, 6.6, 9.9 and 13.3% of the maximum isometric strength! | 
197	and the height of the fall (Vcrkhoshansky, 1977). The experiment showed that an increase in kinetic energy caused 
198	by an increase in the mass of the load decreases the height to which a load is thrown, but an increase in the 
199	distance through which a load falls increases the height to which it is thrown (Fig 4.8a).
200	A similar picture emerges from research on reactive ability (Fig 4.8b). This tendency, in general, is displayed 
201	by movements executed under other conditions, although these have their own peculiarities (Figs 4.9, 4.10). ] 
202	These examples show clearly that it is not beneficial to increase kinetic energy by use o f heavier loads. It is 
203	therefore necessary to examine a better means of increasing the thrust height. 
204	The depth jump which has 
205	immediate practical significance for developing jumping ability is given in the example illustrated in Figure 4.10. 
206	Here maximal force (Fmax) increases up to a height of 1.15 metres, then diminishes sharply, while movement time 
207	begins by changing insignificantly, then increasing sharply. Maximum power and reactivity are achieved using a 
208	drop height of approximately 0.75 metres.
209	Figure 4.8 (a) Changes in height (h2) o f thrown loads of different mass (in terms o f maximum isometric strength Po), after having 
210	fallen from different heights (hi) (b) Changes in reactivity coefficient (RC) with respect to the kinetic energy of the falling load. 
211	(Verkhoshansky, 1977).
212	Thus, the optimal range of depth jumping for the stimulation of muscular activity is 0.75-1.15 metres, because at 
213	the lower end of this range the muscles are working at maximal power and at the upper end they are working at 
214	maximal dynamic force. This finding forms the basis for the recommendations for using depth jumps in the 
215	training of advanced jumpers 
216	(Vcrkhoshansky 1963, 
217	1964, 1966), though it is preferable to err on the 
218	conservative side of using considerably lower jump heights with anyone who is unused to this type of training 
219	and to strictly limit the volume of this type o f ‘shock’ training.
220	Further increases in the height of the depth jump significantly decrease the magnitude of the dynamic 
221	parameters of the take-off. The support time increases quickly, primarily because the phase o f switching from 
222	eccentric to concentric work is lengthened. In addition, the maximum dynamic force of take-off and the speed of 
223	muscular contraction stabilise and do not increase any further.
224	The take-off comprises two distinct actions: amortisation (where the kinetic energy of the fall is absorbed), 
225	and the thrust proper. The amortisation is characterised by the increasing depth of the resulting knee flexion, and 
226	the thrust proper by a fairly constant speed of muscle contraction. 
227	Thus, the positive effect of muscle 
228	stimulation by absorption of kinetic energy from a fall can be used successfully only under certain conditions by 
229	taking into consideration the optimal height of the fall, bodymass, additional load, and any other factors which 
230	may facilitate a quick take-off.
231	However, the state of the neuromuscular system during the amortisation phase of the falling body also can 
232	play an independent training role. Tension developed reflexively during this phase enhances the ability of the 
233	muscles to switch quickly to the active state. Experience indicates that this is not detrimental to speed-strength
234	222
235	
236	
237	===== PDF 234 (printed 223) =====
238	SUPERTRAINING
239	preparation and the musculoskeletal support apparatus, although further research is required in order to make 
240	definitive practical recommendations in this area.
241	Figure 4.10 Take-off characteristics after depth jumping from gradually greater heights (h). RC is the reactivity coefficient, Fmax is 
242	the maximal force and t is the ground contact time. (Vcrkhoshansky, 1977).
243	Therefore, muscle stimulation by the absorption of energy of a falling body can be a very effective method of 
244	loading, the basis of which lies in the ability of the muscles to contract more powerfully after a sharp preliminary 
245	stretch. This mechanism enables one to successfully overcome the force of body inertia in emergency situations, 
246	which proves to be of particular value in sport.
247	Preliminary muscle stretching has a place in a number of strength exercises such as squats and jumps with a 
248	barbell on the shoulders. However, these exercises are not as intensely impulsive as exercises which brake the 
249	velocity of a preliminary fall and display a sharp, shock-like character.
250	Therefore, the method of muscle stimulation by means of absorbing the kinetic energy of a fall, now known 
251	as plyometrics, was originally called the 'shock method' (Verkhoshansky 1966, 1968). 
252	Research by 
253	Vcrkhoshansky (1958, 1976) took the first serious steps in studying and formulating this method and much 
254	subsequent research has corroborated its effectiveness in specific applications (Kuznetsov, 1966; Papysheva, 
255	1966; Chudinov, 1966; Chemesheva, 1967; Semenov, 1967; Tatian, 1974; Khodykin, 1975). However, more 
256	work is needed in the laboratory and under training conditions before its full scope is covered.
257	4.2.4 Isom etric Training
258	In athletics, isometric exercises were very popular in the mid-1950s as a result of the search for economical and 
259	effective methods of developing strength. Hettinger and Muller (1953, 1955) established that one daily effort of 
260	two-thirds of one's maximum exerted for six seconds at a time for 10 weeks will increase strength about 5% per
261	223
262	
263	
264	===== PDF 235 (printed 224) =====
265	SUPERTRAINING
266	week, while Clark et al (1954) found that static strength continues to increase even after the conclusion of a four- 
267	week programme of isomctric exercises.
268	The success of isometric training provoked considerable research, much of it being concerned with the 
269	question of its effectiveness compared with dynamic training. This research produced rather contradictory data 
270	(see review by Verkhoshansky, 1970). However, research produced the general conclusion that isometric training 
271	can be more effective than dynamic exercises in those cases where the specific exercise requires muscle contraction 
272	of large magnitude at a certain stage of a movement or during the early stages of injury rehabilitation.
273	If the specific exercise involves high-speed movement, then sustained isometric training is less effective. 
274	Research indicates that there are distinct differences between the training effects of static and dynamic exercises. 
275	It is important that muscular tension should be increased slowly and be held for a relatively long time when 
276	executing isometric exercises, because the usual purpose of isometric training is to develop absolute strength. 
277	Prolonged maintenance of muscular tension requires an energy expenditure which stimulates adequate adaptation 
278	in the neuromuscular system, thereby determining its strength potential. The increase in strength can be more 
279	significant than that produced by transient dynamic tension. If one notes the fact that some researchers have not 
280	discovered an essential difference in the growth of strength produced by muscle tension of various intensities, 
281	then it is obvious that the fundamental conditioning factor is not so much the magnitude of the isometric tension 
282	as its duration.
283	A technique which may be referred to as oscillatory isometrics may also be useful in producing powerful 
284	contractions over a small range of movement. This is corroborated by research which showed the maximum 
285	tension that can be produced voluntarily during sinusoidally pulsed brief isometric jerks at 5 Hz is the same as the 
286	maximum sustained tension (Soechting & Roberts, 1975). Basmajian (1978) commented that this emphasizes the 
287	importance of muscle fibre recruitment in the gradation of tension and synchronisation of motor unit activity 
288	during the short bursts of loading.
289	In other applications, short periods of low frequency mechanical vibration (10-35 Hz) on the body have been 
290	shown to induce faster recovery, have a positive effect on different body systems, modulate muscle activity, elicit 
291	a higher stable state of strength and power, lower arterial pressure, and enhance oxidative processes (Kopysov, 
292	1978; Lebedev & Peliakov, 1991). More recently, it has been found that powerful whole body vibrations 
293	imposed at 26 Hz through the lower extremities produces marked increases in jumping power (Bosco et al, 1998).
294	These findings may relate to a similar impulsive loading process which is associated with the training effects 
295	of plyometrics, thereby adding further fuel to the debate (Ingen Schcnau ct al, 1997) about which of the following 
296	effects may predominate during plyometrics: elastic energy storage/utilisation in the soft tissues, neural 
297	facilitation or intrinsic muscle changes.
298	At this point it must be stressed that isometric training is not simply a matter o f holding a static muscle 
299	contraction for a given time. Isometric contraction requires a muscle to increase its tension from rest to a 
300	maximum or sub-maximal value over a certain time (rise or ‘attack’ time), to sustain this tension for another period 
301	(the resistance phase) and to decrease this tension to rest or a lower value (decay time). Consequently, one may 
302	distinguish between explosive isometrics, which have a very brief rise time, and slow isometrics, with a much 
303	longer rise time (Fig 4.12). The isometric contraction may be produced by voluntary contraction or involuntarily 
304	by the reflex response of the muscle between the eccentric and concentric phases of plyometric activities such as 
305	the depth jump or weightlifting clean-and-jerk. The different types of isometric contraction are categorised in 
306	Figure 4.11.
307	Each class of isometric training produces its own distinct training effects. If isometric exercises are executed 
308	with the accent on the speed of developing force, then they can be as effective for developing explosive strength 
309	as dynamic exercises. The steepness of the force-time curve (Fig 3.3) and the greater magnitude of maximum 
310	isometric than dynamic maximum force for equivalent joint angles is the basis for this assertion. Therefore, it is 
311	doubtful whether it is always productive to maintain a rigid distinction between dynamic and isometric exercise. In 
312	general, the harder the muscles work in overcoming large resistance, the more closcly the work becomes isometric, 
313	as may be seen from the force-vclocity curves of muscle action (Figs 3.15 & 3.16). In other words, isometric 
314	work is really the limiting case o f dynamic work as the velocity o f movement tends to zero. Furthermore, because 
315	the inhibitory effects usually associated with voluntary muscle action are not encountered in reflexive isometric 
316	contraction, even greater explosive force can be displayed isometrically than dynamically.
317	224
318	
319	
320	===== PDF 236 (printed 225) =====
321	SUPERTRAINING
322	Figure 4.11 Categorisation of the different types of isometric muscle contraction.
323	la connection with this, it makes sense to distinguish isometric training fo r developing absolute strength and 
324	isometric training for developing explosive strength and to use one or the other in the appropriate circumstances. 
325	However, this still requires detailed experimental corroboration. Nevertheless, isometrics should not be neglected 
326	is a means of strength development, so that negative evaluations of this method are premature.
327	Figure 4.12 Comparison o f slow and explosive isometric action, distinguished by their force-time characteristics. The slope of the rise 
328	is even greater and the duration of the resistance phase is much shorter during reflexive explosive isometric action.
329	It is necessary to bear in mind the following advantages of isometric training, as emphasized by its proponents:
330	1. It requires very simple apparatus.
331	2. It can locally exercise any muscle group at a specific joint angle. During dynamic work the display of 
332	maximal effort at the necessary joint angle can be achieved only for a fraction of a second. In some cases, 
333	this is generally not possible since the movement's inertia quickly moves the apparatus through that

363	method involves shifting the load slowly over a wide working range with stops at different joint angles

365	the increase in training weight.

368	idea of the magnitude of the tension. He can lift the weight several times between the stops then execute an

439	Recovery from isometric contraction is different from that of dynamic muscle action. It appears to take place in 
440	three phases (Petrofsky & Phillips, 1986):
441	• Rapid recovery of about 50% of endurance during the first 3 minutes after exercise
442	• A slower recovery lasting about 20 minutes during which recovery reaches about 90% of initial endurance
443	• A complete recovery within at least 24 hours.
444	Interestingly, recovery from low tension isometric contraction is slower during the first phases of recovery. 
445	O th e r  A s p e c ts  o f I s o m e tr ic  A c tiv ity
446	Isometric contraction is always distinguished from the dynamic forms of muscle contraction (concentric and 
447	eccentric), as if it is due to an entirely different process. Irrespective o f whether a muscle contraction produces or 
448	does not produce external movement o f a joint, the process o f contraction remains the same. Nervous impulses 
449	reaching the muscle fibres produce a sliding of myosin and actin filaments relative to one another until fatigue sets 
450	in and relaxation occurs.
451	The difference between static and dynamic muscle contraction lies not in the muscle, but in the nervous 
452	system which controls the intensity, speed, duration, type and pattern of contraction. It is the nervous system 
453	which recruits a specific group and number of muscle fibres at a particular rate, time and sequence. It activates 
454	prime movers, antagonists, assistant movers, emergency muscles and other groups of muscles to produce the 
455	necessary controlled movement of a given joint or series of joints. What needs to be appreciated is the feet that 
456	the concept of isometrics is far broader than is intimated by most texts on training. Little is said about how the 
457	isometric contractions are initiated, controlled or terminated. The main focus appears to be on the intensity and 
458	duration of the contraction rather than on the overall pattern of muscle action from resting state back to resting 
459	state after activity.
460	As discussed earlier, isometric contraction always takes place automatically during some stage of the 
461	transition between concentric and eccentric muscle action. Under voluntary control, isometric contraction may be 
462	initiated or terminated slowly or rapidly, and maintained for a certain duration at a specific percentage of one's 
463	maximal strength for one repetition (for a particular joint action).
464	Maintenance of a maximal isometric contraction, however, depends ultimately on autonomic responses 
465	produced by muscle fatigue or protective reflexes elicited in the muscles or connective tissues. Motivation may 
466	overcome the negative feedback from these tissues for somewhat longer, but voluntary activation of the muscles 
467	eventually becomes impossible and rest becomes necessary.

561	4.2.5 Eccentric Training
562	Eccentric contraction refers to muscle action in which the muscle force succumbs to the imposed load and the 
563	muscle complex lengthens (see 1.10). 
564	Not only is it metabolically much more efficient than concentric 
565	contraction, but it is also capable of generating higher forces (Kaneko et al, 1984; Komi, 1973; Rodgers & Berger,
566	1974). In addition, this difference between concentric and eccentric contractions has been found to depend on the 
567	velocity of contraction (Komi, 1973). As the velocity of contraction increases, so the maximum cccentric force 
568	increases, whereas the maximum concentric force decreases (Fig 3.16), even though the corresponding EMG for 
569	the given muscle group remains reasonably constant.
570	Investigations into the change in strength elicited by concentric and eccentric work are often contradictory. 
571	Johnson et al (1976) found that there were no significant differences between the two methods of training. Komi 
572	and Buskirk (1972), using an isokinetic dynamometer, found that eccentric training produced greater eccentric, 
573	concentric and isometric strength increases than concentric training. 
574	The concentric training increased only 
575	concentric and eccentric strength. Fridcn et al (1983b) found that eccentric training to failure produces marked in­
576	creases in eccentric strength-endurance, but minimal changes in concentric strength-endurance.
577	The high speed, large acceleration SMART (Seated Movement Aerobic and Resistive Training) or 
578	Supersitting system created by Lisa Ericson (1992) for work with the disabled, however, tends to increase both 
579	concentric and eccentric strength-endurance. Other workers have reported adaptation differences relating to 
580	training velocity, measurement velocity and particular muscle groups, while very few studies exist which compare 
581	functional strength and power changes with free weights, auxotonic activities or natural sporting manoeuvres. The 
582	central role played by the specificity principle clearly has a profound effect on the experimental analysis.
583	The ability of a muscle to produce greater eccentric than concentric force may be a result of the tension- 
584	generating capacity of the connective tissues rather than the contractile elements of the muscle. Therefore, the 
585	superior strengthening observed for high velocity (over 180° per second) isokinetic eccentric training may be due 
586	to selective increase in the tensile strength of the tendon and other series elastic components of the muscic 
587	complex. 
588	The training and rehabilitation implication is that high velocity eccentric exercise, applied in a 
589	progressive overload manner, may enable the connective tissue, especially that of the musculotendinous junction, 
590	to resist high impact forces associated with running, jumping and other impulsive actions.

596	Since lengthening of the muscle complex occurs with eccentric contraction, the stretching SEC (series elastic 
597	component) is exposed to greater strain than under concentric conditions and the potential for injury increases. 
598	Thus, it is not surprising to learn that most muscle strains and ruptures occur during the eccentric phase of 
599	movement (Garrett, 1986).
600	It is often been shown that a single session of intense eccentric exercise causes pronounced DOMS (delayed 
601	onset muscle soreness) which peaks between 24-72 hours after exercise and disappears several days later (Fridcn 
602	et al, 1983a). This soreness is accompanied by reduced dynamic strength and damage to the myofibrils and 
603	connective tissue elements such as the Z bands, which are a component of the SEC. Friden et al (1983b) also 
604	examined the effects of longer periods of eccentric exercise (3 sessions a week over a total of 8 weeks) and 
605	discovered that post-exercise soreness not only did not occur after 2-3 weeks, but the ability to perform eccentric 
606	work even increased by 375%. At the same time, biopsies revealed that Z band damage had not taken place, 
607	suggesting that adaptation to eccentric exercise had occurred. This research was corroborated by Schwane and 
608	Armstrong (1983), who found that downhill running in rats produced a superior training effect to level or uphill 
609	training and prevented injury more effectively.

611	and hypertrophy than concentric exercise (Hortobagyi et al, 2000), and it is sometimes suggested that this may be 
612	the result of greater tissue damage being produced under eccentric conditions. Recent work, however, has 
613	discovered that the increase in myofibral cross-sectional area is much the same in unchanged muscle fibres 
614	following concentric exercise as that following eccentric exercise, which is more damaging (Komulainen et al, 
615	2000). These results do not support the hypothesis that fibre hypertrophy depends on the extent of the fibre

619	with determining those regimes which ensure that the athlete's motor potential will be realised to the fullest and

621	research has been done in basically two directions:

632	4.2.6.1 The Isokinetic Training Method
633	The isokinetic method was very popular in the latter part of the 1960's and early 1970's, particularly in the USA 
634	(see 1.10). Essentially this method involves the use of a special device (such as a centrifugal clutch, or hydraulic 
635	system) which automatically adjusts the resistance to the movement, controls its speed and ensures a maximum 
636	load on the muscles throughout the entire working amplitude. In other words, the limiting factor is the speed with 
637	which the exercise is executed, not the magnitude of the resistance as it is for weightlifting exercises. 
638	The 
639	resistance increases as the speed increases.
640	In isokineticSy the resistance is a function of the force applied. Depending on the apparatus, it may be offered 
641	in the form of concentric isokinetics or eccentric isokinetics, although most commercial machines at present offer 
642	only the concentric mode. The isokinetic device controls the velocity of the movement so that the athlete can fully 
643	use the working amplitude of the movement to produce muscular tension. The device is constructed so as to offer 
644	resistance whose magnitude can be varied from the force of finger pressure to hundreds of Newtons. The athlete 
645	attempts to apply maximum force and the device automatically varies the resistance. Because muscular force and 
646	work capacity change during the specific movement, the resistance automatically accommodates to the muscles'

674	3. By using resistance which automatically accommodates to the applied force, significant strength can be

714	Fundamental B iom echanics of Isokinetic Devices
715	The faulty basic assumption is that isokinetic dynamometers are accurately constant angular velocity devices. 
716	The laws of physics deem it impossible to construct any machine which offers purely isokinetic resistance from 
717	beginning to end of motion. When a body is at rest, it has to be accelerated to reach a certain terminal velocity 
718	that can be maintained for a given period of time before it has to be decelerated to return to rest once more. This 
719	means that there is always a period of positive or negative acceleration associated with all movement, isokinetic or 
720	otherwise. The best that manufacturers of isokinetic devices can do is to minimise the duration of these phases, 
721	although they can never entirely eliminate them. To produce entirely isokinetic conditions from beginning to end 
722	of motion would necessitate the production of infinite acceleration, which contradicts the laws of science.
723	Justifiably, it might be asked if the existence of non-isokinetic measuring phases on these machines is 
724	important. This fact is vitally important, because most injuries occur during these transition phases when a limb 
725	is changing its velocity or tension is changing in the musculotendinous system and isokinetic testing can reveal no 
726	useful information about what is happening to the muscles then. A most serious problem is that isokinetic testing 
727	can give no information on the major contribution played by the storage and release of elastic energy in the soft 
728	tissues during dynamic, natural actions such as walking, running, jumping or throwing. Stated simply, isokinetic 
729	testing or training is non-functional, except possibly for swimmers whose movements are approximately 
730	isokinetic over part of their range.
731	Biomechanical analysis of the force-time and rate of force development (RFD) curves for resisted free 
732	movement confirm the existence of vital muscular performance qualities such as maximal strength, starting 
733	strength (at the beginning of a movement), acceleration strength (while the movement is speeding up to maximum 
734	velocity) and explosive strength (see Fig 2.13). The curves obtained isokinetically are so radically different from 
735	tbeir free movement equivalents that they are of minimal value either for functional analysis or specific 
736	neuromuscular conditioning.
737	Recommended Strength Ratios
738	It is often claimed that the optimal ratio of quadriceps to hamstring strength is 60:40, but Russian scientists have 
739	found that this ratio depends on the specific type of sport (Vorobyev, 1978). For example, they have determined 
740	that this ratio (measured when knee extension torque is greatest) should be nearer 80:20 for weightlifters and 
741	lumpers. 
742	Moreover, if the ratio is measured during movement on a treadmill, the ratio for runners is 
743	approximately 50:50. Despite these findings, the traditional 60:40 recommendation is widely accepted and much 
744	rehabilitation is based on restoring this ratio. Another popular belief is that injuries are far more common if the 
745	difference in strength between left and right lower extremities is more than 10%.
746	Recent research, however, has shown that neither of these recommendations is supported by scientifically 
747	controlled experiments which correct torque outputs for the effect of gravity and avoid stretching the hamstrings

Initial Implications of M echanics
Because of their fundamental importance in biomechanics, Newton’s Laws of Motion warrant repetition here:
Newton / (The Law of Inertia): A body will persist in its original state of rest or motion unless acted on by 
an external agency (i.e. a force).
Newton //(The Law of Acceleration): Newton stated it thus: “The change of motion is proportional to the 
motive force impressed; and is made in the direction of the straight line in which that force is impressed” 
(Richards et al, 1962), which in modem terms may be restated as: 
The rate of change of velocity 
(acceleration) is proportional to the resultant force acting on the body and is in the same direction as the force 
or, if suitable units are chosen. Force = Mass x Acceleration ( F = m.a).
Newton ///(The Law of Reaction): For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction.
Despite the familiarity of these laws, some of their implications appear to be forgotten in the practical setting, in 
particular regarding comparison between machine and free weight training. Some machine manufacturers advertise 
that their variable resistance machines are superior to free weights, because, in the latter case, the weight remains 
constant and does not change in response to altering joint leverages throughout range of any movement. 
Newton’s first two laws show clearly that this claim is false, since a load may only be lifted if its weight (due to 
gravitational acceleration) is overcome by the lifter with an acceleration which exceeds that of gravity.
Furthermore, during the lift, proprioceptive feedback makes the athlete aware that the load is changing and 
enables him to intervene voluntarily in the loading process by accelerating or decelerating the bar to increase or 
decrease the force involved. This method is sometimes known as Compensatory Acceleration Training (CAT) 
and can be useful in altering muscle tension or movement velocity to achieve a specific training goal (see Ch 7.1).
Although the role of CAT is well known during concentric movement (in which the load is being overcome), 
its vital role during eccentric movement (in which the load overcomes the propulsive force) is inadequately 
appreciated. In non-ballistic eccentric motion in which muscle contraction continues throughout the movement, 
the muscles try to oppose the effects of the gravity to slow down and ultimately halt the downward motion of 
the bar. In ballistic motion in which muscle action is intermittent, so-called antagonistic muscle action comes into 
play to slow down and halt the limb to ensure that the joint is not dislocated or soft tissues are ruptured.
Even during isometric action (in which there is no external limb movement), compensatory processes are at 
play if no movement is to occur, since neural activation changes due to fatigue, altered mental focus or other 
physiological processes. This means that the athlete has to maintain adequate muscle tension for the entire 
duration of the isometric action, either by means of involuntary conditioned reflex action or by voluntary 
intervention. Thus, it might be preferable for the acronym CAT to stand for ‘Compensatory Action Training’.
Mass and Acceleration Issues
The implication for the well-known Principle of Progressive Overload is that ‘overload’ should refer not simply 
to the use of progressively greater resistance over a given period, but also to the progressive increase in muscle 
tension, which may be produced by involuntary or voluntary processes. This change in tension may be produced 
in ways which relate directly to Newton II and which pose a question which is of fundamental importance to all 
strength training. It is relevant to examine this issue before we go any further.
21


===== PDF 33 (printed 22) =====
SUPERTRAINING
Since force F = m.a, we may apply it to produce the same magnitude of force F in several different ways:
(a) F = M.a 
where the mass M is large and the acceleration is small
(b) F = m.A where the mass is small and the acceleration A is large
(c) F = m.a 
where both mass and acceleration are moderate
To which might be added force production under isometric or isokinetic conditions where acceleration is zero:
(d) F = k.R where k is a factor of proportionality and R is the resistance applied by the apparatus.
This might immediately suggest, since the production of an adequate level of muscle tension is necessary for 
strength training, that all o f these methods of ‘Force Training* are entirely the same and that is just a matter of 
one’s personal choice which method is used. So, the question is: “Does it make any real difference which method 
o f strength training is used, as long as adequate muscle tension is produced?”
If one attempts to answer this question in purely mechanistic terms, one might be tempted to reply “no" and 
qualify one’s reply with qualifying comments about initiating movement against heavy loads with high inertia, 
possible detrimental effects of sustained loads on the soft tissues of the body and duration of loading.
Interestingly, practical experience from three different competitive aspects of strength training, namely 
Olympic weightlifting, powerlifting and bodybuilding, offers some preliminary information. Option (a) with 
very heavy loads is most commonly encountered in powerlifting, while the hypertrophy associated with 
bodybuilding generally is a product of option (c) training with moderate loads performed for about 8-12 
repetitions. Option (b) is characterised by many actions in track and field events. Olympic weightlifting, which 
involves lifting heavy loads rapidly, appears to contradict evidence that velocity decreases with load, but this is 
because weightlifting is ballistic and relies on the quick movement of the lifter under the bar. It may be concluded 
that powerlifting is essentially strength generating, while weightlifting is maximum power generating in nature.
Option (d) occurs only under laboratory conditions using special isokinetic devices to control the motion and 
correlation of results obtained under these and actual sporting conditions tends to be low, although it may 
produce significant increase in non-specific strength (Rosentzweig & Hinson, 1972; Ostemig, 1986).
The practical evidence shows that the above ways of generating force do not produce the same results and 
research reveals that this is because different neural, muscular and metabolic processes are involved in each ease. 
Thus, strength and power training are not simply a matter of using some generalised form of resistance training to 
produce adequate physical loading and muscle tension; the principle of specificity o f training is central to the 
entire issue.
M u scle T e n s io n  a n d  T ra in in g  S tim u lu s
Some coaches maintain that maximal muscle hypertrophy depends on tension time, with continuous tension 
times of 30-60 seconds per set of any exercise being commonly recommended. The observation that the extended 
use of isometric exercises of this magnitude of duration docs not produce the degree of hypertrophy associated 
with dynamic exercise (which includes eccentric action) militates against this simplistic claim. The fact that 
tension fluctuates from low to high values throughout a movement also militates against this idea. Clearly, both 
hypertrophy and strength increase depend on the existence of some minimum level o f tension, but nobody has 
identified what this tension threshold should be in the case of hypertrophy. Moreover, it is well known that 
novices to resistance training respond to much lower intensities o f loading both in terms of hypertrophy and 
strength gains.
Research has shown that the threshold training stimulus necessary for increasing muscular strength in the 
average person should not be less than one-third of the maximal strength (Hettinger & Muller, 1953). As strength 
increases, the intensity of the stimulus required to produce a training effect should be increased, and reach 80- 
95% of the athlete's maximum. It may be appropriate that the strength of the training stimulus sometimes equals 
or even exceeds the level of the competition stimulus of the given exercise (Verkhoshansky, 1977).
Thus, the development of strength requires that the stimulus intensity be gradually increased. 
It was 
discovered that every stimulus has a changing strengthening threshold, the achievement of which fails to elicit any 
further increase in muscular strength (Hettinger, 1961). The less trained the muscles, the further the strengthening 
threshold from the beginning state. The rate at which strength increases from the initial level to the strengthening 
threshold, expressed as a percentage of the current maximum strength, is independent of sex, age, muscle group
22


===== PDF 34 (printed 23) =====
SUPERTRAINING
and the level of the strengthening threshold. After the strengthening threshold has been reached, strength can be 
increased only by intensifying the training.
In this regard, according to Korobkov, Gerasimov and Vasiliev (Verkhoshansky, 1977), strength increases 
relatively uniformly during the initial stages of training, independent of how the load is applied in training, 
whether large or small. Approximately equivalent increases in strength arc obtained with loads of 20, 40, 60 and 
80 percent of IRM (one repetition maximum). An increase in the intensity of training in the initial stages (e.g. 
using a heavier load, faster tempo of movement and shorter intervals between sessions) does not always enhance 
the effectiveness of strength development, this becoming effective only later, as strength increases. This principle 
is corroborated by the training results of weightlifters (Hettinger, 1961; Verkhoshansky, 1977).
Application of Basic Biom echanics
This brings us back to the interesting and vitally important question in strength training which was raised earlier, 
namely: Should a heavy weight be lifted with a small acceleration or should a lighter load be lifted with a greater 
acceleration to produce strength most effectively? Or, is it preferable to train isometrically to produce maximal 
strength gains? In all of these cases the force produced may be exactly the same, but the training effect may be 
entirely different. What training effect is imposed by the duration of muscle tension, especially since the factor of 
strength-endurance becomes increasingly important and maximal strength becomes less important as the duration 
of any contraction increases?
To answer these questions, it is necessary in later chapters to apply the fundamentals of biomechanics to 
strength training (Fig 1.11) and draw a curve of force versus time and examine how each force-time curve or 
appropriate portion of this curve best matches the required strength quality, such as static strength, speed- 
strength, strength-endurance or strength-spced. In other words, the force-time curve may serve as one of the vital 
starting points for understanding the entire phenomenon of sport-specific strength and for prescribing sport- 
specific strength training. This curve is used in later chapters to answer the questions posed above and to act as a 
framework for resolving many other important strength training issues.
Figure 1.11 Summary of the major concepts used in sport biomechanics. Strain is the relative change in length, i.e. the change in 
length of a length of material L caused by a force F relative to its original length, d/dt refers to the first derivative with respect to time. 
] cfe refers to the integral with respect to displacement s.
As mentioned previously, other curves which also provide invaluable information for understanding and 
applying sport-specific strength training are the force (torque) vs angular displacement (for each joint), force 
(torque) vs velocity, endurance vs force and endurance vs velocity graphs. This information, together with a 
knowledge of which muscles are involved statically and dynamically in given complex movements, ftimish the 
minimum requirements for drawing up an effective and safe strength training programme for any sport. It is a 
major intention of this text to provide the reader with a solid understanding of these and other essential 
processes which are central to exercise prescription for enhanced performance or rehabilitation after injury.

1.3 A Philosophy of Physical Training
The success o f any training programme is closely linked to the philosophy of physical training in which it is 
embedded. Since this text draws heavily on Russian exercise science, it is enlightening to examine the overall 
education system in Russia which produced generations of the world's finest athletes in all sports. The excellence 
of their athletes in international competition is a direct result of carefully designed educational programmes aimed 
at employing sport, among other activities, to promote its national aims. Russian sport, like any other class of 
education, follows the same general principles and stages. The Russians distinguish between physical education 
and sport, in that the latter involves specialisation, competition for improving performance, and the acquisition of 
maximum physical and mental drive.
Several authors (Yessis, 1987; Schneidman, 1979; Matveyev, 1981; Vorobyev, 1978) give useful insights 
into the highly organised approach of the Russians, who recognise at least eight interrelated principles in scientific 
sports preparation:
1. T he P rin c ip le  o f A w aren ess
This covers the ideology and the philosophy o f Russian sport as well as the conscious awareness of all processes 
involved in acquiring sporting proficiency. The athlete is required to know himself and understand the 
physiological and psychological processes taking place in his body to enable him to control and evaluate 
objectively his sensations and his capacity for work.
2. T he P rin c ip le  o f A ll-round D e v e lo p m e n t
This entails building a solid physical and mental foundation on which to found other specialised sporting qualities. 
All-round development involves strength, speed, flexibility, endurance, good coordination, strong will-power, and 
exemplary moral and cultural development. Psychological preparation involves persuasion, explanation, example, 
encouragement, group influence, self-motivation and adaptation to stress.
3 . T h e P rin c ip le  o f C o n s e c u tiv e n e s s  (or C o n siste n c y )
This refers to the systematic overloading principle in which the intensity and the volume o f physical work, as 
well as the degree of difficulty of motor skills, is progressively increased. In all aspects, including strength, skill 
and strategy, the athlete moves from the easy to the difficult, from the light to the heavy, from the known to the 
unknown. The same principle in reverse is advised so that physical workouts arc not ended abruptly. The 
harmony of the body must be maintained by slowing down the exercise tempo after every workout and every 
competitive season.
4 . T he P rin c ip le  o f R e p e titio n
This principle is based on Pavlov's three-stage theory for development of conditioned reflexes. Firstly, novel 
activities stimulate large areas of the brain and recruit muscles which are unnecessary for performing a particular 
movement. Next, consistent repetition diminishes spurious neuromuscular activity and enables one to concentrate 
predominantly on the task being learned. Finally, expertise is established and the movement becomes automatic. 
These are the same stages applied in teaching sporting skills, namely:
(a) Development o f knowledge The athlete must understand frilly what must be learned before attempting to 
master it
(b) Development o f motor ability The athlete must acquire the ability to concentrate full attention on 
performance of the required physical manoeuvres
(c) Development o f automatic motor response The athlete no longer needs to concentrate consciously on the 
movements to perform them efficiently. The learned skill has bccome an automatic, conditioned reflex.
Not only repetition of exercises, but also proper sequences of work and rest fatigue and recovery, injury and 
rehabilitation are vital in producing the proficient athlete.
5. T h e P rin c ip le  o f V isu a lisa tio n
The athlete must be able to visualise the correct movements in order to master any sport. He must leam these 
patterns by observing demonstrations by his coach and other experts, studying films, slides and diagrams, and
