ratio varies throughout the range of joint motion, as may be seen in Figure 4.16.
For example, the ratio for the knee at 80° is about 75:25 at 36 degs/sec, whereas it is 68:32 at 180 degs/ sec. 
The only stage at which the ratio is 60:40 occurs at an angle of approximately 50°. Not only does the ratio change 
with joint angle, but it also changes with velocity of measurement, so it is meaningless to prescribe an optimal 
alio for any joint. It would be more relevant to refer to a characteristic curve over a full range of movement for a 
given angular velocity.
4.2.6.2 L im itations of th e Isokinetic M ethod
233


===== PDF 245 (printed 234) =====
SUPERTRAINING
234
Functional Anatomy
Another confounding factor is the influence of the angle of nearby joints on the torque that is produced by given 
muscles about the joint in question. For instance, knee extension torque increases with hip angle, a phenomenon 
that is of immense practical importance to weightlifters, jumpers and sprinters, in particular. These athletes arc 
well aware of operating over optimal ranges of relative knee and hip angle. 
Measurement of the relative 
disposition of these angles forms the basis o f the cyclogram used by biomechanists to study gait efficiency. 
Therapists attempt to solve this problem by immobilising the seated athlete’s hips by using strong inextensiblc 
straps across the upper thighs. 
This immediately creates non-functional conditions for evaluating the 
biomechanics of knee extension/flexion in free space. 
The seated posture produces highly constrained and 
accurate conditions for measuring torque that is specific to the seated posture and not to the posture exhibited 
during any actual sporting action.
Furthermore, seated isokinetic evaluation of knee motion is usually imprecisely controlled, since it is rarely 
combined with electromyography or myotonometry (muscle tension measurement) to ascertain the relative 
contributions made to joint torque by the different muscles comprising the quadriceps and hamstrings. 
Prescription of any exercise regime without knowing precisely which muscles are involved is just as haphazard 
with or without the aid of costly isokinetic devices. What complicates matters farther is that the degree of lateral 
or medial rotation of the lower extremity has a significant effect on the relative involvement of vastus medialis and 
lateralis, so that this variable also needs to be more accurately controlled if isokinetic testing is to become 
scientifically rigorous. Open-chain testing of the lower extremity with the sole of the foot not in contact with the 
ground alters the way in which poplitcus initiates knee flexion or gastrocnemius contributes to knee flexion, two 
actions that are of great importance in running, lifting or jumping.
In addition, seated testing does not take into consideration medial rotation of the knee by sartorius, gracilis, 
semimembranosus or semitendinosus, or lateral rotation by biceps femoris. 
The role of these muscles in 
performance may be largely ignored for the average client, but certainly not in the case of competitive athletes, 
who place maximal demands on their bodies.
The entire system of PNF is based on the importance of specific patterns of joint action and rnusclc 
recruitment in determining movement efficiency and safety, yet therapists with an extensive knowledge of PNF 
unquestioningly accept results produced under the highly unnatural conditions imposed by isokinetic machines. 
They are fully aware that training in a given way produces specific neural changes which become part of the 
central nervous programme that determines all movement efficiency; they meticulously apply the precise 
kinesiological patterns prescribed by Knott and Voss (1977), but they are compelled to ignore this knowledge 
when using isokinetic machines.
Muscle Physiology
Some of the implications of muscle physiology are also relevant to understanding the limitations o f isokinetic 
testing:


===== PDF 246 (printed 235) =====
SUPERTRAINING
• The initial muscular state preceding many sporting actions is intense isometric contraction or explosive 
isomctric contraction accompanied by storage of elastic energy in the tendons (see 1.6.2). This state has a 
profound influence on explosive strength, metabolic efficiency and safety, yet all isokinetic testing or training 
involves insignificant initial levels of isometric contraction.
• The myotatic stretch reflex has great significance for increasing the working effect of concentric muscle action, 
with the greater the rate of stretch, the stronger this reflex. Most explosive movements in running, jumping, 
lifting and throwing rely on intense recruitment of this reflex, which is not possible under isokinetic 
conditions. In fact, the production of powerful, skillful movements in all sports relies on the establishment of 
precise neuromuscular patterns through integration of many different reflexes. The elimination of most of 
these reflex actions by isokinctic apparatus ensures that isokinetic testing and training is only of value during 
the early general conditioning or rehabilitation phase, but of no real significance during the specific 
preparation or competitive phases of sports training.
• Musclcs generally interact to produce two kinds of action: cocontraction or ballistic movement (see 1.8). In 
cocontraction, agonists and antagonists contract simultaneously, with dominance of the former producing the 
external motion. Ballistic movement comprises bursts of agonist activity followed by phases of relaxation 
during which the motion continues due to stored limb momentum. Skilled, rapid ballistic and fast continuous 
movements are preprogrammed in the central nervous system (CNS) and rarely involve feedback during the 
action, whereas slower, discontinuous movements involve cocontraction and ongoing feedback to the CNS 
from the muscles and joints. Isokinetic conditions do not permit the production of ballistic or discontinuous 
cocontractive actions, so that they address only a few of the needs of sports testing and preparation.
• Some authorities maintain that strength is best developed if muscle tension is kept at a maximum throughout 
the movement by the use o f isokinetics (Thistle et al, 1967). This proposition is neither proved nor is it 
universally accepted with reference to all types of strength. Moreover, torque produced under isokinetic 
conditions is usually much lower than that produced isometrically at the same joint angle (Figs 2.8, 2.9).
• If contraction of the agonists is preceded immediately by maximal contraction of the antagonists, the force 
produced by the agonists is increased, a phenomenon often called reciprocal inhibition and regularly used in 
PNF. Most isokinetic devices do not permit this type of motion, which commonly occurs during plyometric 
rebounding activity.
• The patterns of force production are different for bilateral (simultaneous use of both limbs) and unilateral 
(alternate use of each limb) sports, so that isokinetic comparisons of relative limb strength can be very 
misleading. Furthermore, each person has a dominant limb, so that functional asymmetry is perfectly normal. 
This docs not imply that the dominant limb has superior strength; it often displays superiority in skill, 
especially in kicking, jumping and throwing sports. Yet, it is common to find therapists trying to strengthen 
the weaker kicking limb of a footballer isokinetically, although the support leg is meant to produce greater 
stabilising strength.
The Im portance of Specificity
Indiscriminate use of isokinetics neglects the proven principle of specificity (discussed in detail in 1.3) with 
respect to:
• Type of Muscle Contraction 
• Musclc Fibre Recruitment
• Movement Pattern 
• Metabolism
• Region of Movement 
• Biochcmical Adaptation
• Velocity of Movement 
• Flexibility
• Force of Contraction 
• Fatigue
Therefore, it is vital to understand the limitations of using isokinetics to test or train the athlete and appreciate 
that sport specific conditioning has little to do with isokinetic performance. As has been stressed by Sale and 
McDougall (1981), increased strength is apparent only when measured during the same type of movement used in 
training. The importance of training specificity is underlined further by the considerable research of 
Verkhoshansky, which culminated in his formulating the principle o f dynamic correspondence (see 4.3) This 
principle emphasizes that the means of strength training for all sports should enhance the required motor qualities
235


===== PDF 247 (printed 236) =====
SUPERTRAINING
in terms o f factors such as amplitude and direction of movement, and the rate and time of maximal force 
production.
On this basis, as well, isokinetic training and measurement are seen to be so functionally different from 
normal sporting movement as to be relatively useless for giving any information that is accurately applicable to 
the competitive athlete.
Concluding Rem arks
Although technological measurement is invaluable and highly desirable in sport 
and rehabilitation, 
oversimplification of any highly complex situation can lead to serious errors and hinder scientific progress. The 
simplistic central sun and planetary electron model o f the atom was a valuable tool for early 20th century 
physicists, but its replacement by more sophisticated quantum models has advanced our understanding of the 
universe enormously. Unqualified reliance on a single isokinetic model to assess muscular strength and endurance 
is tantamount to permanently accepting the early model of the atom, just because it is easy to work with.
The fact is that human motion involving static and dynamic multiple link components is extremely 
complicated and isokinetic testing can offer only a very simplistic way o f obtaining information on a limited 
number of variables. 
Isokinetic machines are useful for measuring isokinetic actions and changes in two 
dimensions, just as isometric dynamometry is useful for measuring isomctric strength at a given joint angle. 
Extrapolation o f results obtained under these conditions to sporting actions involving other types of muscle 
contraction and patterns of movement is scientifically unacceptable and misleading. Human mobility and stability 
are the integrated result of the appropriate phases of isomctric and non-isokinetic muscle contraction occurring 
with a specific timing in three-dimensional space over specific ranges of joint angle. Multi-faceted human 
movement demands the use of far more versatile and complex technological means, a type of kincsiological 
polygraph which integrates information yielded by concurrent use of devices such as high speed video, EMG, 
myotensiometers, accelerometers and force plates.
The ultimate measure of successful testing and training is unequivocal improvement in the athlete's 
performance, so that sporting movements should still be regarded as the final test of any training or rehabilitation 
regime. In addition, an inexpensive and highly effective alternative to isokinetics is the APRE system based on the 
original work of DeLorme (sec 5.2.2). The convenience of isokinetic testing should be weighed against its high 
cost, limited application and the unsupported claims of manufacturers. The detailed review of the strengths and 
weaknesses of isokinetic methods given by Ostemig (1986) provides further useful information in this regard.
4.2.6.3 S tatic-D ynam ic M ethods
The static-dynamic method of developing muscular strength involves the sequential combination in one exercise of 
isometric and dynamic (auxotonic) muscular activity, each of which can provide its own distinct quantitative 
characteristics. For example, the following variations of static-dynamic exercise have been shown to be effective:
• a 2-3 second isometric contraction (at 80% of one's maximum) is held, followed by explosive concentric 
dynamic work with a load of 30% of maximum
• with both the isometric and dynamic components, a constant load of 75-80% of maximum is used.
In the latter case, for instance, the athlete sinks into the half-squat position with a barbell on his shoulders, holds 
this position for 2 seconds, then with maximal acceleration, jumps upward. After careful landing he repeats the 
exercise.
It has been established experimentally that the first variant of static-dynamic exercise is better than dynamic 
exercise alone for developing speed-strength. The second variant has an equivalent affect on the improvement of 
speed-strength and absolute strength (Dobrovolsky, 1972, 1973).
4.2.6.4 C hoice of M uscle T raining Regim es
One may now ask the question: O f all these regimes, which is the most effective? 
It is difficult to give a 
categorical answer for several reasons:
1. Comprehensive research to evaluate the effectiveness of all the regimes has not been conducted. An attempt, 
for example, to study the effectiveness of eccentric, concentric, isometric and combined regimes revealed
236


===== PDF 248 (printed 237) =====
SUPERTRAINING
some advantages of the concentric over the eccentric and isometric method, but the main method using 
combined regimes showed a clear advantage (Plctnev, 1975).
2. Similar comparative research is difficult with respect to controlling the training loads of the different regimes.
3, It is inappropriate to raise the question of the absolute effectiveness of any specific regime. Each of them 
can be the most effective, depending upon factors such as the situation, stage of the annual cycle, level of the 
athlete, the primary regime of muscular work in the special exercise, and the specificity of the strength ability 
acquired as a result of training.
Today it can be ascertained with reasonable certainty that the most rational means of enhancing the effectiveness 
of special strength preparation is to combine the various regimes of muscular work. This has been corroborated 
by several studies (Vorobyev, 1966; Andrianov & Vorobyev, 1969; Kuznetsov, 1970; Verkhoshansky, 1970, 
1972; Slobodyan, 1972; Tatyan, 1974; Pletnev 1975; Khodykin, 1975; Savin, 1974). Such a training combination 
ts selected by taking into consideration its cumulative effect and its correspondence to the specific conditions of 
the sport.
4.2.7 The Use of Training M achines
Recently, training machines for strength development have become very popular in most modem gymnasia. 
However, before machines are used in training, it is important to understand that there are essentially two distinct 
classes of machine:
• Functional resistance machines, whose purpose is to offer resistance in sport specific patterns
• Non-Junctional resistance machines, whose sole purpose is to offer general resistance in non-sport specific 
patterns
An appreciation o f this distinction is vital for many coaches and athletes in the West, because the impressive 
fitness centres in which they often train are usually entirely equipped with non-functional resistance (NFR) 
nuchincs. In fact, the machine training syndrome has become so popular among the average population that it is 
frequently difficult to find adequate free weights or functional resistance (FR) machines in these 'state-of-the-art' 
ccntres. While the use of NFR machines may be adequate for the casual fitness client, it can be profoundly 
counterproductive for sport specific trainees if used in place of FR machines or free weights. Current commer­
cialised emphasis on circuit and cross training has proliferated the use of NFR machines, so the serious athlete 
should become aware of their limitations in sport and rehabilitation, particularly regarding the detrimental effects 
they can have on the specificity of fitness, proprioceptive efficiency, central nervous programming and sporting 
skills. The remarks of Zatsiorsky (1995) on this issue are highly relevant:
The important limitation o f many strength training machines is that they are designed to train muscles, not 
movement. Because o f this, they are not the most important training tool for athletes.
4.2.7.1 F unctional R esistance M achines
Functional strength (FR) machines are devised to provide resistance to various movements encountered in sport. 
Depending on the setting, sport-specific resistance devices are supposed to imitate or train certain elements of an 
athletic exercise in order to provide the necessary specific loads in the different regimes of muscular work (Ratov, 
1976). Research on the use of FR training devices in athletics has shown them to be very effective for aspects of 
special strength training of many types of athlete (Semenov, 1970; Petrova & Gorbunov, 1970; Vcrkhoshansky, 
1970; Deniskin & Kuznetsov, 1972; Dobrovolski, 1972, 1973; Kuznetsov & Aiunts, 1974; Savin, 1974).
This can be explained by the fact that they permit the strict regulation of the load and the spatial 
characteristics of the movement in order to use extensively the appropriate regimes o f muscular work and to 
programme the characteristics of the force over time. They reproduce stereotypical training movements and are 
economical for the athlete in terms of time and energy.
One of the simplest, cheapest and most versatile of all FR devices is the pulley machine, which used to be 
widely used in gymnasia until supplanted by the more commercially persuasive chromium-plated ’modem' 
machines. The 'hi-Io* pulley machine permits one to use the pulleys in high or low positions for all varieties of 
movement in space and time. Since the handles are attached to ropes unlike the fixed bars and pivots of most 
NFR machines, they can be used to exercise in sport specific patterns of great complexity, if so desired.
237


===== PDF 249 (printed 238) =====
SUPERTRAINING
With appropriate choice and layout of hand grips, bars, pulleys and benches, it is possible to perform dozens 
of different exercises for every body part on a single pulley machine. A fixture of only 4 pulley machines can 
actually provide a circuit training facility which cannot be equalled by fewer than 40 'state of the art’ machines. A 
circuit comprising 10 pulley machines, a few benches, a few jumping boards, a few bars, a few mats, gymnastic 
wall-bars and a few racks can provide more clients with a larger range of exercises than 100 specialised machines- 
at less than 15% of the cost. Even then, the NFR machine-only facility would provide inferior multi-dimensional 
conditioning of the body.
A major advantage of sport-specific FR training devices lies in the fact that it is possible to obtain crucial 
visual and computerised feedback about the qualitative and quantitative characteristics of the movement, as well 
as to control the athlete's special strength training. All of these advantages create significant potential foe 
perfecting the athlete's special strength training programme. Therefore, the design, introduction of various types 
of FR training device becomes a very important task.
In using any machine, however, it is vital to note that simulation of any sporting movement against heavy 
loads can alter the force-time characteristics of the action significantly and disrupt the neuromuscular programmes 
responsible for the movement. The magnitude of the load, the pattern of movement and the principle of dynamic 
correspondence have to be considered carefully if one intends to use machines to simulate actual sporting 
movements in any way. Most important is the fact that functionality is not the automatic consequence of a 
specific exercise, but of the functional objectives associated with using any exercise, irrespective of its similarity 
to any sports action and integrating it effectively into the long-term conditioning programme.
4.2.7.2 N on-Functional R esistance M achines
Non-functional resistance (NFR) machines can play a useful supplementary role to free weight and functional 
machine training, but in general they are unable to provide the same degree of multi-dimensional, full range 
neuromuscular and musculoskeletal training as free weights and ‘functional’ machines.
Very often, NFR machines compel the user to sit or lie, thereby minimising the training effect on the major 
stabilising musclcs of the body and involving fewer of the joints in fewer degrees of freedom of movement While 
this may be valuable in the earlier stages of rehabilitating certain injuries, it is an incomplete way of regularly 
training the body for functional development. One of their major deficiencies for the competitive athlete or average 
person is the limitation they impose on proprioceptive processes and the kinaesthetic sense in 
functional 
strength development. Since machines usually stabilise major regions of the body and limit the number of joints 
which move, they diminish one's ability to exercise freely in three dimensional space and thereby do not 
adequately train balance, coordination and other components of proprioception. 
The dangers of regular 
supplementary circuit training as a form of'cross training' for sporting preparation should then become obvious.
NFR machines may be useful in concentrating more on the development of certain muscle groups for 
supplementing overall bodybuilding training or the primary stages of injury rehabilitation, but they are unsuitable 
for providing all-round conditioning of entire muscle groups, interacting agonist/antagonist muscles and motor 
systems. For instance, there is no single machine that can rival the training effect of a barbell squat, a barbell or 
dumbbell curl, a barbell bench press, a power clean, a standing press, lateral raises with dumbbells or a barbell 
deadlift. On the other hand, one machine, namely the 'lat pulley' machine, is generally more suitable and safer for 
training the latissimus dorsi than the free weights equivalent of bent-over rowing.
It is important to note that, if a machinc compels a user to use fewer joints and muscles than an equivalent 
free weights or pulley exercise, then the stress on all of those structures will be increased proportionately. For 
example, the free standing squat involves three joints (hip, knee and ankle), whereas the seated knee extension 
machinc constrains the body to use only one joint (the knee) in exercising the quadriceps, so that, in producing a 
comparable level of exercise over the same range of movement, this machine increases the shearing force across the 
knee. Moreover, the squat also offers the added advantages of exercising the thigh adductors, the spinal erectors 
and several other stabilising muscles, besides enhancing general balance and bone density (due to longitudinal 
compressive loading of the skeleton).
It is not often appreciated that seated exercise always imposes a greater load on the lumbar spinal discs than 
equivalent standing exercises. Even without an added load, sitting with the back maintaining its neutral curvatures 
increases the lumbar disc pressure by about 40% (Chaffin & Andersson, 1984). If the back is allowed to flex 
forwards, this stress can increase by as much as 90%. An ergonomically designed backrest which adequately 
supports the lumbar region lowers the stress, but even then the lumbar disc pressure can be some 75% greater
238


===== PDF 250 (printed 239) =====
SUPERTRAINING
than during standing. The increase in stress becomes far greater against resistance, particularly if jerky movements 
are used to initiate or terminate the movement. The dangers are exacerbated by sitting, because one is unable to 
absorb any shock loading by flexing the knees, hips or ankles, as is the case when standing.
In the vast majority of cases, NFR machines provide an inferior, incomplete and less efficient way of training 
the musculoskeletal system. This is particularly true regarding the conditioning of the neuromuscular system in 
rapid or explosive movements, as well as the elastic qualities of the tendons and other conncctive tissues which 
ire essential in all sports involving running, jumping, throwing, catching or any other ballistic actions. Isokinetic 
machines can be especially deficient in this regard, so that their appropriateness of use must be clearly understood 
if they are to prove beneficial in sport specific training (see 4.2.6). Nevertheless, some machines may be used 
productively as an occasional form of General Physical Training, rehabilitation or restoration.
4.2.7.3 M achines and th e Variable R esistan ce Philosophy
As discussed elsewhere in this text, the torque produced by a muscle in a particular movement varies with joint 
angle. Many machine manufacturers have used this fact to justify the design of machines whose resistance varies 
in an attempt to match the torque curves of natural joint movement. They maintain that variable resistance 
machines offer superior strength training to free weights and other resistance devices. What they fail to point out 
is that regular training on any machine, whether variable resistance or not, provides inadequate functional 
proprioceptive training and thereby can reduce one's level of motor efficiency, stability and safety.
Their claims are based on the faulty premise that the resistance offered to the muscles by a free weight 
always remains the same. So, for example, if you perform a biceps curl with 50 kg, then it is implied that you are 
exciting a force of 50 kg weight (about 490 Newtons) from beginning to end of movement. 
Machinc 
manufacturers stress that their bicep curl machine offers some form of automatically adjusting resistance to 
account for the variation of strength with joint angle, apparently something that never happens with free weights.
A simple application of Newton's Second Law of Motion (force is proportional to the acceleration of the ob­
ject) reveals that the resistance offered by a free weight changes with acceleration from rest and during any other 
time when the trainee speeds up or slows down the movement when the weight feels lighter or heavier 
respectively. The force exerted by any weight which begins from and returns to rest is always varying, anyway, 
as can easily be demonstrated by force plate, cable tensiometer or high speed video analysis. The skilled trainee is 
able to rely on his proprioceptive apparatus to perceive any changes in force or pattern o f movement so as to 
statically and dynamically vary the resistance and its direction more efficiently than any current machines.
4.2.7.4 The T raining S afety of M achines
It is often claimed that the NFR machines found in most fitness centres are much safer to use than free weights. 
Injuries to the back and knees (on leg press, hack-squat and hip-sled machines), the shoulders and chest (on bench 
press and pec-deck machines), the elbow joint (bicep curl machines), the back (back extension machines) and other 
joints are just as common with machines as with free weights. In fact, many machines, such as the 'pec-dcck', 
bench-prcss, leg press, calf-raise and seated press machines force the user to commence the movement from the 
biomechanically least efficient and potentially most harmful position for the relevant joint. Partners to 'spot' 
machine users are just as necessary as spotters for free weights users. Faulty technique is equally dangerous with 
machines or free weights.
Some machines such as leg extension, lat pulley and seated bicep curl machines are certainly safer if an 
individual is suffering from back weakness or injury. They can be very helpful in the early stages of rehabili­
tation, but are not helpful in the long-term, since continual avoidance of stress to the regions involved eventually 
leads to their progressive weakening. There is a definite supplementary place in a gymnasium for certain NFR 
machines, but they should not replace free weights, pulley machines and other FR devices. A more detailed 
analysis of the safety of training with specific machines is covered later (Ch 8.8).
4.2.7.5 The Efficiency of M achine T raining
Contrary to what the equipment manufacturers state, it takes far longer for NFR machines to provide a similar 
multi-faceted training effect to the equivalent free weights or FR machines. For instance, it requires at least twelve 
NFR machines to approximately equal the training effect of the clean-and-push press, at least four machines to 
rival the training effect of the free standing squat, more than three machines to equal the training effect of the 
standing dumbbell curl, and at least five machines to rival the effectiveness of the flexed-knee deadlift.
239


===== PDF 251 (printed 240) =====
SUPERTRAINING
In other words, more than 24 NFR machines are required to challenge the effectiveness of a circuit 
comprising only four free weights exercises: the clean-and-push press, the squat, deadlift, and biccps curl. In this 
case, the combined cost of these machines is about forty times greater than the combined cost of several sets of 
free weights and the necessary racks. Moreover, the maintenance cost of most NFR machines is considerably 
higher than that of virtually indestructible free weights and the breakdown of machines is a regular occurrence in a 
well-used gymnasium.
4.2.8 The Concept of Sym m etric Training
Asymmetry in leg length, muscle strength, stride length and several other features of human structure and function 
has been blamed as one of the causes of inefficient movement and injury. 
Likewise, imbalances in muscle 
strength between agonists and antagonists, left and right limbs, and in isokinetic muscle endurance, as measured on 
isokinetic devices have been singled out as leading causes of muscle injury (see 4.2.6).
Research, however, has revealed that isokinetically-measurcd discrepancies as large as 10% between 
left/right leg strength and agonist/antagonist strength of the right and left legs do not statistically correlate with a 
major increase in muscular injuries.
The body and its muscles, tendons and bones are characteristically asymmetric and any attempts to produce 
greater anthropomorphic and kinesiological symmetry could cxaccrbate the existing problem or cause new injuries. 
One has to ascertain the degree of asymmetry not only by static measurements of structural features such as leg 
length and spinal curvature, but also by dynamic biomechanical analysis of Junctional features such as force 
distribution, movement patterns, ground reaction force, electrical activity of postural (tonic) and phasic muscle 
groups, and the timing of the different phases of movement.
Differences in structural characteristics including muscle and tendon length, the sites of tendon and ligament 
attachments to bone, and bone size and mass are quite natural in all humans. It is only when these structural 
differences lead to serious Junctional imbalances in movement patterns that surgical or orthotic means may have to 
be implemented to solve the problem. Even then, one has to ensure that the excessive functional asymmetry is 
due primarily to structural and not neuromuscular or central nervous processes. It may be that the centrally 
stored nervous patterns are producing the troublesome kinesiological imperfections, so that the answer lies in 
paying attention to modifying the motor skills required for the specific sport.
It is important to appreciate that there is no perfect way of executing any movement: everyone has an 
individualised version of the supposedly 'ideal' model of every skill. Some sports coaches and aerobic instructors 
place an unnecessarily restrictive emphasis on what they consider to be 'correct' exercise technique and allow 
inadequate latitude for individual interpretation (i.e. style, as opposed to skill). One simply has to examine the 
drastically different walking and running styles of world class athletes to realise that there is no such thing as 
perfect style. There is only an optimal style for each individual, where style refers to the individual expression of 
a motor skill. This style has to be developed on the basis of observing and experimenting with the 'ideal' model 
until the person produces a central nervous programme which suits his or her body.
Recent research by Yushkcvich (1989) supports these points. He analysed the symmetry of leg strength in 
sprinters and concluded that striving for full leg symmetry is inappropriate. He found that the extensors of all the 
joints of the push-off leg generally were significantly stronger than those of the swing-leg, whereas there was no 
definite difference between the flexor strengths of either leg. There were distinct differences in the patterns of 
asymmetry between novice. Class 3, Class 2, Class 1 and more highly qualified athletes. For instance, novices 
displayed greater strength of the hip flexors of the push-off leg than of the swing-leg. The knee flexors of novices, 
Class 3 and Class 2 were stronger in the swing-leg, whereas those of Class I, Master and other more highly 
qualified athletes were stronger in the push-off \cg. Dorsiflexion was stronger in the push-off leg of all athletes 
except novices.
Interestingly, leg strength asymmetry was found to increase as sprinters increase in proficiency, reaching a 
peak among Class 2 athletes, then diminishing again as level of sports mastery increased. 
Furthermore, 
Yushkevich found that good sprint times correlated more closely with swing-leg strength than push-off leg 
strength.
This study concluded that, not only are attempts to produce symmetrical muscle strength ill-advised, but 
that it can be beneficial to perform asymmetric exercises by running or jumping on sloping or inclined tracks, by 
running around curves in both directions, running and jumping in shoes with soles of different thickness, or 
running with leg weights of different mass. Yushkevich (1989) stressed this type of training thus: \Asymmetric 
exercises destabilise the space-time characteristics o f motor acts, thereby helping athletes break speed barriers'.
240


===== PDF 252 (printed 241) =====
SUPERTRAINING
There is an ancient injunction that the weavers of Eastern carpet must include at least one flaw in their 
work to recognisc that perfection is reserved for the Divine and not for humans. The above findings imply that 
ijnilar asymmetry or lack of perfection may be desirable for all human physical performance and training.
4.2.9 The Concept o f M uscle Isolation
Generations of muscle magazine authors have extolled the virtues of special ways of training to isolate specific 
muscle groups. They have advocated certain machines, ways of fixating the joints, precise placement of the limbs 
ud numerous other ingenious manoeuvres to ensure that one muscle is maximally recruited while others remain 
largely dormant.
EMG studies reveal that isolation of minute muscle groups is indeed possible under low intensities of 
loading (e.g. Basmajian, 1978). Intuitively, we are aware that low intensity actions such as eye-blinking, piano- 
playing or relaxed speaking are due to the precise action of specific muscle groups, a fact which the EMG clearly 
corroborates.
However, if large loads are imposed on a given muscle group by intense resistance, isolation becomcs virtu- 
illy impossible. Immediately the load is applied, stabilising muscles become involved to ensure that the body or 
specific joints remain stable, while the prime movers attempt to cope with the load. If the nervous system signals 
that the prime movers are inadequate to execute the desired joint action, assistant movers, shunt muscles, 
emergency muscles and neutralises may all be recruited to augment the action of the prime movers.
Physiotherapists relying on PNF techniques sometimes impose maximal loading on a joint to elicit 
compensatory or overflow activity o f muscles other than the ‘prime movers.* 
This is not possible if the 
resistance imposed is inadequate to overload the ‘prime movers.* Similarly, the weight trainer who wishes to 
increase hypertrophy or strength of a given muscle selects a weight which forces it to operate at high intensity. 
Hie higher the intensity or the greater the duration of the exercise, the less likely is isolation of the prime mover, 
even if certain joints arc restrained as on an isokinetic test machine.
In many cases the tension developed in the stabilisers or assistant stabilisers will equal or exceed that of the 
pnme movers. For example, during heavy standing tricep press-downs with cable machines, the abdominal 
muscles, latissimus dorsi and erector spinae of the back may be as strongly contracted as the triceps, even though 
this is supposedly an isolation exercise for the triceps. Analysis of many seated or reclining isolation exercises on 
machines reveals that isolation simply docs not occur with heavy loads.
This is not to negate the value of so-called isolation exercises. Not only can they be useful during the early 
stages of injury rehabilitation, but overflow to other muscle groups may be very desirable (if the exercise is 
performed safely), sincc it simultaneously offers isometric and dynamic training to many other muscle groups. It 
tsnecessary, however, to clarify the popular misconceptions surrounding the misleading concept of muscle 
isolation still proliferated by numerous instructors and in many training texts.
4.3 Dynamic Correspondence as a Means of S trength 
Training
Devising methods of special strength training is associated firstly with the selection of the means and methods for 
developing muscular strength. 
AH sporting movement is specific and goal-directed. Therefore, the strength 
displayed in the execution of each movement is also specific and goal-directed. One should not refer to strength in 
general, but only in the context of the given task. In other words, the means and methods of strength training 
should provide an adequate conditioning regime for the motor system in the special exercises and thereby ensure 
continued improvement in sporting performance.
The foundation of this assertion lies in the principle o f dynamic correspondence, which emphasizes that the 
means and methods of strength training for specific sports should be chosen to enhance the required motor 
qualities in terms o f :
• The amplitude and direction of movement
• The accentuated region of force production
• The dynamics o f the effort
• The rate and time of maximum force production
• The regime of muscular work
241


===== PDF 253 (printed 242) =====
SUPERTRAINING
4.3.1 The Amplitude and D irection of M ovement
The criterion of correspondence with respect to the amplitude and direction originates from the patterns of the 
movement relative to the adjacent body part. It determines which muscles are involved in the work and allows for 
anatomical peculiarities and the external conditions of work. Thus, the movement of the shoulder girdle of a row« 
or shot putter is about the same in amplitude, but the direction of the working force is different (Fig 4.17). In the 
first case the pulling of the oars involves shoulder extension, whereas in the second case it involves shoulder 
flexion acting in opposition to the force of inertia of the shot.
The importance of the correspondence of muscular work, in terms of the relevant criteria may be illustrated 
by the following example. In track-and-field training, jumpers and sprinters sometimes do exercises to develop the 
hip flexor muscles in a standing position on a hip flexor machine which offers resistance by means of a pad 
pressing against the front of the thigh.
However, the amplitude of thigh movement in running and jumping (when moving the legs forward) ij 
significantly greater than the amplitude of this exercise, and begins at an angle of about 210° in the hip joint, 
relative to the torso. Therefore, the execution of this exercise in the standing position docs not duplicate the 
mcchanism of the movement in the sport specific exercise ( e.g. jumping or sprinting).
Figure 4.17 Working amplitude of shoulder movement of a rower and a shotputter (Siff & Verkhoshansky, 1999).
If the athlete’s position changes (Fig 4.18), the criterion of the correspondence is met, not only with respect to the 
amplitude of the movement, but also to the sporting movement, because the resistance imitates the inertial 
resistance of the mass of the leg rotating about the hip joint in the special exercise. By altering the load, the 
number of repetitions and the tempo of movement, the task of developing the strength to produce the required 
force and strength-endurance, will be solved. Thus, to fulfill the criteria of correspondence with respect to the 
amplitude and direction of movement, it is advisable to select the exact starting position and posture of the ath­
lete, as well as to calculate the direction of action of the forces associated with the working links of the system 
and the additional load.
The line of action of the applied external resistance and of the loaded movement as a whole must also be 
taken into account. For example, in middle-distancc running, skiing and skating, a knapsack full o f sand ora 
weight belt are sometimes used as resistance. However, the muscles which bear the load are those which resist the 
weight o f the body. This can increase the ability to cope with vertical loading and develop general strength- 
endurance, but docs not strengthen those muscles which propel the body horizontally.
Figure 4.18 Exercise for developing hip flexion strength based on consideration for the accentuated part o f the working amplitude and 
the resistance to the force of muscle contraction (SiflF & Verkhoshansky, 1999).
Similarly, a skater may exccute jumps on one leg on the floor or from a bench. These exercises strengthen the leg 
muscles supporting the body and the static-endurance of the back muscles, but do not fully imitate the working of 
the muscles for the push-off, where the force is directed backward.
242

# Hettinger and Muller's Original Isometric-Training Finding: About 5% Strength Gain Per Week From One Daily 6-Second Effort at Two-Thirds Maximum

**What it is** — Isometric exercises became popular in the mid-1950s in the search for
economical, effective strength methods. Hettinger and Muller (1953, 1955) established that
one daily effort at two-thirds of maximum, held for six seconds, performed for 10 weeks,
increases strength by about 5% per week. Separately, Clark et al (1954) found that static
strength continues to increase even after a four-week isometric programme has concluded.
This early success prompted considerable research comparing isometric training's
effectiveness against dynamic training, which produced "rather contradictory data" (see
review by Verkhoshansky, 1970). The authors' general conclusion from that body of research:
isometric training can be more effective than dynamic exercise specifically where the target
exercise requires a large-magnitude muscle contraction at a certain stage of a movement, or
during early-stage injury rehabilitation; if the target exercise involves high-speed
movement, sustained isometric training is less effective. The authors also note that
because isometric training's usual purpose is developing absolute strength, tension should
be increased slowly and held for a relatively long time, since prolonged tension maintenance
demands the energy expenditure that stimulates adequate neuromuscular adaptation; some
researchers found no essential difference in strength gain from varying isometric tension
intensity, from which the authors infer that tension duration, not magnitude, is the
"fundamental conditioning factor." (PDF pp. 235, printed pp. 223-224, "4.2.4 Isometric
Training.")

**Why it works** — The authors' stated reasoning: prolonged maintenance of muscular tension
requires an energy expenditure that "stimulates adequate adaptation in the neuromuscular
system, thereby determining its strength potential," and this can exceed the stimulus from
brief transient dynamic tension. Inference: no cellular or neural mechanism is given for why
duration outweighs magnitude specifically; this is an inference the authors draw from
studies not finding a strength-gain difference across tension intensities, not a stated
physiological pathway.

**When to apply** — Use the 5%-per-week figure and the two-thirds-maximum, 6-second, daily,
10-week protocol as a citable historical anchor for isometric-training dosing, and use the
authors' scoping rule (isometrics favoured for large-magnitude contraction at a specific
movement stage or early rehab; less favoured when the target skill is high-speed) to decide
when isometric work is the better tool versus dynamic resistance training.

**When NOT to apply** — This is single-era data (1950s studies, corroborated only by a 1970
review) without modern replication in this text; treat "5% per week" as specific to
Hettinger and Muller's exact protocol (two-thirds max, 6 seconds, daily, 10 weeks), not a
generalizable isometric-training growth rate. The "contradictory data" comparing isometric
to dynamic training is acknowledged by the authors themselves, so this entry's headline
finding should not be read as settling the isometric-versus-dynamic debate; it explains only
the original claim's origin and the authors' scoping conditions for it.

**Example** — The book's own example is the Hettinger and Muller protocol itself (daily,
6-second, two-thirds-maximum isometric effort for 10 weeks, yielding about 5% weekly
strength gain); no further invented example is added here.

**Related** — [[heuristic--isometric-training-execution-protocol-and-advantages-drawbacks]],
[[claim--isometric-regional-specificity-not-strictly-angular]].

16:**What it is** — Five dials set an isometric stimulus. Natera maps each one to adaptations using a review that the ASR renders as "Orren Schuch." It is almost certainly **Oranchuk, Storey, Nelson & Cronin (2019), *Isometric training and long-term adaptations: effects of muscle length, intensity and intent*** (Scand J Med Sci Sports); two papers in Zotero cite it under that title.
18:- **Muscle length.** Short, moderate or long.
20:- **Intensity.** Low is 30–50% of max; high is 70–100%.
24:- **Muscle mass** is favored by long lengths, higher volume, grind intent and long holds.
25:- **Fascicle length** changes are equivocal, and length does not change the result. Long lengths favor a **pennation angle** increase.
26:- **Tendon cross-sectional area and stiffness** respond to high intensity (≥70%), long lengths and **ballistic intent**. Duration matters little, with long "slightly better" for stiffness.
28:- **Peak force** does not differ by length. Moderate-to-long lengths spread gains across more of the range, and moderate-to-high intensity gives the best gains.
30:- **Dynamic performance** (squat, CMJ) shows little difference by length or intent.
31:- **Angle specificity** holds, with some carryover to both shorter and longer lengths.
37:- **moderate** muscle lengths, avoiding both short lengths and the hypertrophic long end;
41:He says the method came first and he found the evidence afterward. The link between "moderate length + ballistic" and "better sprint tissue" is his inference, not a tested outcome.
45:**When NOT to apply** — This is one coach's paraphrase of one review, heard through ASR. Read Oranchuk 2019 before citing any single cell of the map. Much of the review's evidence comes from single-joint lab studies in untrained or recreationally trained subjects, so how it generalizes to trained sprinters is unknown. Architecture changes are "questionable," as Natera says himself. Tendon claims (intensity ≥70%, ballistic intent) are **tissue-adaptation claims, untested in this context**. Do not apply the early-rehab analgesic-isometric literature (Rio/Cook) here; that is a different goal with different dosing.
47:**Example** — For a DB coming off a patellar tendinopathy flare, pick high intensity (≥70%), ballistic intent, moderate knee angle and short 3 s efforts at low volume. That prescription follows from this map; it is not a validated protocol.
----
15:evidence-locator: page
51:- The framework is explicitly not evidence that one eccentric method is superior; its purpose is terminology and selection clarity. [p. 9]
55:- The paper identifies limitations in earlier models but does not report a systematic search, evidence grading, or comparative intervention. [p. 3]
61:Name the intended eccentric task before selecting an exercise: tolerate and dissipate load, stop rapidly, reverse rapidly, overcome a load, or accept a supramaximal lowering demand. Then choose dose and progression from population-specific evidence rather than assuming the taxonomy proves effectiveness.

69:| Framework purpose and non-superiority statement | p. 9 | limitation and application |

14	# Isometric Endurance Collapses Above 10-15% of Maximal Tension, and Recovers in Three Distinct Phases
15	
16	**What it is** — Isometric endurance at resistance exceeding 10-15% of a muscle's maximal
17	strength is very short compared with dynamic exercise, because of metabolic demand and
18	impaired blood flow to the exercising muscle under sustained contraction (Petrofsky &
19	Phillips, 1986); below that threshold, contractions are considered non-fatiguing, since
20	intramuscular pressure stays low and is readily exceeded by rising mean arterial pressure in
21	the capillaries. Verified against the page image (Fig 4.13, printed p. 227, cat soleus and
22	gastrocnemius, electrically stimulated, based on Petrofsky & Hendershot, 1984): intramuscular
23	pressure rises roughly linearly with muscle tension, from near 0 kPa at rest to over 20 kPa
24	at 100% of maximal strength. As tension rises, intramuscular pressure rises with it and
25	metabolism cannot keep pace, producing a hyperbolic drop in performance and marked fatigue
26	increase (the Rohmert curve, first derived by Monod and Sherrer 1967, later by Rohmert
27	1968). Verified against the page image (Fig 4.14, printed p. 227, finger flexors, based on
28	Petrofsky 1980): endurance time falls hyperbolically as %MVC (maximum voluntary contraction)
29	rises, and females sustain the same tension level for longer than males at every tension
30	level tested, a difference the authors say "has not been adequately explained yet." Muscle
31	temperature also affects isometric endurance: hot packs reduce it and pre-exercise icing
32	increases it, with an optimum core muscle temperature (later work places it near 27-28
33	Celsius, Petrofsky & Phillips, 1986) above and below which endurance drops; higher bodyfat
34	percentage, associated with higher resting muscle temperature, is linked to lower isometric
35	endurance in most situations. Unlike dynamic exercise (which is more efficient at higher
36	temperatures, likely due to reduced tissue viscosity), isometric contraction involves no
37	fibre movement, so viscosity plays an "insignificant role compared with that of muscle
38	metabolism." Recovery from isometric contraction proceeds in three phases (Petrofsky &
39	Phillips, 1986): a rapid recovery of about 50% of endurance in the first 3 minutes; a slower
40	recovery lasting about 20 minutes, reaching about 90% of initial endurance; and complete
41	recovery within at least 24 hours; recovery from low-tension isometric contraction is
42	"interestingly" slower during the initial recovery phases. (PDF pp. 236-239, printed pp.
43	226-228, "4.2.4 Isometric Training," "Isometric Endurance," "Recovery after Isometric
44	Activity," Figs 4.13-4.14.)
45	
46	**Why it works** — The authors' stated mechanism is a mechanical-metabolic one: rising muscle
47	tension raises intramuscular pressure, which above roughly 10-15% of maximal strength begins
48	to exceed the arterial pressure available to perfuse the muscle, choking off the blood flow
49	that metabolism needs to sustain the contraction, producing the hyperbolic Rohmert-curve
50	drop in endurance. No mechanism is given for the sex difference in endurance or for the
51	27-28 Celsius optimum temperature beyond citing the studies that measured them.
52	
53	**When to apply** — Use the 10-15%-of-maximal-strength threshold as a practical dividing line
54	between "non-fatiguing" and rapidly fatiguing isometric holds when designing isometric
55	protocols (e.g. low-level postural holds versus near-maximal strength holds). Use the
56	three-phase recovery timeline (about 50% back in 3 minutes, about 90% back in 20 minutes,
57	full recovery by 24 hours) when spacing repeated maximal isometric efforts within and between
58	sessions.
59	
60	**When NOT to apply** — The intramuscular-pressure data (Fig 4.13) are from electrically
61	stimulated cat soleus and gastrocnemius (Petrofsky & Hendershot, 1984), not human voluntary
62	contraction; treat the specific kPa values as animal-model data illustrating the
63	tension-pressure relationship, not human norms. The Rohmert-curve endurance data (Fig 4.14)
64	are specifically finger-flexor endurance (Petrofsky, 1980), a small, distal muscle group;
65	the shape of the curve (hyperbolic decline, female advantage) should not be assumed to hold
66	identically for large, proximal muscle groups without separate verification. The 27-28
67	Celsius optimum-temperature finding and the bodyfat-endurance link are each from single
68	cited sources without reported effect sizes.
69	
70	**Example** — Inference: a coach prescribing a sustained postural isometric hold (e.g. a
71	plank or wall-sit at low relative intensity) can expect it to be comparatively non-fatiguing
72	per the 10-15%-of-maximum threshold, while a near-maximal isometric mid-thigh pull hold will
73	fatigue rapidly and require the multi-minute recovery windows this entry describes before a
74	comparable maximal effort can be repeated.
75	
76	**Related** — [[heuristic--isometric-training-execution-protocol-and-advantages-drawbacks]],
77	[[principle--breath-holding-and-valsalva-support-spinal-stability-in-maximal-lifting]] (Ch3,
78	a related discussion of intramuscular/intrathoracic pressure during sustained maximal
79	effort).

# Isometric Endurance Collapses Above 10-15% of Maximal Tension, and Recovers in Three Distinct Phases

**What it is** — Isometric endurance at resistance exceeding 10-15% of a muscle's maximal
strength is very short compared with dynamic exercise, because of metabolic demand and
impaired blood flow to the exercising muscle under sustained contraction (Petrofsky &
Phillips, 1986); below that threshold, contractions are considered non-fatiguing, since
intramuscular pressure stays low and is readily exceeded by rising mean arterial pressure in
the capillaries. Verified against the page image (Fig 4.13, printed p. 227, cat soleus and
gastrocnemius, electrically stimulated, based on Petrofsky & Hendershot, 1984): intramuscular
pressure rises roughly linearly with muscle tension, from near 0 kPa at rest to over 20 kPa
at 100% of maximal strength. As tension rises, intramuscular pressure rises with it and
metabolism cannot keep pace, producing a hyperbolic drop in performance and marked fatigue
increase (the Rohmert curve, first derived by Monod and Sherrer 1967, later by Rohmert
1968). Verified against the page image (Fig 4.14, printed p. 227, finger flexors, based on
Petrofsky 1980): endurance time falls hyperbolically as %MVC (maximum voluntary contraction)
rises, and females sustain the same tension level for longer than males at every tension
level tested, a difference the authors say "has not been adequately explained yet." Muscle
temperature also affects isometric endurance: hot packs reduce it and pre-exercise icing
increases it, with an optimum core muscle temperature (later work places it near 27-28
Celsius, Petrofsky & Phillips, 1986) above and below which endurance drops; higher bodyfat
percentage, associated with higher resting muscle temperature, is linked to lower isometric
endurance in most situations. Unlike dynamic exercise (which is more efficient at higher
temperatures, likely due to reduced tissue viscosity), isometric contraction involves no
fibre movement, so viscosity plays an "insignificant role compared with that of muscle
metabolism." Recovery from isometric contraction proceeds in three phases (Petrofsky &
Phillips, 1986): a rapid recovery of about 50% of endurance in the first 3 minutes; a slower
recovery lasting about 20 minutes, reaching about 90% of initial endurance; and complete
recovery within at least 24 hours; recovery from low-tension isometric contraction is
"interestingly" slower during the initial recovery phases. (PDF pp. 236-239, printed pp.
226-228, "4.2.4 Isometric Training," "Isometric Endurance," "Recovery after Isometric
Activity," Figs 4.13-4.14.)

**Why it works** — The authors' stated mechanism is a mechanical-metabolic one: rising muscle
tension raises intramuscular pressure, which above roughly 10-15% of maximal strength begins
to exceed the arterial pressure available to perfuse the muscle, choking off the blood flow
that metabolism needs to sustain the contraction, producing the hyperbolic Rohmert-curve
drop in endurance. No mechanism is given for the sex difference in endurance or for the
27-28 Celsius optimum temperature beyond citing the studies that measured them.

**When to apply** — Use the 10-15%-of-maximal-strength threshold as a practical dividing line
between "non-fatiguing" and rapidly fatiguing isometric holds when designing isometric
protocols (e.g. low-level postural holds versus near-maximal strength holds). Use the
three-phase recovery timeline (about 50% back in 3 minutes, about 90% back in 20 minutes,
full recovery by 24 hours) when spacing repeated maximal isometric efforts within and between
sessions.

**When NOT to apply** — The intramuscular-pressure data (Fig 4.13) are from electrically
stimulated cat soleus and gastrocnemius (Petrofsky & Hendershot, 1984), not human voluntary
contraction; treat the specific kPa values as animal-model data illustrating the
tension-pressure relationship, not human norms. The Rohmert-curve endurance data (Fig 4.14)
are specifically finger-flexor endurance (Petrofsky, 1980), a small, distal muscle group;
the shape of the curve (hyperbolic decline, female advantage) should not be assumed to hold
identically for large, proximal muscle groups without separate verification. The 27-28
Celsius optimum-temperature finding and the bodyfat-endurance link are each from single
cited sources without reported effect sizes.

**Example** — Inference: a coach prescribing a sustained postural isometric hold (e.g. a
plank or wall-sit at low relative intensity) can expect it to be comparatively non-fatiguing
per the 10-15%-of-maximum threshold, while a near-maximal isometric mid-thigh pull hold will
fatigue rapidly and require the multi-minute recovery windows this entry describes before a
comparable maximal effort can be repeated.

**Related** — [[heuristic--isometric-training-execution-protocol-and-advantages-drawbacks]],
[[principle--breath-holding-and-valsalva-support-spinal-stability-in-maximal-lifting]] (Ch3,
a related discussion of intramuscular/intrathoracic pressure during sustained maximal
effort).

13	
14	# Isometric Strength Gains Spread Further From the Training Angle When the Muscle Trains in a Lengthened Position
15	
16	**What it is** — Many studies report isometric training producing maximum strength gains at
17	or very close to the trained joint angle, leading some athletes to avoid isometric training
18	altogether; the authors argue this "angular specificity" framing needs critical revision,
19	citing other studies showing isometric training also produces significant strength increase
20	up to about 15 degrees either side of the training angle. Because every type of muscle
21	contraction has its own force/torque-versus-joint-angle curve (see 2.1.2), the authors argue
22	it is "highly unlikely" that strength gain would be confined to one precise angle and
23	nowhere else, and prefer the term "regional specificity" over "angular specificity" (or
24	muscle-length specificity). Thepault-Mathieu et al (1988) found this regional specificity is
25	strongest when the muscle trains in its most shortened position and weakest when it trains
26	most lengthened: males training isometrically for 5 weeks (5 sets of 5 reps, 5 seconds each,
27	3 times weekly) at 25 degrees of elbow flexion (full extension = 0 degrees) gained 54%
28	strength at the training angle but only about 25% averaged over the rest of the range; a
29	group training at 80 degrees gained 30% at the training angle and about 25% over the rest of
30	the range; a group training at 120 degrees gained 25% at the training angle but only about
31	7% over the rest of the range. The authors' summary: isometric training of a relatively
32	lengthened muscle can produce substantial strength increase "not only near the region of
33	training, but also throughout the range of movement." They caution this finding should not
34	be read as meaning isometric training can replace other strength-training forms, since a
35	specific type of static or dynamic strength depends on the neuromuscular factors governing
36	how force is exerted in a given situation. (PDF pp. 237-238, printed pp. 226-227, "4.2.4
37	Isometric Training," "Isometric Training and Angular Specificity.")
38	
39	**Why it works** — The authors give the biomechanical basis (a distinct force/torque-vs-angle
40	curve exists for every contraction type) for why strict single-angle specificity is
41	implausible, but they do not give a mechanism for why the Thepault-Mathieu et al (1988)
42	lengthened-position condition specifically produced the broadest transfer across the range
43	(54%/25 degrees training angle giving about 25% elsewhere, versus 120 degrees training angle
44	giving only about 7% elsewhere). Inference: a plausible explanation, not stated in the text,
45	is that training at longer muscle lengths recruits a different or broader distribution of
46	sarcomere lengths and joint-angle-dependent moment arms than training at a shortened length,
47	though this is not confirmed by the source.
48	
49	**When to apply** — Use this as a rationale for choosing a relatively lengthened joint
50	position when isometric training is intended to transfer strength gains across a wider
51	portion of the range of motion, rather than assuming isometric work only strengthens the
52	exact trained angle. Use the "regional specificity" framing, not "angular specificity," when
53	discussing isometric training's carryover with coaches or athletes.
54	
55	**When NOT to apply** — This is a single study (Thepault-Mathieu et al, 1988) with a specific
56	protocol (5 weeks, 5x5 at 5 seconds, 3x weekly, elbow flexion only) and three training
57	angles; the specific percentages (54%, 30%, 25% at-angle gains; roughly 25%, 25%, 7%
58	remainder-of-range gains) should not be generalised to other joints, muscle groups, or
59	protocols without direct testing. The authors' own caution stands: this finding does not
60	mean isometric training can substitute for dynamic strength training generally.
61	
62	**Example** — The book's own example is the Thepault-Mathieu et al (1988) three-group study
63	described above; no further invented example is added here.
64	
65	**Related** — [[claim--hettinger-muller-isometric-strength-gain-rate]],
66	[[claim--joint-angle-specific-strength-training-narrows-transfer]] (Ch2, a related but
67	broader claim about joint-angle transfer that this entry's regional-specificity nuance
68	qualifies).
69

# Isometric Strength Gains Spread Further From the Training Angle When the Muscle Trains in a Lengthened Position

**What it is** — Many studies report isometric training producing maximum strength gains at
or very close to the trained joint angle, leading some athletes to avoid isometric training
altogether; the authors argue this "angular specificity" framing needs critical revision,
citing other studies showing isometric training also produces significant strength increase
up to about 15 degrees either side of the training angle. Because every type of muscle
contraction has its own force/torque-versus-joint-angle curve (see 2.1.2), the authors argue
it is "highly unlikely" that strength gain would be confined to one precise angle and
nowhere else, and prefer the term "regional specificity" over "angular specificity" (or
muscle-length specificity). Thepault-Mathieu et al (1988) found this regional specificity is
strongest when the muscle trains in its most shortened position and weakest when it trains
most lengthened: males training isometrically for 5 weeks (5 sets of 5 reps, 5 seconds each,
3 times weekly) at 25 degrees of elbow flexion (full extension = 0 degrees) gained 54%
strength at the training angle but only about 25% averaged over the rest of the range; a
group training at 80 degrees gained 30% at the training angle and about 25% over the rest of
the range; a group training at 120 degrees gained 25% at the training angle but only about
7% over the rest of the range. The authors' summary: isometric training of a relatively
lengthened muscle can produce substantial strength increase "not only near the region of
training, but also throughout the range of movement." They caution this finding should not
be read as meaning isometric training can replace other strength-training forms, since a
specific type of static or dynamic strength depends on the neuromuscular factors governing
how force is exerted in a given situation. (PDF pp. 237-238, printed pp. 226-227, "4.2.4
Isometric Training," "Isometric Training and Angular Specificity.")

**Why it works** — The authors give the biomechanical basis (a distinct force/torque-vs-angle
curve exists for every contraction type) for why strict single-angle specificity is
implausible, but they do not give a mechanism for why the Thepault-Mathieu et al (1988)
lengthened-position condition specifically produced the broadest transfer across the range
(54%/25 degrees training angle giving about 25% elsewhere, versus 120 degrees training angle
giving only about 7% elsewhere). Inference: a plausible explanation, not stated in the text,
is that training at longer muscle lengths recruits a different or broader distribution of
sarcomere lengths and joint-angle-dependent moment arms than training at a shortened length,
though this is not confirmed by the source.

**When to apply** — Use this as a rationale for choosing a relatively lengthened joint
position when isometric training is intended to transfer strength gains across a wider
portion of the range of motion, rather than assuming isometric work only strengthens the
exact trained angle. Use the "regional specificity" framing, not "angular specificity," when
discussing isometric training's carryover with coaches or athletes.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a single study (Thepault-Mathieu et al, 1988) with a specific
protocol (5 weeks, 5x5 at 5 seconds, 3x weekly, elbow flexion only) and three training
angles; the specific percentages (54%, 30%, 25% at-angle gains; roughly 25%, 25%, 7%
remainder-of-range gains) should not be generalised to other joints, muscle groups, or
protocols without direct testing. The authors' own caution stands: this finding does not
mean isometric training can substitute for dynamic strength training generally.

**Example** — The book's own example is the Thepault-Mathieu et al (1988) three-group study
described above; no further invented example is added here.

**Related** — [[claim--hettinger-muller-isometric-strength-gain-rate]],
[[claim--joint-angle-specific-strength-training-narrows-transfer]] (Ch2, a related but
broader claim about joint-angle transfer that this entry's regional-specificity nuance
qualifies).

15	
16	**What it is** — The authors argue isometric training is not simply holding a static
17	contraction for a set time: a true isometric contraction requires the muscle to raise
18	tension from rest to a maximal or sub-maximal value over a rise ("attack") time, sustain
19	that tension for a resistance phase, then decrease it to rest or a lower value over a decay
20	time. Verified against the page image (Fig 4.11, printed p. 225): the authors categorise
21	isometric contraction into voluntary isometrics (splitting further into slow isometrics and

24	produced deliberately; a reflexive one occurs involuntarily via the muscle's reflex response
25	between the eccentric and concentric phases of plyometric activities such as a depth jump or
26	the weightlifting clean-and-jerk. Verified against the page image (Fig 4.12, printed p.
27	225): slow isometrics show a gradual force rise, a longer resistance-phase plateau, and a
28	gradual decay; explosive (reflexive) isometrics show a much steeper rise phase and a
29	substantially shorter resistance phase before decay. The authors argue that because the
30	steepness of the isometric force-time curve, and the higher magnitude of maximum isometric
31	versus dynamic maximum force at equivalent joint angles, both support developing explosive
32	strength isometrically when the training accent is on speed of force development, "it is
33	doubtful whether it is always productive to maintain a rigid distinction between dynamic and
34	isometric exercise": as resistance grows very large, dynamic work becomes progressively more
35	isometric, so isometric work is "really the limiting case of dynamic work as the velocity of
36	movement tends to zero." Because reflexive isometric contraction bypasses the inhibitory
37	effects normally associated with voluntary muscle action, "even greater explosive force can
38	be displayed isometrically than dynamically." A related but separate finding on impulsive
39	loading: short bouts of low-frequency mechanical vibration (10-35 Hz) applied to the body
40	have been shown to speed recovery, modulate muscle activity, raise strength/power stable
41	state, lower arterial pressure and enhance oxidative processes (Kopysov, 1978; Lebedev &
42	Peliakov, 1991), and whole-body vibration at 26 Hz through the lower extremities has been
43	shown to produce marked increases in jumping power (Bosco et al, 1998); the authors note
44	this fuels an open debate about whether plyometric training effects are driven mainly by
45	elastic-energy storage/release, neural facilitation, or intrinsic muscle changes (Ingen
46	Schenau et al, 1997). (PDF pp. 235-236, printed pp. 224-225, "4.2.4 Isometric Training,"
47	Figs 4.11-4.12.)
48	
49	**Why it works** — The authors' mechanism for the voluntary/reflexive distinction is neural:
50	reflexive isometric contraction (occurring automatically between eccentric and concentric
51	phases) escapes voluntary inhibitory control that would otherwise limit force, permitting
52	higher force display than a deliberately initiated voluntary contraction can achieve.
53	Inference: the slow-vs-explosive distinction within each category follows from how quickly
54	neural drive ramps up to the target tension level, which the force-time curve shape (Fig
55	4.12) captures directly.
56	
57	**When to apply** — Use this taxonomy when specifying what kind of isometric work a given
58	drill is training: a sustained maximal hold at a joint angle is a slow voluntary isometric;
59	a deliberately fast ramp to near-maximal tension is a voluntary explosive isometric; the
60	brief isometric moment at the bottom of a depth jump or clean-and-jerk catch is a reflexive
61	(explosive or oscillatory) isometric that the athlete does not consciously initiate. Per the
62	authors, distinguish "isometric training for developing absolute strength" from "isometric
63	training for developing explosive strength" and select the appropriate type for the goal.
64	
65	**When NOT to apply** — The authors themselves flag this distinction as still needing
66	"detailed experimental corroboration." The vibration/whole-body-vibration findings are a
67	separate line of evidence (Bosco et al, 1998, and others) that the authors connect to this
68	discussion only by analogy (impulsive loading), not by stating vibration produces isometric
69	contraction in the sense defined here; treat the two topics as related but distinct.
70	
71	**Example** — The book's own example is the depth-jump and clean-and-jerk catch positions
72	cited as sources of reflexive isometric contraction; no further invented example is added
73	here.
74

14	# External vs Internal Isometrics, and Using a Held Supramaximal Load to Prime the Nervous System
15	
16	**What it is** — The authors distinguish "external isometrics" (contraction exerted against
17	an external load) from "internal isometrics" (contraction exerted against opposing muscles
18	within the body, as in bodybuilders' posing actions; see
19	[[heuristic--loadless-training-broomstick-protocol]]). Isometric contractions can be
20	submaximal or maximal, short or long duration, continuous or intermittent, sequenced across
21	different joint angles, alternated between agonist and antagonist (or adductor/abductor,
22	medial/lateral rotators), and alternated between intensities, including voluntary
23	oscillation between high and low intensity to prolong the total time under tension. A
24	separate practical technique: isometrically holding a heavy load at a "sticking point" can
25	reduce deficiencies in that region or prime the nervous system to cope with greater loading
26	during gradual progressive overload; the authors' specific example is supporting a
27	supramaximal load (120-150% of 1RM) on the shoulders, or performing quasi-isometric movement
28	over the first few degrees of knee flexion in a squat, to "accustom the body neuromuscularly
29	and favourably enhance one's mental perception" for handling future loads only slightly
30	heavier than the current 1RM. The authors also state that isometric contraction released
31	explosively "can decrease the reaction response time by as much as 7%, particularly if
32	associated with a strong pre-stretch," against the traditional coaching belief that
33	movement is most efficient starting from complete relaxation; Verkhoshansky is cited as
34	stressing that a movement produced from complete relaxation is usually slower and less
35	forceful than one that begins from some prior tension. Historically, isometric effort was
36	emphasised heavily by DeLorme, Hettinger and Muller, but with the rise of gymnasium machines
37	and the decline of Charles Atlas's mail-order "dynamic tension" programmes, isometrics
38	largely fell out of popular use, though physical therapists still use it in early
39	injury-rehabilitation stages, and Russian coaches often prescribe a 75% concentric / 15%
40	eccentric / 10% isometric strength-training regime for the average athlete. The authors also
41	note that because one basic PNF principle holds that mobility (dynamic contraction) is more
42	primitive than stability (isometric contraction), stability sits at a "higher level of
43	muscular learning." (PDF pp. 239-240, printed pp. 228-229, "4.2.4 Isometric Training,"
44	"Other Aspects of Isometric Activity.")
45	
46	**Why it works** — For the reaction-time claim, the mechanism given is that reflexive
47	isometric contraction bypasses voluntary inhibition (already stated for explosive isometrics
48	generally, see
49	[[framework--isometric-contraction-categorization-voluntary-reflexive]]), and a strong
50	pre-stretch potentiates this further. For supramaximal holding, no cellular mechanism is
51	given; the stated effect is psychological/neuromuscular familiarisation ("accustom the body
52	neuromuscularly," "favourably enhance one's mental perception") rather than a measured
53	strength-transfer pathway.
54	
55	**When to apply** — Use the external/internal isometrics distinction as vocabulary when
56	specifying whether a drill uses an external load or purely internal agonist-antagonist
57	tensing. Use supramaximal-hold priming (120-150% of 1RM support holds, or partial-range
58	quasi-isometric squat work) as a technique to familiarise an athlete with loads slightly
59	above their current 1RM before attempting a true max attempt. Use the 75/15/10
60	concentric/eccentric/isometric regime as a citable, if dated, historical reference point when
61	discussing how much isometric work a general strength programme might include.
62	
63	**When NOT to apply** — The 7% reaction-time figure and the supramaximal-holding
64	familiarisation effect are stated without reported sample sizes or controlled outcome data
65	in this passage; treat them as the authors' summarised claims, not independently verified
66	percentages. The 75/15/10 regime is attributed generally to "Russian coaches" without a
67	specific citation, so treat it as a reported convention rather than an experimentally
68	validated ratio. Supramaximal holding (120-150% of 1RM) carries obvious injury risk if
69	attempted without adequate rack/spotter safety and should not be treated as a routine
70	prescription without those safeguards, which this passage does not itself discuss.
71	
72	**Example** — Inference: a lifter approaching a new back-squat 1RM attempt could support a
73	supramaximal load (say, 110-120% of the projected new max) in the rack for a brief hold
74	beforehand, per this heuristic's priming logic, to build familiarity with that load level
75	before the actual max attempt; the specific 110-120% figure here is an adapted illustration,
76	not the source's own 120-150% number.
77

79	[[framework--isometric-contraction-categorization-voluntary-reflexive]],
80	[[heuristic--isometric-training-execution-protocol-and-advantages-drawbacks]].
