14	# Isometric Training's Six Advantages, Six Drawbacks, and the Authors' Recommended Execution Protocol
15	
16	**What it is** — The authors list six advantages proponents claim for isometric training:
17	(1) it requires very simple apparatus; (2) it can locally exercise any muscle group at a
18	specific joint angle, which dynamic work can only briefly pass through, since movement
19	inertia usually carries the load past the angle of greatest mechanical effect; (3) it is
20	time-productive, since each 6-second isometric contraction is "equivalent in its effect" to
21	many dynamic ballistic contractions in which maximal force lasts no more than 0.1 second,
22	meaning 10 minutes of targeted isometric tension can replace "a fatiguing hour" of dynamic
23	weight training; (4) it produces an insignificant increase in muscle mass and bodymass
24	compared with dynamic strength work, particularly pressing exercises; (5) it costs far less
25	time and energy than dynamic weight training, letting an athlete preserve a high
26	speed-strength level during a crucial competition period; (6) it offers more potential than
27	dynamic exercise for using visual and kinaesthetic cues to hold a given position, an
28	advantage for studying and correcting technical errors. Six drawbacks are also listed:
29	isometrics fatigue the nervous system; may harm the cardiovascular system in some
30	individuals via prolonged breath-holding and elevated blood pressure; disturb coordination;
31	enhance muscle performance only near the specific trained joint angle; decrease speed of
32	movement; and diminish soft-tissue elasticity and functional range of dynamic movement.
33	Proper breathing, adequate rest/relaxation between exercises, and limiting contraction length
34	to 6 seconds (some authors recommend up to 10) can minimise these harmful after-effects. The
35	authors give four methods of producing isometric tension: (1) pressing against an immovable
36	structure or a partner's resistance, with the drawback that strength change can only be
37	judged subjectively without a dynamometer; (2) holding a raised load for a set period, with a
38	quasi-isometric variant shifting the load slowly across the range with stops at different
39	joint angles; (3) pushing a weight from a lower support up to press against an upper stop
40	(a power rack), giving a brief dynamic phase before the isometric hold and letting the
41	athlete lift several times between stops; (4) using a dynamometer or other resistance
42	device to control and display tension magnitude. For non-explosive isometrics, the authors
43	give a specific protocol: apply force gradually, hold maximal tension no longer than 8
44	seconds, perform 6 repetitions, rest 5-10 seconds between reps, limit total isometric
45	training to 10 minutes per session, and finish with relaxation exercises; for developing
46	explosive strength instead, tension should be generated at maximum speed to 70-80% of
47	maximum strength, and reflexive explosive isometric action from plyometric movements "can be
48	extremely effective" for this. (PDF pp. 236-237, printed pp. 225-226, "4.2.4 Isometric
49	Training.")
50	
51	**Why it works** — The authors give a specific mechanism only for advantage (2), regarding
52	joint-angle specificity of loading, and advantage (3), the time-efficiency claim, which rests
53	on comparing sustained near-maximal isometric tension duration against the brief (about 0.1
54	second) duration of maximal force during a ballistic dynamic contraction. Inference: the
55	remaining advantages and drawbacks are stated as observations rather than derived from a
56	single unifying mechanism.
57	
58	**When to apply** — Use the 8-second hold, 6-repetition, 5-10-second-rest, 10-minute-session
59	protocol as the authors' recommended baseline for non-explosive isometric training aimed at
60	absolute strength, and the 70-80%-max, maximum-speed protocol for explosive-strength-focused
61	isometric work. Weigh the six advantages against the six drawbacks for a given athlete and
62	context: the cardiovascular caution (drawback 2) is particularly relevant for athletes with
63	existing cardiovascular risk factors, and the coordination-disturbance and range-of-movement
64	drawbacks argue for pairing isometric work with dynamic training rather than using it as a
65	sole training means.
66	
67	**When NOT to apply** — This protocol and these advantages/drawbacks are the authors' own
68	synthesis from an era (1950s-1970s citations) predating modern force-plate or dynamometer-based
69	isometric dosing research; do not treat the "equivalent to a fatiguing hour of training"
70	comparison (advantage 3) as a rigorously measured equivalence, since no controlled outcome
71	comparison is cited for that specific claim. The drawbacks (cardiovascular risk, coordination
72	disturbance, reduced movement speed, reduced tissue elasticity) argue against using isometric
73	training as an athlete's sole or dominant training means, per the authors' own framing.
74	
75	**Example** — Inference: a coach using isometric mid-thigh pulls to reinforce a specific
76	sticking-point joint angle is applying advantage (2) directly; the same coach should still
77	program dynamic work elsewhere in the week to offset the coordination and movement-speed

# Isometric Training's Six Advantages, Six Drawbacks, and the Authors' Recommended Execution Protocol

**What it is** — The authors list six advantages proponents claim for isometric training:
(1) it requires very simple apparatus; (2) it can locally exercise any muscle group at a
specific joint angle, which dynamic work can only briefly pass through, since movement
inertia usually carries the load past the angle of greatest mechanical effect; (3) it is
time-productive, since each 6-second isometric contraction is "equivalent in its effect" to
many dynamic ballistic contractions in which maximal force lasts no more than 0.1 second,
meaning 10 minutes of targeted isometric tension can replace "a fatiguing hour" of dynamic
weight training; (4) it produces an insignificant increase in muscle mass and bodymass
compared with dynamic strength work, particularly pressing exercises; (5) it costs far less
time and energy than dynamic weight training, letting an athlete preserve a high
speed-strength level during a crucial competition period; (6) it offers more potential than
dynamic exercise for using visual and kinaesthetic cues to hold a given position, an
advantage for studying and correcting technical errors. Six drawbacks are also listed:
isometrics fatigue the nervous system; may harm the cardiovascular system in some
individuals via prolonged breath-holding and elevated blood pressure; disturb coordination;
enhance muscle performance only near the specific trained joint angle; decrease speed of
movement; and diminish soft-tissue elasticity and functional range of dynamic movement.
Proper breathing, adequate rest/relaxation between exercises, and limiting contraction length
to 6 seconds (some authors recommend up to 10) can minimise these harmful after-effects. The
authors give four methods of producing isometric tension: (1) pressing against an immovable
structure or a partner's resistance, with the drawback that strength change can only be
judged subjectively without a dynamometer; (2) holding a raised load for a set period, with a
quasi-isometric variant shifting the load slowly across the range with stops at different
joint angles; (3) pushing a weight from a lower support up to press against an upper stop
(a power rack), giving a brief dynamic phase before the isometric hold and letting the
athlete lift several times between stops; (4) using a dynamometer or other resistance
device to control and display tension magnitude. For non-explosive isometrics, the authors
give a specific protocol: apply force gradually, hold maximal tension no longer than 8
seconds, perform 6 repetitions, rest 5-10 seconds between reps, limit total isometric
training to 10 minutes per session, and finish with relaxation exercises; for developing
explosive strength instead, tension should be generated at maximum speed to 70-80% of
maximum strength, and reflexive explosive isometric action from plyometric movements "can be
extremely effective" for this. (PDF pp. 236-237, printed pp. 225-226, "4.2.4 Isometric
Training.")

**Why it works** — The authors give a specific mechanism only for advantage (2), regarding
joint-angle specificity of loading, and advantage (3), the time-efficiency claim, which rests
on comparing sustained near-maximal isometric tension duration against the brief (about 0.1
second) duration of maximal force during a ballistic dynamic contraction. Inference: the
remaining advantages and drawbacks are stated as observations rather than derived from a
single unifying mechanism.

**When to apply** — Use the 8-second hold, 6-repetition, 5-10-second-rest, 10-minute-session
protocol as the authors' recommended baseline for non-explosive isometric training aimed at
absolute strength, and the 70-80%-max, maximum-speed protocol for explosive-strength-focused
isometric work. Weigh the six advantages against the six drawbacks for a given athlete and
context: the cardiovascular caution (drawback 2) is particularly relevant for athletes with
existing cardiovascular risk factors, and the coordination-disturbance and range-of-movement
drawbacks argue for pairing isometric work with dynamic training rather than using it as a
sole training means.

**When NOT to apply** — This protocol and these advantages/drawbacks are the authors' own
synthesis from an era (1950s-1970s citations) predating modern force-plate or dynamometer-based
isometric dosing research; do not treat the "equivalent to a fatiguing hour of training"
comparison (advantage 3) as a rigorously measured equivalence, since no controlled outcome
comparison is cited for that specific claim. The drawbacks (cardiovascular risk, coordination
disturbance, reduced movement speed, reduced tissue elasticity) argue against using isometric
training as an athlete's sole or dominant training means, per the authors' own framing.

**Example** — Inference: a coach using isometric mid-thigh pulls to reinforce a specific
sticking-point joint angle is applying advantage (2) directly; the same coach should still
program dynamic work elsewhere in the week to offset the coordination and movement-speed
drawbacks this entry lists.

the cardiovascular/breath-holding caution this entry's drawback 2 overlaps with).

14	# Loadless Training: Tensing Muscles Maximally Against an Unloaded Broomstick to Train Without Equipment
15	
16	**What it is** — "Loadless training" (the Russian term; bodybuilders call the related
17	practice "posing" training) has an athlete voluntarily tense agonists and antagonists
18	maximally at every joint without an external load, imitating a loaded lift's demand through
19	mental effort and tension alone. In the early 1900s Anokhin and Froshek proposed developing
20	strength through motivated tensing of agonists and antagonists at every joint, similar to
21	bodybuilders tensing before judges, but the technique was not studied scientifically until
22	after 1965. Kovalik (1978) ran a doctoral thesis on this "voluntary loadless muscle tensing,"
23	aiming to develop a supplementary training system imposing less joint stress than weight
24	training, particularly for younger lifters whose skeletal systems have not matured. His
25	subjects performed Olympic and supplementary lifts (e.g. snatch pull, front squat) with a
26	broomstick while trying to generate maximum muscle tension as if overcoming a maximal
27	weight; this produced definite muscle strengthening and technical-skill improvement, but
28	Kovalik concluded it must be used cautiously in Olympic weightlifting because it might
29	disrupt optimal extensor-flexor strength ratios. Loadless training is described as
30	especially useful without access to training facilities or during recovery from
31	musculoskeletal injury, and can be performed isometrically (joint held at a specific angle),
32	quasi-isometrically (joint moved powerfully through a full range), or dynamically
33	(imitating a weight-training movement with unloaded muscular tension against a broomstick).
34	Kovalik's recommended protocol: 5 sets per exercise, separated by 3-10 seconds of rest;
35	during quasi-isometric loadless training, avoid long periods of intense breath-holding and
36	instead exhale slowly in synchrony with the slow tensing of each movement; each movement
37	should involve strong simultaneous tension in agonists and antagonists, starting from full
38	extension and ending with stretching beyond full extension and back, over 10-15 seconds; the
39	holding phase at the end of each movement (e.g. the overhead jerk position) should be held
40	with maximal tension for 6-8 seconds; rotating joints in different planes and moving limbs
41	in diagonal/spiral patterns follows PNF principles and can enhance loadless training's
42	effectiveness as a supplementary strengthening method. (PDF pp. 240-241, printed pp.
43	229-230, "4.2.4 Isometric Training," "Loadless Training.")
44	
45	**Why it works** — No cellular mechanism is given beyond the general isometric/quasi-isometric
46	tension logic already stated for the chapter; the authors' stated rationale for loadless
47	training's specific value is reduced joint stress compared with weight training (relevant
48	for immature skeletons or injury recovery) and portability (no equipment required). The
49	caution about disrupting extensor-flexor ratios implies that voluntary tensing without an
50	external load and its accompanying proprioceptive feedback may not reproduce the same
51	relative muscle-group demand as loaded lifting.
52	
53	**When to apply** — Use loadless training as a supplementary strengthening tool when
54	equipment is unavailable (e.g. travel) or during early-stage musculoskeletal injury
55	recovery, and specifically for younger or skeletally immature lifters where reduced joint
56	loading is a priority. Follow Kovalik's protocol details (5 sets, 3-10s rest, slow
57	exhalation during quasi-isometric tensing, 10-15s per movement, 6-8s holding phase) as the
58	authors' cited baseline.
59	
60	**When NOT to apply** — Kovalik's own caution applies directly: use loadless training
61	cautiously in competitive Olympic weightlifting programming specifically, since it may
62	disrupt the optimal extensor-flexor strength ratio the sport requires. This is a single
63	doctoral thesis (Kovalik, 1978) without reported sample size or a control condition compared
64	against standard weight training in this passage; treat it as a supplementary method, not a
65	substitute for loaded resistance training.
66	
67	**Example** — The book's own example is Kovalik's protocol described above (broomstick
68	snatch pull and front squat, maximal tension, 5 sets); no further invented example is added
69	here.
70	
71	**Related** — [[heuristic--isometric-training-execution-protocol-and-advantages-drawbacks]],
72	[[heuristic--isometric-priming-and-external-internal-classification]].

14	# Eccentric Training Damages Tissue and Causes Soreness at First, but Adaptation Removes Both Without Losing the Strength Gain
15	
16	**What it is** — Because the muscle complex lengthens under eccentric contraction, its series
17	elastic component (SEC) is exposed to greater strain than under concentric conditions,
18	raising injury potential; most muscle strains and ruptures occur during the eccentric phase
19	of movement (Garrett, 1986). A single session of intense eccentric exercise commonly causes
20	pronounced delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS), peaking 24-72 hours after exercise and
21	resolving within several days (Friden et al, 1983a), accompanied by reduced dynamic strength
22	and damage to myofibrils and connective-tissue elements such as the Z bands (a SEC
23	component). Friden et al (1983b) also examined longer eccentric-training exposure (3
24	sessions weekly over 8 weeks total) and found post-exercise soreness stopped occurring after
25	2-3 weeks, while the ability to perform eccentric work increased by 375%; biopsies showed no
26	Z-band damage at that point, suggesting adaptation had occurred (the repeated-bout effect).
27	Schwane and Armstrong (1983) corroborated this with downhill running in rats, which produced
28	a superior training effect to level or uphill running and prevented injury more effectively
29	over time. Eccentric exercise is known to produce greater and more rapid strength and
30	hypertrophy increases than concentric exercise (Hortobagyi et al, 2000), and it is sometimes
31	suggested this stems from eccentric exercise's greater tissue damage; however, Komulainen et
32	al (2000) found the increase in myofibrillar cross-sectional area in unchanged (non-damaged)
33	muscle fibres was much the same after concentric exercise as after the more damaging
34	eccentric exercise, a result the authors say "do not support the hypothesis that fibre
35	hypertrophy depends on the extent of the fibre damage in exercised muscles." (PDF pp.
36	241-242, printed pp. 230-231, "4.2.5 Eccentric Training.")
37	
38	**Why it works** — For the soreness/damage mechanism, the stated pathway is mechanical:
39	eccentric lengthening strains the SEC (including the Z bands) more than concentric
40	shortening does, producing microdamage that manifests as DOMS. For the repeated-bout
41	adaptation, no cellular mechanism is given beyond the biopsy finding that Z-band damage no
42	longer occurs after 2-3 weeks of repeated exposure; Inference: this is consistent with a
43	protective structural or neural adaptation (increased sarcomere number in series, improved
44	motor-unit recruitment patterns, or connective-tissue remodelling) that the text does not
45	itself specify. For the Hortobagyi-versus-Komulainen tension, the authors present Komulainen
46	et al's finding as evidence against a damage-drives-hypertrophy causal model, without
47	proposing an alternative mechanism for why eccentric training produces faster
48	strength/hypertrophy gains if not primarily through greater damage.
49	
50	**When to apply** — Use the repeated-bout effect (soreness and Z-band damage both disappear
51	within 2-3 weeks of regular eccentric exposure, while eccentric work capacity rises sharply,
52	here 375% in 8 weeks) as the rationale for introducing eccentric-emphasis training
53	gradually and consistently rather than sporadically, to reach the adapted, lower-injury-risk
54	state faster. Use the downhill-running finding (Schwane & Armstrong, 1983) as a citable
55	rationale for progressive eccentric loading in return-to-running or tendon/muscle
56	rehabilitation programming, alongside the tendon-adaptation hypothesis already noted in
57	[[claim--eccentric-vs-concentric-training-adaptation-contradictory-findings]].
58	
59	**When NOT to apply** — The rat downhill-running data (Schwane & Armstrong, 1983) is an
60	animal model; do not assume the same magnitude of protective adaptation transfers directly
61	to human eccentric training without separate verification. The Komulainen et al (2000)
62	finding that hypertrophy does not depend on damage extent contradicts the popular
63	"damage-drives-adaptation" narrative for eccentric training; do not cite eccentric training's
64	greater soreness or damage as itself the reason to prefer it for hypertrophy, since this
65	specific study found comparable myofibrillar growth in undamaged fibres regardless of
66	contraction type. The 375% eccentric-work-capacity increase is from one study (Friden et al,
67	1983b) with a specific 8-week, 3x-weekly protocol; it measures work capacity, not maximal
68	strength specifically.
69	
70	**Example** — Inference: introducing a new eccentric-emphasis exercise (e.g. slow eccentric
71	Nordic curls) should start conservatively and progress gradually over roughly the first 2-3
72	weeks, per Friden et al's repeated-bout timeline, before expecting soreness to diminish and
73	before assuming the tissue has reached its adapted, more damage-resistant state.

13	
14	# Eccentric-Training Studies Disagree on Whether It Beats Concentric Training for Strength Gains
15	
16	**What it is** — Eccentric contraction is metabolically more efficient than concentric
17	contraction and capable of generating higher forces (Kaneko et al, 1984; Komi, 1973; Rodgers
18	& Berger, 1974), and the concentric-eccentric force gap widens as contraction velocity
19	increases: maximum eccentric force rises while maximum concentric force falls as velocity
20	increases, even though EMG for the muscle group stays reasonably constant (Komi, 1973; see
21	also [[claim--eccentric-strength-and-energetics-vs-concentric]] for the underlying
22	force/energy-cost data from Ch3). Training-adaptation findings, however, are described as
23	"often contradictory": Johnson et al (1976) found no significant difference between
24	concentric and eccentric training methods; Komi and Buskirk (1972), using an isokinetic
25	dynamometer, found eccentric training produced greater eccentric, concentric AND isometric
26	strength increases than concentric training, while concentric training increased only
27	concentric and eccentric strength; Friden et al (1983b) found eccentric training to failure
28	produced marked increases in eccentric strength-endurance but minimal change in concentric
29	strength-endurance. The high-speed, large-acceleration SMART (Seated Movement Aerobic and
30	Resistive Training, "Supersitting") system created by Lisa Ericson (1992) for work with
31	disabled populations tends to increase both concentric and eccentric strength-endurance
32	together. The authors note other researchers report adaptation differences tied to training
33	velocity, measurement velocity and the specific muscle group tested, while very few studies
34	compare functional strength and power changes across free weights, auxotonic (variable
35	resistance) activities, or natural sporting movements, concluding "the central role played
36	by the specificity principle clearly has a profound effect on the experimental analysis." A
37	separate mechanistic note: the superior eccentric strengthening seen at high isokinetic
38	velocities (over 180 degrees/second) may reflect selective tensile-strength increase in
39	tendon and other series elastic components rather than the contractile elements, with a
40	training/rehabilitation implication that high-velocity progressive-overload eccentric work
41	may build the musculotendinous junction's capacity to resist high-impact forces from
42	running, jumping and other impulsive actions. (PDF p. 241, printed p. 230, "4.2.5 Eccentric
43	Training.")
44	
45	**Why it works** — The authors give a partial mechanism for the velocity-dependent
46	concentric-eccentric force gap (already established in Ch3's force-velocity treatment, see
47	[[claim--eccentric-strength-and-energetics-vs-concentric]] and
48	[[framework--force-time-curve-adaptation-pattern-by-movement-type]]), but give no mechanism
49	reconciling why different training studies (Johnson 1976 vs Komi & Buskirk 1972 vs Friden
50	1983b) reach different conclusions about which training mode transfers best; the authors'
51	own explanation is methodological (differing velocities, populations, and measurement
52	specificity across studies), not physiological.
53	
54	**When to apply** — Inference: when deciding between eccentric-emphasis and concentric-emphasis
55	training for a given goal, treat "eccentric training is superior" as a contested claim
56	depending heavily on which outcome is measured (eccentric strength specifically tends to
57	respond best to eccentric training across these studies; broader transfer to concentric or
58	functional strength is less consistent). The high-velocity eccentric/tendon-adaptation
59	hypothesis is a plausible rationale for progressive high-velocity eccentric work in tendon
60	rehabilitation (e.g. patellar or Achilles tendinopathy), consistent with modern eccentric
61	tendon-loading protocols, though the authors do not cite such protocols directly.
62	
63	**When NOT to apply** — This entry summarises training-adaptation studies from a narrow era
64	(1972-1992) with small, heterogeneous samples and differing protocols (isokinetic dynamometer
65	training in Komi & Buskirk; training-to-failure in Friden; a seated aerobic-resistive system
66	in Ericson) that are not directly comparable to one another. Do not treat "eccentric training
67	increases concentric, eccentric and isometric strength" (Komi & Buskirk's specific finding)
68	as a settled general principle; Johnson et al (1976) found no such advantage under a
69	different protocol. The tendon-adaptation hypothesis for high-velocity eccentric work is
70	explicitly framed as a possible explanation ("may be due to"), not a confirmed mechanism.
71	
72	**Example** — Inference: a rehabilitation programme using slow, controlled eccentric squats

# Eccentric-Training Studies Disagree on Whether It Beats Concentric Training for Strength Gains

**What it is** — Eccentric contraction is metabolically more efficient than concentric
contraction and capable of generating higher forces (Kaneko et al, 1984; Komi, 1973; Rodgers
& Berger, 1974), and the concentric-eccentric force gap widens as contraction velocity
increases: maximum eccentric force rises while maximum concentric force falls as velocity
increases, even though EMG for the muscle group stays reasonably constant (Komi, 1973; see
also [[claim--eccentric-strength-and-energetics-vs-concentric]] for the underlying
force/energy-cost data from Ch3). Training-adaptation findings, however, are described as
"often contradictory": Johnson et al (1976) found no significant difference between
concentric and eccentric training methods; Komi and Buskirk (1972), using an isokinetic
dynamometer, found eccentric training produced greater eccentric, concentric AND isometric
strength increases than concentric training, while concentric training increased only
concentric and eccentric strength; Friden et al (1983b) found eccentric training to failure
produced marked increases in eccentric strength-endurance but minimal change in concentric
strength-endurance. The high-speed, large-acceleration SMART (Seated Movement Aerobic and
Resistive Training, "Supersitting") system created by Lisa Ericson (1992) for work with
disabled populations tends to increase both concentric and eccentric strength-endurance
together. The authors note other researchers report adaptation differences tied to training
velocity, measurement velocity and the specific muscle group tested, while very few studies
compare functional strength and power changes across free weights, auxotonic (variable
resistance) activities, or natural sporting movements, concluding "the central role played
by the specificity principle clearly has a profound effect on the experimental analysis." A
separate mechanistic note: the superior eccentric strengthening seen at high isokinetic
velocities (over 180 degrees/second) may reflect selective tensile-strength increase in
tendon and other series elastic components rather than the contractile elements, with a
training/rehabilitation implication that high-velocity progressive-overload eccentric work
may build the musculotendinous junction's capacity to resist high-impact forces from
running, jumping and other impulsive actions. (PDF p. 241, printed p. 230, "4.2.5 Eccentric
Training.")

**Why it works** — The authors give a partial mechanism for the velocity-dependent
concentric-eccentric force gap (already established in Ch3's force-velocity treatment, see
[[claim--eccentric-strength-and-energetics-vs-concentric]] and
[[framework--force-time-curve-adaptation-pattern-by-movement-type]]), but give no mechanism
reconciling why different training studies (Johnson 1976 vs Komi & Buskirk 1972 vs Friden
1983b) reach different conclusions about which training mode transfers best; the authors'
own explanation is methodological (differing velocities, populations, and measurement
specificity across studies), not physiological.

**When to apply** — Inference: when deciding between eccentric-emphasis and concentric-emphasis
training for a given goal, treat "eccentric training is superior" as a contested claim
depending heavily on which outcome is measured (eccentric strength specifically tends to
respond best to eccentric training across these studies; broader transfer to concentric or
functional strength is less consistent). The high-velocity eccentric/tendon-adaptation
hypothesis is a plausible rationale for progressive high-velocity eccentric work in tendon
rehabilitation (e.g. patellar or Achilles tendinopathy), consistent with modern eccentric
tendon-loading protocols, though the authors do not cite such protocols directly.

**When NOT to apply** — This entry summarises training-adaptation studies from a narrow era
(1972-1992) with small, heterogeneous samples and differing protocols (isokinetic dynamometer
training in Komi & Buskirk; training-to-failure in Friden; a seated aerobic-resistive system
in Ericson) that are not directly comparable to one another. Do not treat "eccentric training
increases concentric, eccentric and isometric strength" (Komi & Buskirk's specific finding)
as a settled general principle; Johnson et al (1976) found no such advantage under a
different protocol. The tendon-adaptation hypothesis for high-velocity eccentric work is
explicitly framed as a possible explanation ("may be due to"), not a confirmed mechanism.

**Example** — Inference: a rehabilitation programme using slow, controlled eccentric squats
for general lower-body strength is applying a different training stimulus than one using
fast, high-velocity eccentric work (over 180 degrees/second) aimed at tendon/musculotendinous
junction adaptation; per this entry, the evidence for broad strength transfer is
stronger in some cited studies than others, while the tendon-specific rationale applies
mainly to the high-velocity case.

**Related** — [[claim--eccentric-strength-and-energetics-vs-concentric]] (Ch3, the
underlying force-magnitude and energy-cost data this entry's training studies build on),
[[claim--eccentric-training-damage-adaptation-and-injury-risk-tradeoff]] (this section's
companion entry on DOMS, tissue damage and the repeated-bout effect).

14	# The Isokinetic Training Method: How It Works, and Five Advantages Claimed by Its Early Proponents
15	
16	**What it is** — The isokinetic method, popular in the USA in the late 1960s and early
17	1970s, uses a device (e.g. a centrifugal clutch or hydraulic system) that automatically
18	adjusts resistance to control movement speed and, in principle, keep a maximal load on the
19	muscles throughout the full working range; the limiting factor is movement speed, not the
20	magnitude of resistance as in weightlifting, and resistance rises as speed rises. Depending
21	on the apparatus, isokinetics may be concentric or eccentric, though most commercial
22	machines of the era offered only the concentric mode; the device's resistance
23	automatically accommodates each joint angle to the muscle's momentary capability, provided
24	the athlete sustains sufficient motivation. Counsilman (1971, 1972), an early populariser
25	for athletic training, claimed the isokinetic method's basic advantage over others is that
26	it forces maximal-effort work throughout, producing larger, faster strength increases for
27	particular actions even in very strong athletes; the authors state this specific claim "is
28	incorrect," since isokinetic force is usually lower than isometric force throughout the
29	range of joint movement, and maximal strength production is not possible under isokinetic
30	conditions. Even so, the authors report some isokinetic benefits have been corroborated in
31	specific sports (swimming, rowing) by considerable research (Chu & Smith, 1971;
32	Rosentsweig & Hinson, 1972; Hinson & Rosentsweig, 1972; Wilson, 1972), which promote five
33	advantages: (1) the device accommodates to the athlete's own capability throughout the
34	range rather than the athlete accommodating to a fixed resistance, automatically adjusting
35	for fatigue, pain or strength gain and thereby minimising injury risk; (2) prolonged warm-up
36	becomes largely unnecessary, and a demanding workout is possible in five minutes, with no
37	per-athlete adjustment needed on team equipment; (3) fewer repetitions can produce
38	significant strength gains, since each repetition loads the muscle intensively throughout
39	the full range; (4) real-time results display (computer monitor or graph) lets the athlete
40	compete against themselves or others; (5) eliminating most eccentric activity on most
41	isokinetic machines reduces post-exercise soreness. The authors caution that the studies
42	behind these five points were not conducted with top-level international athletes, and did
43	not specify training-phase context (general versus specific preparation). Several studies
44	comparing isometric, dynamic and isokinetic regimes (Thistle et al, 1967; Rosentsweig &
45	Hinson, 1972) found isokinetic exercise produced the greatest electrical (EMG) activity,
46	largest muscle hypertrophy, and most effective maintenance of strength for specific muscle
47	groups in the average person, with more significant strength gains in shorter periods and
48	shorter sessions than other regimes in laboratory studies; transfer of this effect to
49	multi-dimensional functional sporting activity, or across athletes of different
50	qualification, "has not been proved." Isokinetic training also gives limited speed
51	specificity over some ranges of sporting movement, since the trainer can control joint-action
52	speed, but cannot reproduce force-time curves matching specific sports movements. (PDF pp.
53	243-244, printed pp. 232-233, "4.2.6 Isokinetic and Other Training Means," "4.2.6.1 The
54	Isokinetic Training Method.")
55	
56	**Why it works** — The authors state the accommodating-resistance mechanism directly
57	(resistance adjusts automatically to applied force at each joint angle), but immediately
58	qualify Counsilman's stronger claim (that this guarantees superior, faster strength gains)
59	as incorrect on physiological grounds, since isokinetic force output is lower than isometric
60	force at the same joint angle throughout the range.
61	
62	**When to apply** — Use this framework's five advantages as the historical case FOR
63	isokinetic training, while treating Counsilman's "forces maximal effort throughout, superior
64	to other methods" claim as specifically refuted by the authors. Inference: the swimming and
65	rowing support cited here is consistent with isokinetics being most defensible for sports
66	whose own movements are already closer to constant-velocity through part of their range (see
67	[[heuristic--isokinetic-testing-limitations-for-functional-sport-specificity]], which notes
68	isokinetic testing/training is "non-functional, except possibly for swimmers").
69	
70	**When NOT to apply** — The cited supporting studies used non-elite athlete samples and did
71	not report training-phase context, per the authors' own caution; do not extend these
72	findings to elite/international athletes or to specific-preparation training phases without
73	separate verification. This entry's advantages should be read alongside
74	[[claim--isokinetic-devices-cannot-be-truly-isokinetic-physics-limitation]] and
75	[[heuristic--isokinetic-testing-limitations-for-functional-sport-specificity]], both of which
76	the authors use to substantially qualify how much practical value these advantages carry for
77	competitive athletes.
78	
79	**Example** — The book's own example is the swimming and rowing research cited above (Chu &
80	Smith 1971; Rosentsweig & Hinson 1972; Hinson & Rosentsweig 1972; Wilson 1972); no further
81	invented example is added here.
82

85	[[heuristic--isometric-dynamometry-misrepresents-dynamic-functional-strength]] (Ch2, a
86	related caution against inferring dynamic functional strength from isometric or isokinetic
87	dynamometer output).

14	# There Is No Single "Optimal" Quadriceps:Hamstring Ratio: It Changes With Sport, Joint Angle and Test Velocity
15	
16	**What it is** — It is often claimed the optimal quadriceps-to-hamstring strength ratio is
17	60:40, but Russian scientists found this ratio depends on the specific sport (Vorobyev,
18	1978): measured at the joint angle of greatest knee-extension torque, the ratio should be
19	nearer 80:20 for weightlifters and jumpers, while a treadmill-movement measurement gives
20	runners a ratio near 50:50. A related popular belief, that injuries become far more common
21	once left/right lower-extremity strength differs by more than 10%, is also questioned.
22	Recent research (as of the text) found neither recommendation supported by scientifically
23	controlled experiments that correct torque outputs for gravity's effect and avoid
24	stretching the hamstrings during measurement (Stephens & Reid, 1988). The
25	flexor/extensor-ratio recommendation is additionally vague because the ratio varies across
26	the joint's range of motion. Verified against the page image (Fig 4.16, printed p. 234,
27	Cybex dynamometer data at 36, 108 and 180 degrees/second): the ratio at the knee measured
28	at 80 degrees is about 75:25 at 36 degrees/second but 68:32 at 180 degrees/second; the ratio
29	equals the traditional 60:40 figure only at approximately 50 degrees of joint angle. Since
30	the ratio changes with both joint angle and measurement velocity, the authors conclude "it
31	is meaningless to prescribe an optimal ratio for any joint," and it would be more accurate
32	to refer to a full-range characteristic curve for a given angular velocity than to a single
33	number. (PDF pp. 244, 245-246, printed pp. 233-234, "4.2.6.1 The Isokinetic Training
34	Method," "Recommended Strength Ratios," Fig 4.16.)
35	
36	**Why it works** — No physiological mechanism is given for why the ratio shifts with sport,
37	joint angle or velocity beyond the general fact that different muscles' torque-generating
38	capacity varies differently across the range of motion and across contraction speed, so any
39	single-number ratio necessarily averages over that variation in a way that hides it.
40	
41	**When to apply** — Use this as a caution against citing a single flexor/extensor or
42	left/right strength-ratio target (e.g. "60:40 quad:hamstring," "no more than 10% L/R
43	difference") as universally optimal or diagnostic of injury risk. If a ratio must be used,
44	specify the joint angle and angular velocity it was measured at, per this claim, and prefer a
45	full-range curve over a single number when data allow. **Eric's baseline:** this bears on how
46	isokinetic or ForceFrame-style ratio data should be interpreted for return-to-play decisions;
47	the corpus does not document a specific flexor/extensor ratio target
48	(`method-baseline.md`).
49	
50	**When NOT to apply** — This is single-source, era-specific data (Vorobyev, 1978; Stephens &
51	Reid, 1988) using a Cybex dynamometer at three specific velocities on an unspecified
52	population; the specific ratio-versus-angle values (75:25 at 36 degrees/second, 68:32 at 180
53	degrees/second) should not be treated as universal constants for every athlete or joint. Do
54	not use this entry to conclude ratio testing is worthless; the claim is that a single
55	"optimal ratio" number is misleading, not that ratio measurement itself carries no
56	information (see [[claim--natural-asymmetry-caution-against-isokinetic-symmetry-correction]]
57	for the related but distinct caution about using isokinetic ratios to drive "correction").
58	
59	**Example** — Inference: a rehabilitation report citing "this athlete's quad:hamstring ratio
60	is below the healthy 60:40 standard" should specify the joint angle and test velocity the
61	ratio was measured at, per this claim, since the same athlete could show a ratio at or above
62	60:40 at one angle/velocity and below it at another, without any change in underlying
63	tissue health.
64	
65	**Related** — [[claim--natural-asymmetry-caution-against-isokinetic-symmetry-correction]]
66	(Ch3.3.4.4, a related caution against using isokinetic ratios to "correct" asymmetry),
67	[[heuristic--isokinetic-testing-limitations-for-functional-sport-specificity]].

13	
14	# No Machine Can Be Truly Isokinetic: The Physics of Acceleration Means Injuries and Elastic Energy Happen Exactly Where Isokinetic Testing Cannot See
15	
16	**What it is** — The authors call the assumption that isokinetic dynamometers offer
17	accurately constant angular velocity from start to finish a "faulty basic assumption": the
18	laws of physics make it impossible, since a body at rest must accelerate to reach a terminal
19	velocity, sustain it, then decelerate back to rest, meaning every movement (isokinetic or
20	otherwise) has periods of positive or negative acceleration; producing truly isokinetic
21	conditions throughout would require infinite acceleration, which "contradicts the laws of
22	science." Manufacturers can only minimise, never eliminate, these non-isokinetic transition
23	phases. The authors argue this matters critically because most injuries occur during exactly
24	these transition phases, when a limb is changing velocity or musculotendinous tension is
25	changing, and isokinetic testing "can reveal no useful information about what is happening
26	to the muscles then." A further limitation: isokinetic testing gives no information on the
27	major contribution of elastic-energy storage and release in soft tissue during dynamic,
28	natural actions like walking, running, jumping or throwing. The authors' summary: "isokinetic
29	testing or training is non-functional, except possibly for swimmers whose movements are
30	approximately isokinetic over part of their range." Biomechanical analysis of force-time and
31	rate-of-force-development curves for resisted free movement confirms distinct qualities
32	(maximal strength, starting strength, acceleration strength, explosive strength, see Fig
33	2.13) that isokinetic curves, being "so radically different from their free movement
34	equivalents," capture poorly, limiting their value for functional analysis or specific
35	neuromuscular conditioning. (PDF pp. 244-245, printed pp. 233-234, "4.2.6.2 Limitations of
36	the Isokinetic Method," "Fundamental Biomechanics of Isokinetic Devices.")
37	
38	**Why it works** — The mechanism is pure Newtonian mechanics: any object moving from rest,
39	sustaining a velocity, and returning to rest must accelerate and decelerate, and true
40	isokinetic motion throughout would demand infinite (physically impossible) acceleration at
41	the start and end. Because injuries and elastic-energy exchange concentrate in these
42	non-constant-velocity transition phases (and in general dynamic movement, which is rarely
43	constant-velocity at all), a device measuring only the constant-velocity middle portion
44	misses the biomechanically important parts of most natural movements.
45	
46	**When to apply** — Use this as the physics-level foundation for treating isokinetic test or
47	training data as descriptive of a narrow, artificial condition (the device's controlled
48	constant-velocity phase) rather than as a general index of an athlete's dynamic capability.
49	Inference: this reinforces the terminology point already in this library (see
50	[[framework--precise-muscle-action-terminology]]) that commercial "isokinetic" devices are
51	more accurately "quasi-isokinetic."
52	
53	**When NOT to apply** — The authors' own exception is swimming, where movement is
54	"approximately isokinetic over part of their range," making isokinetic testing/training
55	comparatively more relevant there than for running, jumping, throwing or lifting. Do not read
56	this entry as claiming isokinetic devices provide zero useful information; the claim is
57	narrower: they provide no useful information specifically about the transition
58	(acceleration/deceleration) phases where most injuries occur and where elastic energy
59	storage/release happens, which is where much of natural dynamic movement's biomechanical
60	significance lies.
61	
62	**Example** — Inference: a hamstring isokinetic strength test at a fixed angular velocity

# No Machine Can Be Truly Isokinetic: The Physics of Acceleration Means Injuries and Elastic Energy Happen Exactly Where Isokinetic Testing Cannot See

**What it is** — The authors call the assumption that isokinetic dynamometers offer
accurately constant angular velocity from start to finish a "faulty basic assumption": the
laws of physics make it impossible, since a body at rest must accelerate to reach a terminal
velocity, sustain it, then decelerate back to rest, meaning every movement (isokinetic or
otherwise) has periods of positive or negative acceleration; producing truly isokinetic
conditions throughout would require infinite acceleration, which "contradicts the laws of
science." Manufacturers can only minimise, never eliminate, these non-isokinetic transition
phases. The authors argue this matters critically because most injuries occur during exactly
these transition phases, when a limb is changing velocity or musculotendinous tension is
changing, and isokinetic testing "can reveal no useful information about what is happening
to the muscles then." A further limitation: isokinetic testing gives no information on the
major contribution of elastic-energy storage and release in soft tissue during dynamic,
natural actions like walking, running, jumping or throwing. The authors' summary: "isokinetic
testing or training is non-functional, except possibly for swimmers whose movements are
approximately isokinetic over part of their range." Biomechanical analysis of force-time and
rate-of-force-development curves for resisted free movement confirms distinct qualities
(maximal strength, starting strength, acceleration strength, explosive strength, see Fig
2.13) that isokinetic curves, being "so radically different from their free movement
equivalents," capture poorly, limiting their value for functional analysis or specific
neuromuscular conditioning. (PDF pp. 244-245, printed pp. 233-234, "4.2.6.2 Limitations of
the Isokinetic Method," "Fundamental Biomechanics of Isokinetic Devices.")

**Why it works** — The mechanism is pure Newtonian mechanics: any object moving from rest,
sustaining a velocity, and returning to rest must accelerate and decelerate, and true
isokinetic motion throughout would demand infinite (physically impossible) acceleration at
the start and end. Because injuries and elastic-energy exchange concentrate in these
non-constant-velocity transition phases (and in general dynamic movement, which is rarely
constant-velocity at all), a device measuring only the constant-velocity middle portion
misses the biomechanically important parts of most natural movements.

**When to apply** — Use this as the physics-level foundation for treating isokinetic test or
training data as descriptive of a narrow, artificial condition (the device's controlled
constant-velocity phase) rather than as a general index of an athlete's dynamic capability.
Inference: this reinforces the terminology point already in this library (see
[[framework--precise-muscle-action-terminology]]) that commercial "isokinetic" devices are
more accurately "quasi-isokinetic."

**When NOT to apply** — The authors' own exception is swimming, where movement is
"approximately isokinetic over part of their range," making isokinetic testing/training
comparatively more relevant there than for running, jumping, throwing or lifting. Do not read
this entry as claiming isokinetic devices provide zero useful information; the claim is
narrower: they provide no useful information specifically about the transition
(acceleration/deceleration) phases where most injuries occur and where elastic energy
storage/release happens, which is where much of natural dynamic movement's biomechanical
significance lies.

**Example** — Inference: a hamstring isokinetic strength test at a fixed angular velocity
(e.g. 60 degrees/second) can characterise force output during that constant-velocity phase,
but per this claim it cannot characterise what happens during the initial acceleration into
that velocity or the deceleration out of it, which is where a sprinting hamstring's peak
eccentric strain and injury risk concentrate.

**Related** — [[framework--precise-muscle-action-terminology]] (Ch1, "isokinetic" as a
misleading term for the same physical reason given here),
[[heuristic--isometric-dynamometry-misrepresents-dynamic-functional-strength]] (Ch2),
[[heuristic--isokinetic-testing-limitations-for-functional-sport-specificity]].

17	[[claim--isokinetic-devices-cannot-be-truly-isokinetic-physics-limitation]]), the authors
18	give a detailed, itemised critique of relying on isokinetic dynamometers (e.g. Cybex,
19	Orthotron) for testing and rehabilitation. (1) **Functional anatomy**: nearby-joint angle
20	changes the torque produced about the joint in question (e.g. hip angle changes knee
21	extension torque, important to weightlifters, jumpers and sprinters), but seated isokinetic
22	testing typically immobilises the hips with straps, creating "non-functional conditions" that

24	also rarely combined with EMG or myotonometry to identify which specific muscles (e.g.
25	vastus medialis vs lateralis, affected by lateral/medial rotation) actually contribute to the
26	measured torque, and open-chain testing (foot not contacting the ground) alters how popliteus
27	and gastrocnemius contribute to knee flexion, both important in running, lifting and jumping;
28	seated testing also ignores medial rotation contributions (sartorius, gracilis,
29	semimembranosus, semitendinosus) and lateral rotation (biceps femoris). (2) **Muscle
30	physiology**: most sporting actions begin from intense isometric or explosive-isometric
31	contraction with stored tendon elastic energy, a state isokinetic testing/training involves
32	only insignificantly; the myotatic stretch reflex (stronger with faster stretch) is central
33	to explosive running, jumping, lifting and throwing but cannot be recruited under isokinetic
34	conditions; agonist-antagonist cocontraction and ballistic (preprogrammed,
35	feedback-independent) movement are both common in sport but isokinetic conditions permit
36	neither; torque under isokinetic conditions is usually much lower than isometric torque at
37	the same joint angle, contradicting the claim (Thistle et al, 1967) that isokinetics keeps
38	tension maximal throughout; reciprocal inhibition (antagonist pre-contraction raising
39	agonist force, used in PNF and common in plyometric rebounding) is not permitted by most
40	isokinetic devices; and bilateral versus unilateral force-production patterns differ, so
41	isokinetic limb-to-limb comparisons "can be very misleading," since a dominant limb's
42	superiority is often one of skill, not strength (e.g. it is common, but the authors imply
43	misguided, for therapists to isokinetically strengthen a footballer's weaker kicking limb
44	when the support leg's job is producing stabilising strength). (3) **Specificity**:
45	indiscriminate isokinetic use neglects the specificity principle across ten dimensions (type
46	of muscle contraction, movement pattern, region of movement, velocity of movement, force of
47	contraction, muscle fibre recruitment, metabolism, biochemical adaptation, flexibility,
48	fatigue), citing Sale and McDougall (1981) that strength gains are apparent only when
49	measured during the same movement type used in training; this specificity concern
50	"culminated" in Verkhoshansky's principle of dynamic correspondence (see 4.3, not yet
51	ingested in this pass). The authors' concluding analogy: relying on a single isokinetic model
52	to assess strength and endurance is "tantamount to permanently accepting" the early
53	planetary-electron atomic model just because it is easy to work with; a more versatile,
54	"kinesiological polygraph" combining high-speed video, EMG, myotensiometers, accelerometers
55	and force plates is what multi-faceted human movement actually demands, and sporting
56	performance itself remains the ultimate test of any training or rehabilitation regime. The
57	authors also name the APRE system (based on DeLorme's original work, see 5.2.2) as an
58	inexpensive, effective alternative to isokinetics, and point to Ostering (1986) for a
59	detailed review of isokinetic strengths and weaknesses. (PDF pp. 245-247, printed pp.
60	234-236, "4.2.6.2 Limitations of the Isokinetic Method," "Functional Anatomy," "Muscle
61	Physiology," "The Importance of Specificity," "Concluding Remarks.")

64	inline): joint-coupling effects on torque, missing EMG/myotonometry verification, absent
65	elastic-energy and stretch-reflex contribution, absent cocontraction/ballistic patterning,
66	absent reciprocal inhibition, and bilateral-versus-unilateral force-pattern differences. The
67	authors' unifying argument is that isokinetic devices remove or distort each of these
68	naturally-occurring features of dynamic sport movement, so a test built on removing them
69	cannot validly characterise performance that depends on them.
70

72	specific isokinetic finding (a strength deficit, an asymmetry, a rehabilitation
73	"clearance" threshold) should influence a functional/sport-specific training or return-to-play
74	decision: check whether the isokinetic condition tested (seated, seat-strapped, single-joint,
75	no elastic energy, no stretch reflex, no cocontraction, no reciprocal inhibition, bilateral
76	comparison) resembles the sporting movement in question closely enough for the finding to

87	[[heuristic--isokinetic-strength-ratios-vary-by-angle-and-velocity]]) to establish real

90	(the authors themselves call them "useful for measuring isokinetic actions... in two
91	dimensions"); the claim is that extrapolating isokinetic results to full sporting movement
92	"is scientifically unacceptable and misleading."

95	kicking (non-support) leg, per the authors' own named example, may be targeting the wrong
96	quality if the support leg's job (stabilising strength under bilateral/unilateral,
97	cocontractive demand) is actually more functionally relevant to on-field performance than the

14	# The Static-Dynamic Method: Pairing a Brief Isometric Hold With Explosive Concentric Work in One Repetition
15	
16	**What it is** — The static-dynamic method sequentially combines isometric and dynamic
17	(auxotonic) muscular activity within one exercise. Two variants are given as experimentally
18	effective: (1) a 2-3 second isometric contraction at 80% of maximum, immediately followed by
19	explosive concentric dynamic work with a 30%-of-maximum load; (2) a constant load of 75-80%
20	of maximum used for both the isometric and dynamic components, illustrated with a half-squat
21	example: the athlete sinks into a half-squat with a barbell on the shoulders, holds that
22	position for 2 seconds, then jumps upward with maximal acceleration before landing carefully
23	and repeating. Experimentally, variant (1) proved better than dynamic exercise alone for
24	developing speed-strength; variant (2) had an effect on speed-strength and absolute strength
25	improvement roughly equivalent to dynamic exercise alone (Dobrovolsky, 1972, 1973). (PDF p.
26	247, printed p. 236, "4.2.6.3 Static-Dynamic Methods.")
27	
28	**Why it works** — No specific mechanism is given for why pairing a brief isometric hold with
29	subsequent explosive concentric work outperforms dynamic-only training for speed-strength in
30	variant (1); Inference: this is plausibly related to the same explosive-isometric-to-concentric
31	transition mechanism already described for depth jumps and the shock method (see
32	[[framework--kinetic-energy-stimulation-mechanical-basis-and-advantages]] and
33	[[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]]), where the isometric phase primes the
34	neuromuscular system immediately before the explosive concentric effort, though the authors
35	do not state this connection explicitly for the static-dynamic method here.
36	
37	**When to apply** — Use variant (1) (2-3s isometric hold at 80% max, then explosive
38	concentric at 30% max) when the specific goal is speed-strength development, per the cited
39	finding that it outperformed dynamic-only training for that quality. Use variant (2) (a
40	half-squat-and-jump at 75-80% max) as an option with roughly equivalent
41	speed-strength-and-absolute-strength effect to dynamic training alone, useful mainly for
42	variety or when the loaded-jump movement pattern itself is desired.
43	
44	**When NOT to apply** — This is a single-source finding (Dobrovolsky, 1972, 1973) without
45	reported sample size, training-age context, or long-term outcome data beyond the immediate
46	comparison to dynamic-only training; treat the specific load percentages (80%/30%, 75-80%)
47	as the cited protocol's own parameters, not universally optimal figures. Variant (2)'s
48	half-squat-and-jump with load requires careful technique and landing control, which this
49	passage does not itself detail as a safety protocol.
50	
51	**Example** — The book's own example is the half-squat-hold-then-jump description above
52	(variant 2); no further invented example is added here.

14	# No Single Training Regime Is "Most Effective": Combining Regimes Consistently Outperforms Any One Alone
15	
16	**What it is** — Asked which of the chapter's several muscular-work regimes (concentric,
17	eccentric, isometric, isokinetic, static-dynamic, and combinations) is most effective, the
18	authors argue a categorical answer is not possible, for three reasons: (1) comprehensive
19	research comparing all regimes has not been conducted; one study comparing eccentric,
20	concentric, isometric and combined regimes found some advantage of concentric over eccentric
21	and isometric methods individually, but the combined-regime method showed "a clear
22	advantage" over all of them (Pletnev, 1975); (2) comparative research is inherently difficult
23	because training loads are hard to equate across different regimes; (3) it is
24	"inappropriate to raise the question of the absolute effectiveness of any specific regime,"
25	since each regime can be the most effective depending on the training situation, stage of
26	the annual cycle, athlete level, the primary regime of muscular work demanded by the specific
27	sport exercise, and the specific strength quality being trained. The authors' overall
28	conclusion, stated with "reasonable certainty": the most rational way to enhance special
29	strength preparation is to combine the various regimes of muscular work, a conclusion
30	corroborated by multiple studies (Vorobyev, 1966; Andrianov & Vorobyev, 1969; Kuznetsov,
31	1970; Verkhoshansky, 1970, 1972; Slobodyan, 1972; Tatyan, 1974; Pletnev, 1975; Khodykin,
32	1975; Savin, 1974). Such a combination should be selected by considering its cumulative
33	effect (see [[framework--acute-delayed-particular-cumulative-training-effect-taxonomy]]) and
34	its correspondence to the specific conditions of the sport. (PDF pp. 247-248, printed pp.
35	236-237, "4.2.6.4 Choice of Muscle Training Regimes.")
36	
37	**Why it works** — No single mechanism is given for why combined regimes outperform any one
38	regime alone; Inference: a plausible explanation, not stated in the text, is that different
39	regimes stress different components of the strength system (contractile tissue,
40	elastic/connective tissue, neural drive, fibre-type-specific adaptation) somewhat
41	independently, so combining them addresses more of the system than repeatedly stressing only
42	one component.
43	
44	**When to apply** — Use this heuristic to resist single-method dogma ("isokinetics is best,"
45	"only free weights work," "eccentric training is superior") when programming special
46	strength training; per this section, the authors' own multi-study conclusion favours

# No Single Training Regime Is "Most Effective": Combining Regimes Consistently Outperforms Any One Alone

**What it is** — Asked which of the chapter's several muscular-work regimes (concentric,
eccentric, isometric, isokinetic, static-dynamic, and combinations) is most effective, the
authors argue a categorical answer is not possible, for three reasons: (1) comprehensive
research comparing all regimes has not been conducted; one study comparing eccentric,
concentric, isometric and combined regimes found some advantage of concentric over eccentric
and isometric methods individually, but the combined-regime method showed "a clear
advantage" over all of them (Pletnev, 1975); (2) comparative research is inherently difficult
because training loads are hard to equate across different regimes; (3) it is
"inappropriate to raise the question of the absolute effectiveness of any specific regime,"
since each regime can be the most effective depending on the training situation, stage of
the annual cycle, athlete level, the primary regime of muscular work demanded by the specific
sport exercise, and the specific strength quality being trained. The authors' overall
conclusion, stated with "reasonable certainty": the most rational way to enhance special
strength preparation is to combine the various regimes of muscular work, a conclusion
corroborated by multiple studies (Vorobyev, 1966; Andrianov & Vorobyev, 1969; Kuznetsov,
1970; Verkhoshansky, 1970, 1972; Slobodyan, 1972; Tatyan, 1974; Pletnev, 1975; Khodykin,
1975; Savin, 1974). Such a combination should be selected by considering its cumulative
effect (see [[framework--acute-delayed-particular-cumulative-training-effect-taxonomy]]) and
its correspondence to the specific conditions of the sport. (PDF pp. 247-248, printed pp.
236-237, "4.2.6.4 Choice of Muscle Training Regimes.")

**Why it works** — No single mechanism is given for why combined regimes outperform any one
regime alone; Inference: a plausible explanation, not stated in the text, is that different
regimes stress different components of the strength system (contractile tissue,
elastic/connective tissue, neural drive, fibre-type-specific adaptation) somewhat
independently, so combining them addresses more of the system than repeatedly stressing only
one component.

**When to apply** — Use this heuristic to resist single-method dogma ("isokinetics is best,"
"only free weights work," "eccentric training is superior") when programming special
strength training; per this section, the authors' own multi-study conclusion favours
deliberately combining regimes (concentric, eccentric, isometric, static-dynamic,
resistance, kinetic-energy) rather than committing to one, selected for cumulative effect
and sport-specific correspondence.

**When NOT to apply** — The nine corroborating citations (Vorobyev 1966 through Savin 1974)
give no individual effect sizes or protocols in this passage; treat "combining regimes is
most rational" as the authors' summary conclusion across a body of era-specific Soviet sport
science, not a single quantified finding. This heuristic does not specify which combination,
in what proportion, or in what sequence to use for a given sport or athlete; it establishes
only the general principle that combination beats any single regime, leaving the specific
combination as a separate programming decision guided by cumulative-effect and
dynamic-correspondence principles (see 4.3, not yet ingested in this pass).

occasional isometric holds at sticking points, and periodic eccentric-emphasis work (rather

sport-specificity criteria the authors name.

20	Western "state-of-the-art" fitness centres are usually equipped almost entirely with NFR
21	machines, so much so that adequate free weights or FR machines can be hard to find in them;
22	they quote Zatsiorsky (1995) directly: "the important limitation of many strength training
23	machines is that they are designed to train muscles, not movement. Because of this, they are
24	not the most important training tool for athletes." FR devices (guided by Ratov, 1976) are
25	reported effective for aspects of special strength training across many athlete types
26	(Semenov, 1970; Petrova & Gorbunov, 1970; Verkhoshansky, 1970; Deniskin & Kuznetsov, 1972;
27	Dobrovolski, 1972, 1973; Kuznetsov & Aiunts, 1974; Savin, 1974), because they permit strict
28	regulation of load and the movement's spatial characteristics, letting a coach use the
29	appropriate regime of muscular work and programme force-over-time characteristics while
30	reproducing stereotypical training movements economically. The authors' example of a
31	simple, cheap, versatile FR device is the "hi-lo" pulley machine, whose rope-attached
32	handles (unlike fixed bars and pivots on most NFR machines) allow sport-specific movement
33	patterns of great complexity; they estimate a circuit of just four pulley machines can
34	provide training capacity that would otherwise need more than 40 "state of the art" NFR
35	machines, and that a circuit of 10 pulley machines plus a few benches, jumping boards, bars,
36	mats and wall-bars can serve more clients with a larger range of exercises than 100
37	specialised machines, at under 15% of the cost, though even this pulley-based facility would
38	give inferior multi-dimensional conditioning compared with an NFR-machine-only facility on

40	quality and quantity for controlling training. The authors caution that simulating a sport
41	movement against heavy machine loads can still significantly alter the movement's

65	remain appropriate despite this section's general preference for FR devices and free
66	weights.

14	# NFR Machines: Real Limitations on Proprioception and Joint Loading, but Not Actually Safer Than Free Weights
15	
16	**What it is** — Non-functional resistance (NFR) machines can play a useful supplementary
17	role but generally cannot match free weights and FR machines for multi-dimensional,
18	full-range neuromuscular and musculoskeletal training. Many NFR machines force the user to
19	sit or lie, minimising training effect on major stabilising muscles and involving fewer
20	joints through fewer degrees of freedom; while potentially valuable early in rehabilitation,
21	this is an incomplete way of training the body for functional development, since machines
22	that stabilise major body regions and limit the number of moving joints diminish the
23	capacity to train balance, coordination and proprioception. The authors give a worked
24	example: a free-standing squat involves three joints (hip, knee, ankle), while a seated knee
25	extension machine constrains the body to one joint (knee) to exercise the quadriceps, so for
26	a comparable exercise intensity over the same range of motion, the machine increases
27	shearing force across the knee; the squat additionally exercises the thigh adductors, spinal
28	erectors and other stabilisers, and enhances balance and (via longitudinal compressive
29	loading) bone density. Seated exercise also always imposes a greater lumbar-disc load than
30	equivalent standing exercise: maintaining a neutral spinal curve while seated raises lumbar
31	disc pressure by about 40% (Chaffin & Andersson, 1984); allowing the back to flex forward can
32	raise this by as much as 90%; a well-designed lumbar-supporting backrest lowers the stress
33	but lumbar disc pressure can still run about 75% higher than standing; stress increases
34	further against resistance, especially with jerky movements, and seated positions cannot
35	absorb shock loading via knee/hip/ankle flexion the way standing can. On safety
36	specifically, the authors reject the common claim that NFR machines are much safer than free
37	weights: injuries to the back and knees (leg press, hack-squat, hip-sled), shoulders and
38	chest (bench press, pec-deck), elbow (bicep curl machines) and back (back-extension
39	machines) are "just as common with machines as with free weights," and many machines (pec
40	deck, bench press, leg press, calf raise, seated press) force the movement to start from the
41	biomechanically least efficient, most harmful position for the relevant joint; spotters are
42	just as necessary for machines as for free weights, and faulty technique is equally dangerous
43	with either. Some machines (leg extension, lat pulley, seated bicep curl) genuinely are safer
44	for someone with back weakness or injury, and can help in early rehabilitation, but
45	"continual avoidance of stress to the regions involved eventually leads to their progressive
46	weakening" if relied on long-term. NFR machines remain useful for isolating specific muscle
47	groups (bodybuilding-style supplementary training) or for the primary stages of injury
48	rehabilitation, but not as an all-round conditioning replacement for free weights and FR
49	devices; one exception noted is the lat-pulley machine, generally more suitable and safer
50	than the free-weight equivalent (bent-over rowing) for training latissimus dorsi. (PDF pp.
51	249-250, printed pp. 238-240, "4.2.7.2 Non-Functional Resistance Machines," "4.2.7.4 The
52	Training Safety of Machines.")
53	
54	**Why it works** — The proprioception/stability mechanism is that fixing more joints and
55	supporting more of the body's weight through the machine itself removes the balance,
56	coordination and multi-joint stabilisation demand that free, standing exercise imposes. The
57	single-joint-versus-multi-joint mechanism is straightforward: constraining a comparable
58	training stimulus to fewer joints concentrates the same relative stress onto those joints'
59	structures (illustrated by the squat-versus-knee-extension shearing-force example). The
60	lumbar-disc mechanism is postural: seated positions load the discs differently than standing,
61	and cannot use lower-body joint flexion to absorb shock the way standing positions can.
62	
63	**When to apply** — Use NFR machines for early-stage rehabilitation of a specific injured
64	joint or muscle group, for supplementary bodybuilding-style isolation work, or when back
65	weakness/injury makes a machine (leg extension, lat pulley, seated bicep curl) genuinely
66	safer than the free-weight equivalent. **Eric's baseline:** the department's testing
67	protocols already run standard CMJ family tests and mid-thigh pull on ForceDecks rather than
68	seated machine-based strength testing (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular
69	monitoring"), consistent with this section's general preference for standing, multi-joint,
70	free assessment over seated/constrained machine testing.
71	
72	**When NOT to apply** — Do not rely on NFR machines long-term as a substitute for free
73	weights or FR devices in a healthy, competitive athlete's programme, since progressive
74	avoidance of stress to a region "eventually leads to... progressive weakening." Do not
75	assume NFR machines are inherently safer than free weights; per the authors' own comparison,
76	injury rates and biomechanically poor starting positions are comparable across both,
77	technique quality and spotting matter more than equipment choice.
78	
79	**Example** — Inference: using a seated knee-extension machine during the first two weeks
80	after a knee injury (early rehabilitation, single-joint control) while progressing toward a
81	free-standing squat as tolerance improves applies this heuristic's appropriate-use window; continuing
82	to rely on the knee-extension machine as the primary quadriceps exercise once the athlete
83	returns to full training would not, per the "progressive weakening" caution above.
84	
85	**Related** — [[framework--functional-vs-nonfunctional-resistance-machines]],
86	[[claim--nfr-machine-marketing-claims-examined]].
87

13	
14	# Variable-Resistance Machines' Core Marketing Claim Rests on a Physics Error, and NFR Machines Need Many More Units to Match Free Weights
15	
16	**What it is** — Many machine manufacturers design variable-resistance machines to match a
17	joint's natural torque curve, claiming superiority over free weights and other resistance
18	devices on this basis. The authors identify a flawed premise behind this claim: manufacturers
19	imply a free weight's resistance stays constant throughout a lift (e.g. a 50 kg biceps curl
20	is presented as exerting a constant 50 kg / about 490 Newton force from start to finish). A
21	simple application of Newton's Second Law (force proportional to acceleration) shows this is
22	false: the resistance a free weight offers changes with acceleration from rest and at any
23	point the trainee speeds up or slows down, "as can easily be demonstrated by force plate,
24	cable tensiometer or high speed video analysis"; a skilled trainee already uses proprioception
25	to perceive these changes and adjust resistance and direction more efficiently, the authors
26	argue, than current machines can. Separately, on training efficiency, the authors give
27	several specific machine-count comparisons: it takes at least 12 NFR machines to
28	approximately equal the training effect of the clean-and-push-press, at least 4 to rival the
29	free-standing squat, more than 3 to equal the standing dumbbell curl, and at least 5 to
30	rival the flexed-knee deadlift; in total, more than 24 NFR machines are required to match the
31	combined training effect of just four free-weight exercises (clean-and-push-press, squat,
32	deadlift, biceps curl), at roughly 40 times the combined cost of the equivalent free weights
33	and racks, with NFR machines also carrying higher maintenance costs and more frequent
34	breakdowns in a well-used gymnasium than "virtually indestructible" free weights. (PDF pp.
35	250-251, printed pp. 239-240, "4.2.7.3 Machines and the Variable Resistance Philosophy,"
36	"4.2.7.5 The Efficiency of Machine Training.")
37	
38	**Why it works** — For the variable-resistance critique, the mechanism is Newtonian: force
39	equals mass times acceleration, so any free weight's true resistance already varies with the
40	trainee's own acceleration/deceleration throughout the lift, contradicting the marketing
41	premise that free weights offer constant resistance needing a machine's correction. For the
42	machine-count comparison, the implied mechanism is that a free-weight compound exercise
43	recruits and trains many more muscle groups, movement patterns and stabilising demands
44	simultaneously than any single-joint NFR machine, so many NFR machines are needed in
45	combination to approach the same total training stimulus.
46	
47	**When to apply** — Use the Newtonian-mechanics point directly to counter variable-resistance
48	machine marketing claims that free weights offer "constant" resistance needing a machine's
49	correction; a skilled lifter's own proprioceptive control of bar speed already varies the
50	true resistance throughout the lift (see also

# Variable-Resistance Machines' Core Marketing Claim Rests on a Physics Error, and NFR Machines Need Many More Units to Match Free Weights

**What it is** — Many machine manufacturers design variable-resistance machines to match a
joint's natural torque curve, claiming superiority over free weights and other resistance
devices on this basis. The authors identify a flawed premise behind this claim: manufacturers
imply a free weight's resistance stays constant throughout a lift (e.g. a 50 kg biceps curl
is presented as exerting a constant 50 kg / about 490 Newton force from start to finish). A
simple application of Newton's Second Law (force proportional to acceleration) shows this is
false: the resistance a free weight offers changes with acceleration from rest and at any
point the trainee speeds up or slows down, "as can easily be demonstrated by force plate,
cable tensiometer or high speed video analysis"; a skilled trainee already uses proprioception
to perceive these changes and adjust resistance and direction more efficiently, the authors
argue, than current machines can. Separately, on training efficiency, the authors give
several specific machine-count comparisons: it takes at least 12 NFR machines to
approximately equal the training effect of the clean-and-push-press, at least 4 to rival the
free-standing squat, more than 3 to equal the standing dumbbell curl, and at least 5 to
rival the flexed-knee deadlift; in total, more than 24 NFR machines are required to match the
combined training effect of just four free-weight exercises (clean-and-push-press, squat,
deadlift, biceps curl), at roughly 40 times the combined cost of the equivalent free weights
and racks, with NFR machines also carrying higher maintenance costs and more frequent
breakdowns in a well-used gymnasium than "virtually indestructible" free weights. (PDF pp.
250-251, printed pp. 239-240, "4.2.7.3 Machines and the Variable Resistance Philosophy,"
"4.2.7.5 The Efficiency of Machine Training.")

**Why it works** — For the variable-resistance critique, the mechanism is Newtonian: force
equals mass times acceleration, so any free weight's true resistance already varies with the
trainee's own acceleration/deceleration throughout the lift, contradicting the marketing
premise that free weights offer constant resistance needing a machine's correction. For the
machine-count comparison, the implied mechanism is that a free-weight compound exercise
recruits and trains many more muscle groups, movement patterns and stabilising demands
simultaneously than any single-joint NFR machine, so many NFR machines are needed in
combination to approach the same total training stimulus.

**When to apply** — Use the Newtonian-mechanics point directly to counter variable-resistance
machine marketing claims that free weights offer "constant" resistance needing a machine's
correction; a skilled lifter's own proprioceptive control of bar speed already varies the
true resistance throughout the lift (see also
[[framework--compensatory-acceleration-training]], Ch1). Use the machine-count/cost
comparison when evaluating equipment-purchase decisions for a training facility: a small set
of free-weight stations and racks may replicate the combined training effect of a much
larger, more expensive NFR machine circuit, per this section's specific figures.

**When NOT to apply** — The specific machine-count figures (12, 4, 3+, 5, 24+, roughly 40x
cost) are the authors' own estimates for approximating specific free-weight exercises' total
training effect with combinations of NFR machines; they do not cite a controlled study
establishing these exact ratios, so treat them as illustrative rather than precisely
measured. This entry does not argue variable-resistance machines have zero value, only that
their core "free weights are constant resistance" marketing premise is physically incorrect;
some variable-resistance designs may still offer useful features (feedback display, joint
isolation for rehabilitation) independent of that specific flawed premise.

**Example** — Inference: a facility manager comparing the cost of building a small free-weight
area (barbells, plates, a rack, a platform) against an equivalent machine circuit covering
the same major lift patterns should expect, per this section's estimates, the free-weight
option to require far fewer total pieces of equipment and far lower combined cost.

[[heuristic--nfr-machine-limitations-safety-and-appropriate-use]],

resistance already varies via the lifter's own acceleration).

15
