17	(see
18	[[claim--natural-asymmetry-caution-against-isokinetic-symmetry-correction]]), which deferred
19	"The Concept of Symmetric Training" to this section. Asymmetry in leg length, muscle
20	strength, stride length and other structural/functional features has been blamed for
21	inefficient movement and injury, and imbalances in agonist/antagonist and left/right strength
22	(including isokinetically-measured muscular endurance imbalances) have been singled out as
23	leading causes of muscle injury. However, research shows isokinetically-measured left/right
24	leg-strength or agonist/antagonist discrepancies as large as 10% do not statistically
25	correlate with a major increase in muscular injuries. Because the body, its muscles, tendons
26	and bones are characteristically asymmetric, attempts to force greater anthropomorphic and
27	kinesiological symmetry "could exacerbate the existing problem or cause new injuries";
28	assessing asymmetry properly requires both static structural measurement (leg length, spinal
29	curvature) and dynamic biomechanical analysis (force distribution, movement patterns, ground
30	reaction force, postural/phasic muscle EMG, movement-phase timing). Structural differences
31	in muscle/tendon length, tendon and ligament attachment sites, and bone size/mass are
32	"quite natural in all humans"; surgical or orthotic correction is warranted only when such
33	structural differences cause serious functional movement imbalances, and even then only
34	after confirming the asymmetry is primarily structural rather than a centrally-stored
35	neuromuscular pattern (in which case the answer is modifying the motor skill itself, not
36	correcting the body). There is "no perfect way" to execute any movement; style is the
37	individualised expression of a motor skill and should be developed by observing and
38	experimenting against an "ideal" model until the athlete's own central nervous programme
39	fits their body, rather than enforcing one rigid technique standard. Yushkevich (1989)
40	analysed leg-strength symmetry in sprinters and concluded striving for full leg symmetry is
41	inappropriate: extensors of all joints of the push-off leg were generally significantly
42	stronger than the swing leg's, with no consistent flexor-strength difference between legs.

44	flexors than swing-leg; novice, Class 3 and Class 2 athletes showed stronger swing-leg knee
45	flexors, while Class 1, Master and higher-qualified athletes showed stronger push-off-leg
46	knee flexors; dorsiflexion was stronger in the push-off leg for all athletes except novices.
47	Leg-strength asymmetry increased with sprint proficiency, peaking among Class 2 athletes,
48	then diminishing again with further mastery. Good sprint times correlated more closely with
49	swing-leg strength than push-off-leg strength. Yushkevich's conclusion: not only is
50	symmetrical muscle strength a misguided target, but deliberately asymmetric exercise
51	(running or jumping on sloping/inclined tracks, running curves in both directions, running or
52	jumping in shoes with soles of different thickness, or running with unevenly-weighted legs)
53	can be beneficial, since "asymmetric exercises destabilise the space-time characteristics of
54	motor acts, thereby helping athletes break speed barriers." The authors close with an analogy
55	to the tradition that Eastern-carpet weavers deliberately include at least one flaw, since
56	"perfection is reserved for the Divine," implying similar asymmetry or imperfection may be
57	desirable in human physical performance and training generally. (PDF pp. 251-252, printed pp.

64	symmetry-forcing backfires" claim, the implied mechanism is that the body's natural asymmetry
65	already reflects functional adaptation (dominant-limb skill specialisation, individualised

14	# "Muscle Isolation" Works at Low Loads, but Heavy Resistance Recruits Stabilisers Until Isolation Is Essentially Impossible
15	
16	**What it is** — Generations of bodybuilding-magazine authors have advocated specific
17	machines, joint-fixation methods, precise limb placement and other techniques claimed to
18	maximally recruit one muscle group while others stay "largely dormant." EMG studies confirm
19	isolation of small muscle groups is genuinely possible under low loading intensity
20	(Basmajian, 1978): low-intensity actions like eye-blinking, piano-playing or relaxed speech
21	rely on precise, isolated action of specific small muscle groups. However, once a large load
22	is imposed on a target muscle group by intense resistance, isolation becomes "virtually
23	impossible": as soon as the load is applied, stabilising muscles engage to keep the body or
24	specific joints stable while prime movers cope with the load, and if the nervous system
25	signals the prime movers are inadequate, assistant movers, shunt muscles, emergency muscles
26	and neutralisers may all be recruited to help. The authors' worked example: during heavy
27	standing triceps push-downs on a cable machine, the abdominals, latissimus dorsi and erector
28	spinae may contract nearly as strongly as the triceps, despite this being nominally a
29	triceps-isolation exercise; analysis of many seated or reclining "isolation" machine
30	exercises shows isolation simply does not occur under heavy load, even when joints are
31	restrained (as on an isokinetic test machine). This is the same load-dependent
32	proximal/distal recruitment shift already noted earlier in the chapter (see
33	[[claim--muscle-recruitment-consistency-and-proximal-distal-shift-with-load]]), where the
34	authors explicitly forward-referenced this section. This does not negate the value of
35	isolation-style exercises: they can be useful in early injury rehabilitation, and the
36	overflow to other muscle groups at higher loads can itself be desirable (if performed
37	safely), since it simultaneously offers isometric and dynamic training to those other muscle
38	groups. The authors' stated purpose for this section is to correct the "misleading concept
39	of muscle isolation" still promoted by many instructors and training texts. (PDF p. 252,
40	printed p. 241, "4.2.9 The Concept of Muscle Isolation.")
41	
42	**Why it works** — The mechanism given is neuromuscular: as external load rises, the central
43	nervous system recruits whatever additional muscle groups (stabilisers, assistant movers,
44	emergency muscles, neutralisers) are needed to keep the targeted joint and the body stable
45	and to complete the movement, since a single "isolated" muscle group's own capacity is
46	insufficient against a heavy load; at low loads, this recruitment is unnecessary, so true
47	isolation (confirmed by EMG) is achievable.
48	
49	**When to apply** — Use this claim to correctly interpret what a "muscle isolation" exercise
50	is actually training at a given load: at rehabilitation-level, low-intensity loading, genuine
51	isolation is achievable and useful for targeted, precise re-education of a specific muscle
52	(consistent with [[claim--irradiation-effect-raises-prime-mover-force-and-endurance]]'s
53	adjacent finding that effort and tension spread between muscle groups). At hypertrophy- or
54	strength-level heavy loading, expect and potentially embrace the overflow to stabilisers and
55	assistant movers as additional, simultaneous isometric/dynamic training for those muscle
56	groups rather than treating it as a programming failure.
57	
58	**When NOT to apply** — Do not describe a heavy-load exercise (a heavy cable push-down, a
59	heavy leg-extension set) as "isolating" the target muscle group in marketing, coaching cues,
60	or programme design; per this claim and its EMG evidence, that description is only accurate
61	at low training intensities. Do not assume the specific triceps push-down example
62	generalises identically to every "isolation" exercise; the authors give it as one worked
63	illustration, not a universally quantified finding across exercises.
64	
65	**Example** — The book's own example is the heavy triceps push-down engaging abdominals,
66	latissimus dorsi and erector spinae described above; no further invented example is added
67	here.
68	
69	**Related** — [[claim--muscle-recruitment-consistency-and-proximal-distal-shift-with-load]]
70	(this chapter's own forward reference to this entry, 4.2.2),
71	[[claim--irradiation-effect-raises-prime-mover-force-and-endurance]] (Ch3, a related finding
72	on how tension in one muscle group affects others).

# Hettinger and Muller's Original Isometric-Training Finding: About 5% Strength Gain Per Week From One Daily 6-Second Effort at Two-Thirds Maximum

**What it is** — Isometric exercises became popular in the mid-1950s in the search for
economical, effective strength methods. Hettinger and Muller (1953, 1955) established that
one daily effort at two-thirds of maximum, held for six seconds, performed for 10 weeks,
increases strength by about 5% per week. Separately, Clark et al (1954) found that static
strength continues to increase even after a four-week isometric programme has concluded.
This early success prompted considerable research comparing isometric training's
effectiveness against dynamic training, which produced "rather contradictory data" (see
review by Verkhoshansky, 1970). The authors' general conclusion from that body of research:
isometric training can be more effective than dynamic exercise specifically where the target
exercise requires a large-magnitude muscle contraction at a certain stage of a movement, or
"during the early stages of injury rehabilitation"; if the target exercise involves
high-speed movement, sustained isometric training is less effective. The authors also note
that because isometric training's usual purpose is developing absolute strength, tension
should be increased slowly and held for a relatively long time, since prolonged tension
maintenance demands the energy expenditure that stimulates adequate neuromuscular
adaptation; some researchers found no essential difference in strength gain from varying
isometric tension intensity, from which the authors infer that "the fundamental
conditioning factor is not so much the magnitude of the isometric tension as its duration."
(PDF pp. 234-235, printed pp. 223-224, "4.2.4 Isometric Training.")

**Why it works** — The authors' stated reasoning: prolonged maintenance of muscular tension
requires an energy expenditure that "stimulates adequate adaptation in the neuromuscular
system, thereby determining its strength potential," and this can exceed the stimulus from
brief transient dynamic tension. The authors give no cellular or neural mechanism for why
duration outweighs magnitude; their conclusion rests on studies that did not find a
strength-gain difference across tension intensities (p.224), not on a stated physiological
pathway.

**When to apply** — Use the 5%-per-week figure and the two-thirds-maximum, 6-second, daily,
10-week protocol as a citable historical anchor for isometric-training dosing, and use the
authors' scoping rule (isometrics favoured for large-magnitude contraction at a specific
movement stage or early rehab; less favoured when the target skill is high-speed) to decide
when isometric work is the better tool versus dynamic resistance training.

**When NOT to apply** — This is 1950s data; the authors say later comparisons of isometric
and dynamic training produced "rather contradictory data" (Verkhoshansky 1970 review, PDF
235, printed p.224), and the text reports no modern replication. Treat "5% per week" as
specific to Hettinger and Muller's exact protocol (two-thirds max, 6 seconds, daily, 10
weeks), not a generalizable isometric-training growth rate. The "duration not magnitude"
inference (PDF 235, printed p.224) sits against other statements in the same book and the
library. On PDF 33, printed p.22, the authors cite Hettinger and Muller (1953) for a
threshold stimulus of "not ... less than one-third of the maximal strength" for the average
person, and add that as strength increases the stimulus "should be increased, and reach
80-95% of the athlete's maximum" (see [[claim--strength-training-threshold-stimulus]]); on
PDF 34, printed p.23, Korobkov, Gerasimov and Vasiliev (via Verkhoshansky 1977) report
"approximately equivalent increases in strength" with loads of 20, 40, 60 and 80% of 1RM in
the initial stages of training, which partly agrees with the p.224 inference for beginners.
The book's own isometric protocol also sets explosive work at "70-80% of one's maximum
strength" (PDF 237, printed p.226). Natera, as relayed in
[[framework--isometric-training-variables-and-adaptations]] (Moyer), reports Oranchuk 2019
as finding that "moderate-to-high intensity gives the best" peak-force gains. Hold length
also differs across the section: 6 s here; "no more than 6 seconds (some authors recommend
10 seconds)" and "no longer than 8 seconds" for non-explosive maximal holds (both PDF 237,
printed p.226).

**Example** — The book's own example is the Hettinger and Muller protocol itself (daily,
6-second, two-thirds-maximum isometric effort for 10 weeks, yielding about 5% weekly
strength gain); no further invented example is added here.

**Related** — [[heuristic--isometric-training-execution-protocol-and-advantages-drawbacks]],
[[claim--isometric-regional-specificity-not-strictly-angular]],
[[claim--strength-training-threshold-stimulus]] (Ch1, the intensity-threshold rule this
entry's duration inference sits against),
[[framework--isometric-training-variables-and-adaptations]] (Moyer, Oranchuk 2019 as
relayed).

# Hettinger and Muller's Original Isometric-Training Finding: About 5% Strength Gain Per Week From One Daily 6-Second Effort at Two-Thirds Maximum

**What it is** — Isometric exercises became popular in the mid-1950s in the search for
economical, effective strength methods. Hettinger and Muller (1953, 1955) established that
one daily effort at two-thirds of maximum, held for six seconds, performed for 10 weeks,
increases strength by about 5% per week. Separately, Clark et al (1954) found that static
strength continues to increase even after a four-week isometric programme has concluded.
This early success prompted considerable research comparing isometric training's
effectiveness against dynamic training, which produced "rather contradictory data" (see
review by Verkhoshansky, 1970). The authors' general conclusion from that body of research:
isometric training can be more effective than dynamic exercise specifically where the target
exercise requires a large-magnitude muscle contraction at a certain stage of a movement, or
during early-stage injury rehabilitation; if the target exercise involves high-speed
movement, sustained isometric training is less effective. The authors also note that
because isometric training's usual purpose is developing absolute strength, tension should
be increased slowly and held for a relatively long time, since prolonged tension maintenance
demands the energy expenditure that stimulates adequate neuromuscular adaptation; some
researchers found no essential difference in strength gain from varying isometric tension
intensity, from which the authors infer that tension duration, not magnitude, is the
"fundamental conditioning factor." (PDF pp. 235, printed pp. 223-224, "4.2.4 Isometric
Training.")

**Why it works** — The authors' stated reasoning: prolonged maintenance of muscular tension
requires an energy expenditure that "stimulates adequate adaptation in the neuromuscular
system, thereby determining its strength potential," and this can exceed the stimulus from
brief transient dynamic tension. Inference: no cellular or neural mechanism is given for why
duration outweighs magnitude specifically; this is an inference the authors draw from
studies not finding a strength-gain difference across tension intensities, not a stated
physiological pathway.

**When to apply** — Use the 5%-per-week figure and the two-thirds-maximum, 6-second, daily,
10-week protocol as a citable historical anchor for isometric-training dosing, and use the
authors' scoping rule (isometrics favoured for large-magnitude contraction at a specific
movement stage or early rehab; less favoured when the target skill is high-speed) to decide
when isometric work is the better tool versus dynamic resistance training.

**When NOT to apply** — This is single-era data (1950s studies, corroborated only by a 1970
review) without modern replication in this text; treat "5% per week" as specific to
Hettinger and Muller's exact protocol (two-thirds max, 6 seconds, daily, 10 weeks), not a
generalizable isometric-training growth rate. The "contradictory data" comparing isometric
to dynamic training is acknowledged by the authors themselves, so this entry's headline
finding should not be read as settling the isometric-versus-dynamic debate; it explains only
the original claim's origin and the authors' scoping conditions for it.

**Example** — The book's own example is the Hettinger and Muller protocol itself (daily,
6-second, two-thirds-maximum isometric effort for 10 weeks, yielding about 5% weekly
strength gain); no further invented example is added here.

**Related** — [[heuristic--isometric-training-execution-protocol-and-advantages-drawbacks]],
[[claim--isometric-regional-specificity-not-strictly-angular]].

# Isometric Endurance Collapses Above 10-15% of Maximal Tension, and Recovers in Three Distinct Phases

**What it is** — Isometric endurance at resistance exceeding 10-15% of a muscle's maximal
strength is very short compared with dynamic exercise, because of metabolic demand and
impaired blood flow to the exercising muscle under sustained contraction (Petrofsky &
Phillips, 1986); below that threshold, contractions are considered non-fatiguing, since
intramuscular pressure stays low and is readily exceeded by rising mean arterial pressure in
the capillaries. Verified against the page image (Fig 4.13, PDF p. 238, printed p. 227, cat
soleus and gastrocnemius, electrically stimulated, based on Petrofsky & Hendershot, 1984):
intramuscular pressure rises roughly linearly with muscle tension, from about 0 kPa at 0%
to about 20 kPa at 100% of maximal strength. As tension rises, intramuscular pressure rises
with it and metabolism cannot keep pace, producing a hyperbolic drop in performance and
marked fatigue increase (the Rohmert curve, first derived by Monod and Sherrer 1967, later
by Rohmert 1968). Verified against the page image (Fig 4.14, PDF p. 238, printed p. 227,
finger flexors, based on Petrofsky 1980): endurance time falls hyperbolically as %MVC
(maximum voluntary contraction) rises, and females sustain the same tension level for
longer than males at every tension level tested, a difference the authors say "has not
been adequately explained yet." Muscle temperature also affects isometric endurance: hot
packs reduce it and pre-exercise icing increases it. The authors write that "Research by
Clarke et al (1958) discovered that there is an optimum core muscle temperature" above and
below which isometric endurance fairly rapidly decreases, "with others later showing that
this optimal temperature lies around 27-28 Celsius (Petrofsky & Phillips, 1986)." Higher
bodyfat percentage, associated with higher resting muscle temperature, is linked to lower
isometric endurance in most situations. Dynamic exercise takes place more efficiently at
higher temperatures, "apparently because of reduced environmental tissue viscosity," but in
isometric contraction muscle fibres do not move, so viscosity plays an "insignificant role
compared with that of muscle metabolism" (Petrofsky & Phillips, 1986). Recovery from
isometric contraction proceeds in three phases (Petrofsky & Phillips, 1986): a rapid
recovery of about 50% of endurance in the first 3 minutes; a slower recovery lasting about
20 minutes, reaching about 90% of initial endurance; and complete recovery within at least
24 hours; recovery from low-tension isometric contraction is slower during the first phases
of recovery. (PDF pp. 238-239, printed pp. 227-228, "Isometric Endurance," "Recovery after
Isometric Activity," Figs 4.13-4.14.)

**Why it works** — The authors' stated mechanism is a mechanical-metabolic one: rising muscle
tension raises intramuscular pressure, and above roughly 10-15% of maximal strength the
contraction impairs the blood flow that metabolism needs, so the metabolism "is unable to
meet the physiological demands of the exercise," producing the hyperbolic Rohmert-curve drop
in endurance (PDF p. 238, printed p. 227). No mechanism is given for the sex difference in
endurance or for the 27-28 Celsius optimum temperature beyond citing the studies that
measured them.

**When to apply** — Use the 10-15%-of-maximal-strength threshold as the authors' dividing
line between "non-fatiguing" and rapidly fatiguing isometric holds when designing isometric
protocols. Inference: use the three-phase timeline (about 50% back in 3 minutes, about 90%
back in 20 minutes, full recovery by 24 hours) as the recovery of isometric endurance after
a fatiguing sustained contraction; the source reports recovery "of endurance" (PDF p. 239,
printed p. 228) and does not test brief maximal efforts.

**When NOT to apply** — The intramuscular-pressure data (Fig 4.13) are from electrically
stimulated cat soleus and gastrocnemius (Petrofsky & Hendershot, 1984), not human voluntary
contraction; treat the specific kPa values as animal-model data illustrating the
tension-pressure relationship, not human norms. The Rohmert-curve endurance data (Fig 4.14)
are specifically finger-flexor endurance (Petrofsky, 1980), a small, distal muscle group;
the shape of the curve (hyperbolic decline, female advantage) should not be assumed to hold
identically for large, proximal muscle groups without separate verification. The 27-28
Celsius optimum-temperature finding and the bodyfat-endurance link are each from single
cited sources without reported effect sizes. The text points to "(Fig 4.14)" for the
temperature optimum (PDF p. 238, printed p. 227), but Fig 4.14 plots endurance against %MVC
and shows no temperature data; do not cite the figure for the temperature claim.

**Example** — Inference: a coach prescribing a sustained isometric hold at low relative
intensity could expect it to be comparatively non-fatiguing per the 10-15%-of-maximum
threshold, while a sustained near-maximal hold held to fatigue would need the multi-minute
recovery windows this entry describes before endurance returns. Whether a given hold is
under 10-15% of maximum is not shown in the source.

**Related** — [[heuristic--isometric-training-execution-protocol-and-advantages-drawbacks]],
[[principle--breath-holding-and-valsalva-support-spinal-stability-in-maximal-lifting]] (Ch3,
a related discussion of intramuscular/intrathoracic pressure during sustained maximal
effort).

# Isometric Endurance Collapses Above 10-15% of Maximal Tension, and Recovers in Three Distinct Phases

**What it is** — Isometric endurance at resistance exceeding 10-15% of a muscle's maximal
strength is very short compared with dynamic exercise, because of metabolic demand and
impaired blood flow to the exercising muscle under sustained contraction (Petrofsky &
Phillips, 1986); below that threshold, contractions are considered non-fatiguing, since
intramuscular pressure stays low and is readily exceeded by rising mean arterial pressure in
the capillaries. Verified against the page image (Fig 4.13, printed p. 227, cat soleus and
gastrocnemius, electrically stimulated, based on Petrofsky & Hendershot, 1984): intramuscular
pressure rises roughly linearly with muscle tension, from near 0 kPa at rest to over 20 kPa
at 100% of maximal strength. As tension rises, intramuscular pressure rises with it and
metabolism cannot keep pace, producing a hyperbolic drop in performance and marked fatigue
increase (the Rohmert curve, first derived by Monod and Sherrer 1967, later by Rohmert
1968). Verified against the page image (Fig 4.14, printed p. 227, finger flexors, based on
Petrofsky 1980): endurance time falls hyperbolically as %MVC (maximum voluntary contraction)
rises, and females sustain the same tension level for longer than males at every tension
level tested, a difference the authors say "has not been adequately explained yet." Muscle
temperature also affects isometric endurance: hot packs reduce it and pre-exercise icing
increases it, with an optimum core muscle temperature (later work places it near 27-28
Celsius, Petrofsky & Phillips, 1986) above and below which endurance drops; higher bodyfat
percentage, associated with higher resting muscle temperature, is linked to lower isometric
endurance in most situations. Unlike dynamic exercise (which is more efficient at higher
temperatures, likely due to reduced tissue viscosity), isometric contraction involves no
fibre movement, so viscosity plays an "insignificant role compared with that of muscle
metabolism." Recovery from isometric contraction proceeds in three phases (Petrofsky &
Phillips, 1986): a rapid recovery of about 50% of endurance in the first 3 minutes; a slower
recovery lasting about 20 minutes, reaching about 90% of initial endurance; and complete
recovery within at least 24 hours; recovery from low-tension isometric contraction is
"interestingly" slower during the initial recovery phases. (PDF pp. 236-239, printed pp.
226-228, "4.2.4 Isometric Training," "Isometric Endurance," "Recovery after Isometric
Activity," Figs 4.13-4.14.)

**Why it works** — The authors' stated mechanism is a mechanical-metabolic one: rising muscle
tension raises intramuscular pressure, which above roughly 10-15% of maximal strength begins
to exceed the arterial pressure available to perfuse the muscle, choking off the blood flow
that metabolism needs to sustain the contraction, producing the hyperbolic Rohmert-curve
drop in endurance. No mechanism is given for the sex difference in endurance or for the
27-28 Celsius optimum temperature beyond citing the studies that measured them.

**When to apply** — Use the 10-15%-of-maximal-strength threshold as a practical dividing line
between "non-fatiguing" and rapidly fatiguing isometric holds when designing isometric
protocols (e.g. low-level postural holds versus near-maximal strength holds). Use the
three-phase recovery timeline (about 50% back in 3 minutes, about 90% back in 20 minutes,
full recovery by 24 hours) when spacing repeated maximal isometric efforts within and between
sessions.

**When NOT to apply** — The intramuscular-pressure data (Fig 4.13) are from electrically
stimulated cat soleus and gastrocnemius (Petrofsky & Hendershot, 1984), not human voluntary
contraction; treat the specific kPa values as animal-model data illustrating the
tension-pressure relationship, not human norms. The Rohmert-curve endurance data (Fig 4.14)
are specifically finger-flexor endurance (Petrofsky, 1980), a small, distal muscle group;
the shape of the curve (hyperbolic decline, female advantage) should not be assumed to hold
identically for large, proximal muscle groups without separate verification. The 27-28
Celsius optimum-temperature finding and the bodyfat-endurance link are each from single
cited sources without reported effect sizes.

**Example** — Inference: a coach prescribing a sustained postural isometric hold (e.g. a
plank or wall-sit at low relative intensity) can expect it to be comparatively non-fatiguing
per the 10-15%-of-maximum threshold, while a near-maximal isometric mid-thigh pull hold will
fatigue rapidly and require the multi-minute recovery windows this entry describes before a
comparable maximal effort can be repeated.

**Related** — [[heuristic--isometric-training-execution-protocol-and-advantages-drawbacks]],
[[principle--breath-holding-and-valsalva-support-spinal-stability-in-maximal-lifting]] (Ch3,
a related discussion of intramuscular/intrathoracic pressure during sustained maximal
effort).

# Isometric Contraction Is Not One Thing: Voluntary vs Reflexive, Slow vs Explosive

**What it is** — The authors argue isometric training is not simply holding a static
contraction for a set time: a true isometric contraction requires the muscle to raise
tension from rest to a maximal or sub-maximal value over a rise ("attack") time, sustain
that tension for a resistance phase, then decrease it to rest or a lower value over a decay
time. Verified against the page image (Fig 4.11, PDF p. 236, printed p. 225): the authors
categorise isometric contraction into voluntary isometrics (splitting further into slow
isometrics and voluntary explosive isometrics) and reflexive isometrics (splitting further
into reflexive explosive isometrics and oscillatory isometrics). A voluntary isometric
contraction can be produced deliberately; a reflexive one occurs involuntarily via the
muscle's reflex response between the eccentric and concentric phases of plyometric
activities such as the depth jump or weightlifting clean-and-jerk. Verified against the page
image (Fig 4.12, PDF p. 236, printed p. 225): the figure contrasts slow isometrics (gradual
rise, long resistance plateau) with explosive isometrics (steep rise, short resistance
phase); the caption says reflexive explosive action has an even steeper rise and a much
shorter resistance phase ("The slope of the rise is even greater and the duration of the
resistance phase is much shorter during reflexive explosive isometric action"). On
oscillatory isometrics, the authors say the technique "may also be useful in producing
powerful contractions over a small range of movement," citing research showing that "the
maximum tension that can be produced voluntarily during sinusoidally pulsed brief isometric
jerks at 5 Hz is the same as the maximum sustained tension" (Soechting & Roberts, 1975);
Basmajian (1978) read this as emphasising fibre recruitment and motor-unit synchronisation
(PDF p. 235, printed p. 224). That is the only evidence the book gives for the oscillatory
box, and it describes voluntarily produced jerks, while Fig 4.11 (PDF p. 236, printed p.
225) files oscillatory isometrics under reflexive isometrics; the book does not reconcile
the two. The authors argue that because the steepness of the isometric force-time curve,
and the higher magnitude of maximum isometric versus dynamic maximum force at equivalent
joint angles, both support developing explosive strength isometrically when the training
accent is on speed of force development, "it is doubtful whether it is always productive to
maintain a rigid distinction between dynamic and isometric exercise": as resistance grows
very large, dynamic work becomes progressively more isometric, so isometric work is "really
the limiting case of dynamic work as the velocity of movement tends to zero." Because the
inhibitory effects usually associated with voluntary muscle action are not encountered in
reflexive isometric contraction, "even greater explosive force can be displayed
isometrically than dynamically." The authors add that "negative evaluations of this method
are premature" (PDF p. 236, printed p. 225). A related but separate finding on impulsive
loading: short bouts of low-frequency mechanical vibration (10-35 Hz) applied to the body
have been shown to speed recovery, modulate muscle activity, raise strength/power stable
state, lower arterial pressure and enhance oxidative processes (Kopysov, 1978; Lebedev &
Peliakov, 1991), and whole-body vibration at 26 Hz through the lower extremities has been
shown to produce marked increases in jumping power (Bosco et al, 1998); the authors note
this fuels an open debate about whether plyometric training effects are driven mainly by
elastic-energy storage/release, neural facilitation, or intrinsic muscle changes (Ingen
Schenau et al, 1997). (PDF pp. 235-236, printed pp. 224-225, "4.2.4 Isometric Training,"
Figs 4.11-4.12.)

**Why it works** — The authors' mechanism for the voluntary/reflexive distinction is neural:
reflexive isometric contraction does not encounter the inhibitory effects usually associated
with voluntary muscle action, permitting higher explosive force display (PDF p. 235, printed
p. 224). Inference: the slow-vs-explosive distinction within each category follows from how
quickly neural drive ramps up to the target tension level, which the force-time curve shape
(Fig 4.12) captures directly.

**When to apply** — Use this taxonomy when specifying what kind of isometric work a given
drill is training: a sustained maximal hold at a joint angle is a slow voluntary isometric;
a deliberately fast ramp to near-maximal tension is a voluntary explosive isometric; the
brief isometric moment between the eccentric and concentric phases of a depth jump or
clean-and-jerk is, per the authors, a reflexive explosive isometric that the athlete does
not consciously initiate. Per the authors, distinguish "isometric training for developing
absolute strength" from "isometric training for developing explosive strength" and select
the appropriate type for the goal.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors say the absolute-strength versus explosive-strength
split within isometric training "still requires detailed experimental corroboration" (PDF p.
236, printed p. 225). The oscillatory category rests on one cited study of voluntary 5 Hz
jerks (Soechting & Roberts, 1975), so its placement under reflexive isometrics is not
supported by the evidence the book gives. The vibration/whole-body-vibration findings are a
separate line of evidence (Bosco et al, 1998, and others) that the authors connect to this
discussion only by analogy (impulsive loading), not by stating vibration produces isometric
contraction in the sense defined here; treat the two topics as related but distinct.

**Example** — The book's own example is the depth jump and the weightlifting clean-and-jerk
cited as sources of reflexive isometric contraction; no further invented example is added
here.

**Related** — [[framework--precise-muscle-action-terminology]] (Ch1, the broader
concentric/eccentric/isometric/quasi-isometric terminology this taxonomy sits within),
[[heuristic--isometric-training-execution-protocol-and-advantages-drawbacks]].

# Isometric Contraction Is Not One Thing: Voluntary vs Reflexive, Slow vs Explosive

**What it is** — The authors argue isometric training is not simply holding a static
contraction for a set time: a true isometric contraction requires the muscle to raise
tension from rest to a maximal or sub-maximal value over a rise ("attack") time, sustain
that tension for a resistance phase, then decrease it to rest or a lower value over a decay
time. Verified against the page image (Fig 4.11, printed p. 225): the authors categorise
isometric contraction into voluntary isometrics (splitting further into slow isometrics and
voluntary explosive isometrics) and reflexive isometrics (splitting further into reflexive
explosive isometrics and oscillatory isometrics). A voluntary isometric contraction can be
produced deliberately; a reflexive one occurs involuntarily via the muscle's reflex response
between the eccentric and concentric phases of plyometric activities such as a depth jump or
the weightlifting clean-and-jerk. Verified against the page image (Fig 4.12, printed p.
225): slow isometrics show a gradual force rise, a longer resistance-phase plateau, and a
gradual decay; explosive (reflexive) isometrics show a much steeper rise phase and a
substantially shorter resistance phase before decay. The authors argue that because the
steepness of the isometric force-time curve, and the higher magnitude of maximum isometric
versus dynamic maximum force at equivalent joint angles, both support developing explosive
strength isometrically when the training accent is on speed of force development, "it is
doubtful whether it is always productive to maintain a rigid distinction between dynamic and
isometric exercise": as resistance grows very large, dynamic work becomes progressively more
isometric, so isometric work is "really the limiting case of dynamic work as the velocity of
movement tends to zero." Because reflexive isometric contraction bypasses the inhibitory
effects normally associated with voluntary muscle action, "even greater explosive force can
be displayed isometrically than dynamically." A related but separate finding on impulsive
loading: short bouts of low-frequency mechanical vibration (10-35 Hz) applied to the body
have been shown to speed recovery, modulate muscle activity, raise strength/power stable
state, lower arterial pressure and enhance oxidative processes (Kopysov, 1978; Lebedev &
Peliakov, 1991), and whole-body vibration at 26 Hz through the lower extremities has been
shown to produce marked increases in jumping power (Bosco et al, 1998); the authors note
this fuels an open debate about whether plyometric training effects are driven mainly by
elastic-energy storage/release, neural facilitation, or intrinsic muscle changes (Ingen
Schenau et al, 1997). (PDF pp. 235-236, printed pp. 224-225, "4.2.4 Isometric Training,"
Figs 4.11-4.12.)

**Why it works** — The authors' mechanism for the voluntary/reflexive distinction is neural:
reflexive isometric contraction (occurring automatically between eccentric and concentric
phases) escapes voluntary inhibitory control that would otherwise limit force, permitting
higher force display than a deliberately initiated voluntary contraction can achieve.
Inference: the slow-vs-explosive distinction within each category follows from how quickly
neural drive ramps up to the target tension level, which the force-time curve shape (Fig
4.12) captures directly.

**When to apply** — Use this taxonomy when specifying what kind of isometric work a given
drill is training: a sustained maximal hold at a joint angle is a slow voluntary isometric;
a deliberately fast ramp to near-maximal tension is a voluntary explosive isometric; the
brief isometric moment at the bottom of a depth jump or clean-and-jerk catch is a reflexive
(explosive or oscillatory) isometric that the athlete does not consciously initiate. Per the
authors, distinguish "isometric training for developing absolute strength" from "isometric
training for developing explosive strength" and select the appropriate type for the goal.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors themselves flag this distinction as still needing
"detailed experimental corroboration." The vibration/whole-body-vibration findings are a
separate line of evidence (Bosco et al, 1998, and others) that the authors connect to this
discussion only by analogy (impulsive loading), not by stating vibration produces isometric
contraction in the sense defined here; treat the two topics as related but distinct.

**Example** — The book's own example is the depth-jump and clean-and-jerk catch positions
cited as sources of reflexive isometric contraction; no further invented example is added
here.

concentric/eccentric/isometric/quasi-isometric terminology this taxonomy sits within),
[[heuristic--isometric-training-execution-protocol-and-advantages-drawbacks]].

# External vs Internal Isometrics, and Using a Held Supramaximal Load to Prime the Nervous System

**What it is** — The authors distinguish "external isometrics" (contraction exerted against
an external load) from "internal isometrics" (contraction exerted against opposing muscles
within the body, as in bodybuilders' posing actions; see
[[heuristic--loadless-training-broomstick-protocol]]). Isometric contractions can be
submaximal or maximal, short or long duration, continuous or intermittent, sequenced across
different joint angles, alternated between agonist and antagonist (or adductor/abductor,
medial/lateral rotators), and alternated between intensities, including voluntary
oscillation between high and low intensity to prolong the period of application. A
separate practical technique: isometrically holding a heavy load at a "sticking point" can
"decrease any deficiencies in that region or prime the nervous system to cope with greater
levels of loading which will eventually be encountered during the process of gradual
progressive overload"; the authors' specific example is "the mere supporting of a
supramaximal load (e.g. 120-150% of one's 1RM) on the shoulders or quasi-isometric movement
over the first few degrees of knee flexion of a squat," which can "accustom the body
neuromuscularly and favourably enhance one's mental perception to undertake future squats
which are going to be only slightly heavier than one's current 1RM." The authors also state
that, "as pointed out earlier," isometric contraction released explosively "can decrease the
reaction response time by as much as 7%, particularly if associated with a strong
pre-stretch," against the traditional coaching belief that movement is most efficient
starting from complete relaxation; "Verkhoshansky stresses" that a movement produced from
complete relaxation is usually slower and less forceful. Historically, isometric effort was
emphasised heavily by DeLorme, Hettinger and Muller, but with the rise of gymnasium machines
and the decline of Charles Atlas's mail-order "dynamic tension" programmes, isometrics
largely fell out of popular use, though physical therapists still use it in early
injury-rehabilitation stages, and Russian coaches often prescribe the 75% concentric / 15%
eccentric / 10% isometric strength-training regime "advocated by their scientists" for the
average athlete. The authors also note that because one basic PNF principle holds that
mobility (dynamic contraction) is more primitive than stability (isometric contraction),
stability sits at a "higher level of muscular learning." (PDF p. 240, printed p. 229,
"Other Aspects of Isometric Activity," "4.2.4 Isometric Training.")

**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism for the 7% reaction-time figure (PDF p.
240, printed p. 229). Inference: it may connect to the earlier argument that reflexive
isometric contraction escapes the inhibition associated with voluntary action (PDF p. 235,
printed p. 224; see [[framework--isometric-contraction-categorization-voluntary-reflexive]]),
but that argument is about force, and the text does not link the two. For supramaximal
holding, no cellular mechanism is given; the stated effect is neuromuscular and perceptual
familiarisation ("accustom the body neuromuscularly," "favourably enhance one's mental
perception") rather than a measured strength-transfer pathway.

**When to apply** — Use the external/internal isometrics distinction as vocabulary when
specifying whether a drill uses an external load or purely internal agonist-antagonist
tensing. Use supramaximal-hold work (120-150% of 1RM support holds, or quasi-isometric
movement over the first few degrees of a squat) as a progressive-overload step that
accustoms the athlete to loads slightly above current 1RM (PDF p. 240, printed p. 229). Use
the 75/15/10 concentric/eccentric/isometric regime as a citable, if dated, historical
reference point when discussing how much isometric work a general strength programme might
include.

**When NOT to apply** — The 7% reaction-time figure and the supramaximal-holding
familiarisation effect are stated without reported sample sizes or controlled outcome data
in this passage; treat them as the authors' summarised claims, not independently verified
percentages. The 75/15/10 regime is attributed generally to Russian coaches and "their
scientists" without a specific citation, so treat it as a reported convention rather than
an experimentally validated ratio. Inference: supramaximal holding (120-150% of 1RM) carries
obvious injury risk without adequate rack and spotter safety, which this passage does not
discuss.

**Example** — The book's own example is the 120-150% 1RM shoulder support and the
quasi-isometric first degrees of a squat, used to prepare for future squats only slightly
heavier than the current 1RM (PDF p. 240, printed p. 229); no further invented example is
added here.

**Related** — [[heuristic--loadless-training-broomstick-protocol]],
[[framework--isometric-contraction-categorization-voluntary-reflexive]],
[[heuristic--isometric-training-execution-protocol-and-advantages-drawbacks]].

# External vs Internal Isometrics, and Using a Held Supramaximal Load to Prime the Nervous System

**What it is** — The authors distinguish "external isometrics" (contraction exerted against
an external load) from "internal isometrics" (contraction exerted against opposing muscles
within the body, as in bodybuilders' posing actions; see
[[heuristic--loadless-training-broomstick-protocol]]). Isometric contractions can be
submaximal or maximal, short or long duration, continuous or intermittent, sequenced across
different joint angles, alternated between agonist and antagonist (or adductor/abductor,
medial/lateral rotators), and alternated between intensities, including voluntary
oscillation between high and low intensity to prolong the period of application. A
separate practical technique: isometrically holding a heavy load at a "sticking point" can
"decrease any deficiencies in that region or prime the nervous system to cope with greater
levels of loading which will eventually be encountered during the process of gradual
progressive overload"; the authors' specific example is "the mere supporting of a
supramaximal load (e.g. 120-150% of one's 1RM) on the shoulders or quasi-isometric movement
over the first few degrees of knee flexion of a squat," which can "accustom the body
neuromuscularly and favourably enhance one's mental perception to undertake future squats
which are going to be only slightly heavier than one's current 1RM." The authors also state
that, "as pointed out earlier," isometric contraction released explosively "can decrease the
reaction response time by as much as 7%, particularly if associated with a strong
pre-stretch," against the traditional coaching belief that movement is most efficient
starting from complete relaxation; "Verkhoshansky stresses" that a movement produced from
complete relaxation is usually slower and less forceful. Historically, isometric effort was
emphasised heavily by DeLorme, Hettinger and Muller, but with the rise of gymnasium machines
and the decline of Charles Atlas's mail-order "dynamic tension" programmes, isometrics
largely fell out of popular use, though physical therapists still use it in early
injury-rehabilitation stages, and Russian coaches often prescribe the 75% concentric / 15%
eccentric / 10% isometric strength-training regime "advocated by their scientists" for the
average athlete. The authors also note that because one basic PNF principle holds that
mobility (dynamic contraction) is more primitive than stability (isometric contraction),
stability sits at a "higher level of muscular learning." (PDF p. 240, printed p. 229,
"Other Aspects of Isometric Activity," "4.2.4 Isometric Training.")

**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism for the 7% reaction-time figure (PDF p.
240, printed p. 229). Inference: it may connect to the earlier argument that reflexive
isometric contraction escapes the inhibition associated with voluntary action (PDF p. 235,
printed p. 224; see [[framework--isometric-contraction-categorization-voluntary-reflexive]]),
but that argument is about force, and the text does not link the two. For supramaximal
holding, no cellular mechanism is given; the stated effect is neuromuscular and perceptual
familiarisation ("accustom the body neuromuscularly," "favourably enhance one's mental
perception") rather than a measured strength-transfer pathway.

**When to apply** — Use the external/internal isometrics distinction as vocabulary when
specifying whether a drill uses an external load or purely internal agonist-antagonist
tensing. Use supramaximal-hold work (120-150% of 1RM support holds, or quasi-isometric
movement over the first few degrees of a squat) as a progressive-overload step that
accustoms the athlete to loads slightly above current 1RM (PDF p. 240, printed p. 229). Use
the 75/15/10 concentric/eccentric/isometric regime as a citable, if dated, historical
reference point when discussing how much isometric work a general strength programme might
include.

**When NOT to apply** — The 7% reaction-time figure and the supramaximal-holding
familiarisation effect are stated without reported sample sizes or controlled outcome data
in this passage; treat them as the authors' summarised claims, not independently verified
percentages. The 75/15/10 regime is attributed generally to Russian coaches and "their
scientists" without a specific citation, so treat it as a reported convention rather than
an experimentally validated ratio. Inference: supramaximal holding (120-150% of 1RM) carries
obvious injury risk without adequate rack and spotter safety, which this passage does not
discuss.

**Example** — The book's own example is the 120-150% 1RM shoulder support and the
quasi-isometric first degrees of a squat, used to prepare for future squats only slightly
heavier than the current 1RM (PDF p. 240, printed p. 229); no further invented example is
added here.

[[framework--isometric-contraction-categorization-voluntary-reflexive]],
[[heuristic--isometric-training-execution-protocol-and-advantages-drawbacks]].

supramaximal load (120-150% of 1RM) on the shoulders, or performing quasi-isometric movement

forceful than one that begins from some prior tension. Historically, isometric effort was
emphasised heavily by DeLorme, Hettinger and Muller, but with the rise of gymnasium machines

largely fell out of popular use, though physical therapists still use it in early

eccentric / 10% isometric strength-training regime for the average athlete. The authors also
note that because one basic PNF principle holds that mobility (dynamic contraction) is more
primitive than stability (isometric contraction), stability sits at a "higher level of
muscular learning." (PDF pp. 239-240, printed pp. 228-229, "4.2.4 Isometric Training,"
"Other Aspects of Isometric Activity.")

**Why it works** — For the reaction-time claim, the mechanism given is that reflexive
isometric contraction bypasses voluntary inhibition (already stated for explosive isometrics
generally, see
[[framework--isometric-contraction-categorization-voluntary-reflexive]]), and a strong
pre-stretch potentiates this further. For supramaximal holding, no cellular mechanism is
given; the stated effect is psychological/neuromuscular familiarisation ("accustom the body
neuromuscularly," "favourably enhance one's mental perception") rather than a measured
strength-transfer pathway.

familiarisation effect are stated without reported sample sizes or controlled outcome data

specific citation, so treat it as a reported convention rather than an experimentally
validated ratio. Supramaximal holding (120-150% of 1RM) carries obvious injury risk if
attempted without adequate rack/spotter safety and should not be treated as a routine
prescription without those safeguards, which this passage does not itself discuss.

# Isometric Training's Six Advantages, Six Drawbacks, and the Authors' Recommended Execution Protocol

**What it is** — The authors list six advantages proponents claim for isometric training:
(1) it requires very simple apparatus; (2) it can locally exercise any muscle group at a
specific joint angle, which dynamic work can only briefly pass through, since movement
inertia usually carries the load past the angle of greatest mechanical effect; (3) it is
time-productive, since each 6-second isometric contraction is "equivalent in its effect" to
many dynamic ballistic contractions in which maximal force lasts no more than 0.1 second,
meaning 10 minutes of targeted isometric tension can replace "a fatiguing hour" of dynamic
weight training; (4) it produces an insignificant increase in muscle mass and bodymass
compared with dynamic strength work, particularly pressing exercises; (5) it costs far less
time and energy than dynamic weight training, letting an athlete preserve a high
speed-strength level during a crucial competition period; (6) it offers more potential than
dynamic exercise for using visual and kinaesthetic cues to hold a given position, an
advantage for studying and correcting technical errors. Six drawbacks are also listed:
isometrics fatigue the nervous system; may harm the cardiovascular system in some
individuals via prolonged breath-holding and elevated blood pressure; disturb coordination;
enhance muscle performance only near the specific trained joint angle; decrease speed of
movement; and diminish soft-tissue elasticity and functional range of dynamic movement.
Proper breathing, adequate rest/relaxation between exercises, and limiting contraction length
to 6 seconds (some authors recommend up to 10) can minimise these harmful after-effects. The
authors give four methods of producing isometric tension: (1) pressing against an immovable
structure or a partner's resistance, with the drawback that strength change can only be
judged subjectively without a dynamometer; (2) holding a raised load for a set period, with a
quasi-isometric variant shifting the load slowly across the range with stops at different
joint angles; (3) pushing a weight from a lower support up to press against an upper stop
(a power rack), giving a brief dynamic phase before the isometric hold and letting the
athlete lift several times between stops; (4) using a dynamometer or other resistance
device to control and display tension magnitude. For non-explosive isometrics, the authors
give a specific protocol: apply force gradually, hold maximal tension no longer than 8
seconds, perform 6 repetitions, rest 5-10 seconds between reps, limit total isometric
training to 10 minutes per session, and finish with relaxation exercises; for developing
explosive strength instead, tension should be generated at maximum speed to 70-80% of
maximum strength, and reflexive explosive isometric action from plyometric movements "can be
extremely effective" for this. (PDF pp. 236-237, printed pp. 225-226, "4.2.4 Isometric
Training.")

**Why it works** — The authors give a specific mechanism only for advantage (2), regarding
joint-angle specificity of loading, and advantage (3), the time-efficiency claim, which rests
on comparing sustained near-maximal isometric tension duration against the brief (about 0.1
second) duration of maximal force during a ballistic dynamic contraction. Inference: the
remaining advantages and drawbacks are stated as observations rather than derived from a
single unifying mechanism.

**When to apply** — Use the 8-second hold, 6-repetition, 5-10-second-rest, 10-minute-session
protocol as the authors' recommended baseline for non-explosive isometric training aimed at
absolute strength, and the 70-80%-max, maximum-speed protocol for explosive-strength-focused
isometric work. Weigh the six advantages against the six drawbacks for a given athlete and
context: the cardiovascular caution (drawback 2) is particularly relevant for athletes with
existing cardiovascular risk factors, and the coordination-disturbance and range-of-movement
drawbacks argue for pairing isometric work with dynamic training rather than using it as a
sole training means.

**When NOT to apply** — This protocol and these advantages/drawbacks are the authors' own
synthesis from an era (1950s-1970s citations) predating modern force-plate or dynamometer-based
isometric dosing research; do not treat the "equivalent to a fatiguing hour of training"
comparison (advantage 3) as a rigorously measured equivalence, since no controlled outcome
comparison is cited for that specific claim. The drawbacks (cardiovascular risk, coordination
disturbance, reduced movement speed, reduced tissue elasticity) argue against using isometric
training as an athlete's sole or dominant training means, per the authors' own framing.

**Example** — Inference: a coach using isometric mid-thigh pulls to reinforce a specific
sticking-point joint angle is applying advantage (2) directly; the same coach should still
program dynamic work elsewhere in the week to offset the coordination and movement-speed
drawbacks this entry lists.

[[claim--hettinger-muller-isometric-strength-gain-rate]],
[[principle--breath-holding-and-valsalva-support-spinal-stability-in-maximal-lifting]] (Ch3,
the cardiovascular/breath-holding caution this entry's drawback 2 overlaps with).

# Loadless Training: Tensing Muscles Maximally Against an Unloaded Broomstick to Train Without Equipment

**What it is** — "Loadless training" (the Russian term; bodybuilders' "posing" training is
the related practice) has an athlete voluntarily tense agonists and antagonists maximally
without an external load, as if overcoming a maximal weight. In the early 1900s Anokhin and
Froshek proposed developing strength through motivated tensing of agonists and antagonists
at every joint, as bodybuilders do when tensing before judges, but the technique was not
studied scientifically until after 1965. Kovalik (1978) ran a doctoral thesis on this
"voluntary loadless muscle tensing," aiming to develop a supplementary training system
imposing less joint stress than weight training, particularly for younger lifters whose
skeletal systems have not matured. His subjects performed Olympic and supplementary lifts
(e.g. snatch pull, front squat) with a broomstick while trying to generate maximum muscle
tension as if overcoming a maximal weight; this produced definite muscle strengthening and
technical-skill improvement, but Kovalik concluded it must be used cautiously in Olympic
weightlifting because it might disrupt optimal extensor-flexor strength ratios. Loadless
training is described as "especially useful if one has no access to training facilities or
if one is recuperating from musculoskeletal injuries"; "combined with pushups and
free-standing squats, loadless training can be used to good effect on trips away from
home." It can be performed isometrically (joint held at a specific angle),
quasi-isometrically (joint moved powerfully through a full range), or dynamically (imitating
a weight-training movement with unloaded muscular tension against a broomstick). Kovalik
recommended 5 sets per exercise; the authors add that "research indicates" 3-10 s rest
between sets, and they give, without a source, the rest of the protocol: during
quasi-isometric loadless training, avoid long periods of intense breath-holding and instead
breathe out slowly in synchrony with the slow tensing of each movement; each movement
should involve strong simultaneous tension in agonists and antagonists, starting from full
extension and ending with stretching beyond full extension and back, over 10-15 seconds;
the holding phase at the end of each movement (e.g. the overhead jerk position) should be
held with maximal tension for 6-8 seconds. Rotating joints in different planes and moving
limbs in diagonal and spiral patterns follows PNF principles and can enhance loadless
training as supplementary strengthening. The authors also describe tensing several muscle
groups while clearly visualising sporting movements: this "active visualisation, as opposed
to the passive, relaxed visualisation recommended by many sports psychologists, can be
useful adjunct to skills training, provided it does not alter the dynamic structure of
normal competitive patterns." (PDF pp. 240-241, printed pp. 229-230, "Loadless Training.")

**Why it works** — The authors' stated support is that "the value of this type of training
is corroborated by research which has revealed that dynamic stretching against resistance
may strengthen muscle and connective tissue" (PDF p. 241, printed p. 230; no citation
given), plus Kovalik's finding of strengthening and technical-skill improvement. Their
stated rationale for its specific value is reduced joint stress compared with weight
training (relevant for immature skeletons or injury recovery) and portability (no equipment
required). Inference: the caution about disrupting extensor-flexor ratios may reflect that
voluntary tensing without an external load, and without the proprioceptive feedback a load
gives, does not reproduce the same relative muscle-group demand as loaded lifting; the book
gives no reason for the caution.

**When to apply** — Use loadless training as a supplementary strengthening tool when
equipment is unavailable (e.g. travel, combined with pushups and free-standing squats) or
while recuperating from musculoskeletal injuries, and for younger or skeletally immature
lifters where reduced joint loading is a priority. Follow the protocol given on PDF p. 241,
printed p. 230 (Kovalik's 5 sets; 3-10 s rest; slow exhalation during quasi-isometric
tensing; 10-15 s per movement; 6-8 s holding phase).

**When NOT to apply** — Kovalik's own caution applies directly: use loadless training
cautiously in competitive Olympic weightlifting programming specifically, since it may
disrupt the optimal extensor-flexor strength ratio the sport requires. This is a single
doctoral thesis (Kovalik, 1978) without reported sample size or a control condition compared
against standard weight training in this passage; treat it as a supplementary method, not a
substitute for loaded resistance training. The authors' own proviso on active visualisation
also applies: it should not alter the dynamic structure of normal competitive patterns.

**Example** — The book's own example is Kovalik's broomstick snatch pull and front squat,
performed with maximal tension as if overcoming a maximal weight; no further invented
example is added here.

**Related** — [[heuristic--isometric-training-execution-protocol-and-advantages-drawbacks]],
[[heuristic--isometric-priming-and-external-internal-classification]].

# Loadless Training: Tensing Muscles Maximally Against an Unloaded Broomstick to Train Without Equipment

**What it is** — "Loadless training" (the Russian term; bodybuilders call the related
practice "posing" training) has an athlete voluntarily tense agonists and antagonists
maximally at every joint without an external load, imitating a loaded lift's demand through
mental effort and tension alone. In the early 1900s Anokhin and Froshek proposed developing
strength through motivated tensing of agonists and antagonists at every joint, similar to
bodybuilders tensing before judges, but the technique was not studied scientifically until
after 1965. Kovalik (1978) ran a doctoral thesis on this "voluntary loadless muscle tensing,"
aiming to develop a supplementary training system imposing less joint stress than weight
training, particularly for younger lifters whose skeletal systems have not matured. His
subjects performed Olympic and supplementary lifts (e.g. snatch pull, front squat) with a
broomstick while trying to generate maximum muscle tension as if overcoming a maximal
weight; this produced definite muscle strengthening and technical-skill improvement, but
Kovalik concluded it must be used cautiously in Olympic weightlifting because it might
disrupt optimal extensor-flexor strength ratios. Loadless training is described as
especially useful without access to training facilities or during recovery from
musculoskeletal injury, and can be performed isometrically (joint held at a specific angle),
quasi-isometrically (joint moved powerfully through a full range), or dynamically
(imitating a weight-training movement with unloaded muscular tension against a broomstick).
Kovalik's recommended protocol: 5 sets per exercise, separated by 3-10 seconds of rest;
during quasi-isometric loadless training, avoid long periods of intense breath-holding and
instead exhale slowly in synchrony with the slow tensing of each movement; each movement
should involve strong simultaneous tension in agonists and antagonists, starting from full
extension and ending with stretching beyond full extension and back, over 10-15 seconds; the
holding phase at the end of each movement (e.g. the overhead jerk position) should be held
with maximal tension for 6-8 seconds; rotating joints in different planes and moving limbs
in diagonal/spiral patterns follows PNF principles and can enhance loadless training's
effectiveness as a supplementary strengthening method. (PDF pp. 240-241, printed pp.
229-230, "4.2.4 Isometric Training," "Loadless Training.")

**Why it works** — No cellular mechanism is given beyond the general isometric/quasi-isometric
tension logic already stated for the chapter; the authors' stated rationale for loadless
training's specific value is reduced joint stress compared with weight training (relevant
for immature skeletons or injury recovery) and portability (no equipment required). The
caution about disrupting extensor-flexor ratios implies that voluntary tensing without an
external load and its accompanying proprioceptive feedback may not reproduce the same
relative muscle-group demand as loaded lifting.

**When to apply** — Use loadless training as a supplementary strengthening tool when
equipment is unavailable (e.g. travel) or during early-stage musculoskeletal injury
recovery, and specifically for younger or skeletally immature lifters where reduced joint
loading is a priority. Follow Kovalik's protocol details (5 sets, 3-10s rest, slow
exhalation during quasi-isometric tensing, 10-15s per movement, 6-8s holding phase) as the
authors' cited baseline.

**When NOT to apply** — Kovalik's own caution applies directly: use loadless training
cautiously in competitive Olympic weightlifting programming specifically, since it may
disrupt the optimal extensor-flexor strength ratio the sport requires. This is a single
doctoral thesis (Kovalik, 1978) without reported sample size or a control condition compared
against standard weight training in this passage; treat it as a supplementary method, not a
substitute for loaded resistance training.

**Example** — The book's own example is Kovalik's protocol described above (broomstick
snatch pull and front squat, maximal tension, 5 sets); no further invented example is added
here.

[[heuristic--isometric-priming-and-external-internal-classification]].

# Eccentric Training Damages Tissue and Causes Soreness at First, but Adaptation Removes Both Within 2-3 Weeks While Eccentric Work Capacity Rises

**What it is** — Because the muscle complex lengthens under eccentric contraction, its series
elastic component (SEC) is exposed to greater strain than under concentric conditions,
raising injury potential; most muscle strains and ruptures occur during the eccentric phase
of movement (Garrett, 1986). A single session of intense eccentric exercise commonly causes
pronounced delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS), peaking 24-72 hours after exercise and
resolving within several days (Friden et al, 1983a), accompanied by reduced dynamic strength
and damage to myofibrils and connective-tissue elements such as the Z bands (a SEC
component). Friden et al (1983b) also examined longer eccentric-training exposure (3
sessions weekly over 8 weeks total) and found post-exercise soreness stopped occurring after
2-3 weeks, while the ability to perform eccentric work increased by 375%; biopsies showed no
Z-band damage at that point, suggesting adaptation had occurred (the repeated-bout effect).
Schwane and Armstrong (1983) corroborated this with downhill running in rats, which produced
a superior training effect to level or uphill running and prevented injury more effectively.
The authors state that "eccentric exercise tends to produce greater and more rapid increases
in muscle strength and hypertrophy than concentric exercise (Hortobagyi et al, 2000)". The
book states this on p.231 after calling the comparative training findings "often
contradictory" on p.230 (PDF p. 241); see
[[claim--eccentric-vs-concentric-training-adaptation-contradictory-findings]]. It is sometimes
suggested this stems from eccentric exercise's greater tissue damage; however, Komulainen et
al (2000) found the increase in myofibrillar cross-sectional area in unchanged (non-damaged)
muscle fibres was much the same after concentric exercise as after the more damaging
eccentric exercise, a result the authors say "do not support the hypothesis that fibre
hypertrophy depends on the extent of the fibre damage in exercised muscles." (PDF p. 242,
printed p. 231, "4.2.5 Eccentric Training.")

**Why it works** — The authors give a partial mechanism for the velocity-dependent
concentric-eccentric force gap (already established in Ch3's force-velocity treatment, see
[[claim--eccentric-strength-and-energetics-vs-concentric]] and
[[framework--force-time-curve-adaptation-pattern-by-movement-type]]), but give no mechanism
reconciling why different training studies (Johnson 1976 vs Komi & Buskirk 1972 vs Friden
1983b) reach different conclusions about which training mode transfers best; the authors'
own explanation is methodological (training velocity, measurement velocity, particular
muscle groups, and the specificity principle; PDF p. 241, printed p. 230), not
physiological.

**When to apply** — Inference: when deciding between eccentric-emphasis and concentric-emphasis
training for a given goal, treat "eccentric training is superior" as a contested claim
depending heavily on which outcome is measured (eccentric strength specifically tends to
respond best to eccentric training across these studies; broader transfer to concentric or
functional strength is less consistent). The high-velocity eccentric/tendon-adaptation
hypothesis is the authors' stated "training and rehabilitation implication" for
progressive high-velocity eccentric work (PDF p. 241, printed p. 230); applying it to a
specific tendinopathy (e.g. patellar or Achilles) is an extension the book does not make.

**When NOT to apply** — Contested because the book calls the findings "often contradictory"
(PDF p. 241, printed p. 230) and then states eccentric superiority as known (PDF p. 242,
printed p. 231). Handford et al 2024
([[research-papers/handford-2024-a-conceptual-framework-of-different-eccentric-training-methods]])
states its eccentric taxonomy is not evidence that any one method is superior (its p. 9).
This entry summarises training-adaptation studies from a narrow era (1972-1992) with sample
sizes not given in the text and differing protocols (isokinetic dynamometer
training in Komi & Buskirk; training-to-failure in Friden; a seated aerobic-resistive system
in Ericson) that are not directly comparable to one another. Do not treat "eccentric training
increases concentric, eccentric and isometric strength" (Komi & Buskirk's specific finding)
as a settled general principle; Johnson et al (1976) found no such advantage under a
different protocol. The tendon-adaptation hypothesis for high-velocity eccentric work is
explicitly framed as a possible explanation ("may be due to"), not a confirmed mechanism.

**Example** — Inference: a rehabilitation programme using slow, controlled eccentric squats
for general lower-body strength is applying a different training stimulus than one using
fast, high-velocity eccentric work (over 180 degrees/second) aimed at tendon/musculotendinous
junction adaptation; per this entry, the evidence for broad strength transfer is
stronger in some cited studies than others, while the tendon-specific rationale applies
mainly to the high-velocity case.

---
type: library-entry
kind: heuristic
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
chapter: "4.2.6.1"
topic: quadriceps-hamstring ratio myths
category: [isokinetics, testing, rehabilitation]
confidence: supported
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-27
---

# There Is No Single "Optimal" Quadriceps:Hamstring Ratio: It Changes With Sport, Joint Angle and Test Velocity

**What it is** — It is often claimed the optimal quadriceps-to-hamstring strength ratio is
60:40, but Russian scientists found this ratio depends on the specific sport (Vorobyev,
1978): they "determined that this ratio (measured when knee extension torque is greatest)
should be nearer 80:20 for weightlifters and jumpers," while a treadmill-movement
measurement gives runners a ratio of approximately 50:50. A related popular belief, that
injuries are far more common once left/right lower-extremity strength differs by more than
10%, is also questioned. The authors cite "recent research" finding that neither
recommendation is supported by scientifically controlled experiments that correct torque
outputs for the effect of gravity and avoid stretching the hamstrings (Stephens & Reid,
1988). The flexor/extensor-ratio recommendation is additionally vague because the ratio
varies across the joint's range of motion. Verified against the page image (Fig 4.16, PDF p.
245, printed p. 234): the figure plots the ratio of isokinetic knee-extensor to knee-flexor
torque (y-axis 0.5 to 3.5) against joint angle at 36, 108 and 180 degrees/second, from
Cybex dynamometer data; the caption gives no source and no population, and states that
"joint angle varies between partial knee flexion in the seated position to full extension
at 90 degrees." The text reads the figure: the ratio at the knee at 80 degrees (in Fig 4.16's
convention, where 90 degrees is full extension, so near full extension) is about 75:25 at 36
degrees/second (a ratio near 3.0 on the figure) but 68:32 at 180 degrees/second (near 2.1);
the ratio equals the traditional 60:40 figure (1.5) only at approximately 50 degrees. Since
the ratio changes with both joint angle and measurement velocity, the authors conclude "it
is meaningless to prescribe an optimal ratio for any joint," and it would be more relevant
to refer to a characteristic curve over a full range of movement for a given angular
velocity. The page is internally inconsistent: it reports Vorobyev's sport-specific targets
(80:20, 50:50) as what the ratio "should be," then calls any optimal ratio "meaningless"
(both PDF p. 244, printed p. 233). (PDF pp. 244-245, printed pp. 233-234, "Recommended
Strength Ratios," Fig 4.16.)

**Why it works** — The authors give no physiological mechanism for why the ratio shifts with
sport, joint angle or velocity. Their argument is empirical: the figure shows the ratio
changing across angle and velocity, so a single number cannot describe it. Inference: a
single-number ratio averages over torque variation that differs between the extensors and
flexors across the range and across contraction speed.

**When to apply** — Use this as a caution against citing a single flexor/extensor or
left/right strength-ratio target (e.g. "60:40 quad:hamstring," "no more than 10% L/R
difference") as universally optimal or diagnostic of injury risk. If a ratio must be used,
specify the joint angle, the angle convention and the angular velocity it was measured at,
and prefer a full-range characteristic curve over a single number when data allow, per the
authors.

Eric's baseline: NordBord hamstring testing is "explicitly retained for smaller, targeted
return-to-play groups paired with joint-specific isometric testing (ForceFrame-style)"
(`method-baseline.md`, Rehab and return to play); the corpus sets no flexor/extensor ratio
target.

Inference: this section bears on how such ratio data are read for return-to-play decisions.

**When NOT to apply** — Fig 4.16 is uncited Cybex data at 36, 108 and 180 degrees/second on
an unspecified population; Vorobyev (1978) supplies the sport-specific ratios and Stephens &
Reid (1988) the gravity-correction critique. The specific ratio-versus-angle values should
not be treated as universal constants for every athlete or joint, and they use a convention
(90 degrees = full extension) opposite to the common 0 degrees = extension convention. Do
not use this entry to conclude ratio testing is worthless; the claim is that a single
"optimal ratio" number is misleading, not that ratio measurement itself carries no
information (see [[claim--natural-asymmetry-caution-against-isokinetic-symmetry-correction]]
for the related but distinct caution about using isokinetic ratios to drive "correction").
Note that the Vorobyev targets were measured at a named point (greatest knee-extension
torque), which partly meets the authors' angle objection but not their velocity objection.

**Example** — Inference: a rehabilitation report citing "this athlete's quad:hamstring ratio
is below the healthy 60:40 standard" should specify the joint angle and test velocity the
ratio was measured at, since per Fig 4.16 the same limb could show a ratio above 60:40 at
one angle/velocity and at or below it at another.

**Related** — [[claim--natural-asymmetry-caution-against-isokinetic-symmetry-correction]]
(Ch3.3.4.4, a related caution against using isokinetic ratios to "correct" asymmetry),
[[heuristic--isokinetic-testing-limitations-for-functional-sport-specificity]],
[[claim--pursuing-perfect-bilateral-symmetry-can-be-counterproductive]].
